statement:
In people aged 12 and older, mostly young to middle-aged adults in New Zealand, the United States and Ontario, many of whom also smoked tobacco, smoking cannabis (self-reported; mostly light or infrequent in CARDIA, the long US cohort, and in the Ontario cohort) compared with not smoking cannabis is associated with more cough, phlegm, wheeze and bronchitis episodes. In CARDIA, lung function was not lower at light cumulative exposure, and in the Ontario cohort respiratory emergency visits and admissions over 12 months were not more frequent; what heavy smoking over many years does to lung function is not known. The evidence is a 2018 systematic review of 22 studies, CARDIA (5,115 adults followed 20 years), the Ontario record-linkage cohort (12 months of follow-up) and the 2017 National Academies committee's review (a narrative review, read here for its conclusions and the studies under them). The systematic review and the committee draw on some of the same cohorts (CARDIA, Dunedin, Los Angeles), so they are not independent confirmations of each other; a 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route of use (42 sources, 15 of them empirical studies; nothing pooled, no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies reported, and its search string excluded the term tobacco) adds no independent cohort, since its lung studies are CARDIA, Dunedin, Los Angeles, NHANES and Vancouver, and is used here only for its comparisons of routes and the figures it relays.

Symptoms. In the review's pooled comparisons of people who smoked cannabis with people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco, 4 cross-sectional studies gave risk ratios of 4.37 (95% CI 1.71–11.19) for cough, 3.40 (1.99–5.79) for phlegm and 2.83 (1.89–4.23) for wheeze, and 2 prospective cohorts (Dunedin, followed 15 years on average, and Los Angeles, 9.8 years with 49% lost to follow-up) gave 2.04 (1.02–4.06) for cough and 3.84 (1.62–9.07) for phlegm; these two pooled estimates were not significant after the review's small-sample adjustment (P = 0.10 and 0.20), although its abstract reports the intervals as showing an increased risk. The Los Angeles cohort found more bronchitis episodes (odds ratio 2.3, 1.2–4.4), and both cohorts found fewer symptoms after people stopped. In a convenience sample of 339 people in Wellington (the committee's account), cough was reported by 29% of people who smoked cannabis against 5% of people who did not, wheeze by 27% against 11% and chronic bronchitis symptoms by 19% against 3%. The committee graded the evidence for an association between long-term cannabis smoking and worse symptoms and more bronchitis episodes 'substantial', and for improvement after stopping 'moderate' (its wording; mostly cross-sectional studies and two cohorts, with self-reported use, incomplete control for tobacco and, in one cohort, high loss to follow-up). The review rated its own evidence for cough, phlegm and wheeze 'low'. In NHANES (US adults, 2007 to 2010, cross-sectional; the 2024 review's account, percentages not adjusted), cough, cold, phlegm or a respiratory illness in the past week was reported by 16.9% of people who had not smoked cannabis in the past 30 days against 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% of those who smoked it on 1 to 5, 6 to 20 and more than 20 days, and wheeze in the past year by 12.4% against 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5%.

Lung function. In CARDIA (5,115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start; spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20; 69% still taking part at year 20; use mostly light, a median of 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days among people who smoked cannabis), with tobacco counted in the same model, people currently smoking cannabis only did not differ from people smoking neither (FEV1 +0.7 mL, 95% CI −12 to 13), and more lifetime exposure up to about 7 joint-years (one joint-year is 365 joints) went with slightly higher, not lower, FEV1 (net +53 mL, 28 to 79) and FVC (+64 mL, 36 to 92) than none. Beyond that the estimates were imprecise and flattened or turned negative (FEV1 +27 mL, −10 to 64, at 20 joint-years; −39 mL, −141 to 64, at 50), from few people with heavy cannabis exposure and no tobacco (40 with more than 20 joint-years). Other cohorts were not uniform: Dunedin (10 years) found no change in FEV1 and Los Angeles (8 years) no significant fall, while Tucson (4 to 5 cannabis cigarettes a week) found lower FEV1 after 1 year. The review rated the evidence on FEV1, FVC and the FEV1/FVC ratio 'insufficient'. The committee rated the evidence of higher FVC 'moderate' and wrote that it is unclear whether cannabis smoking is associated with worse lung function; it also graded the evidence on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in people who smoke cannabis occasionally when tobacco was controlled for 'limited', on admissions for COPD 'insufficient' and on asthma 'no or insufficient'.

Hospital use. In an Ontario record-linkage cohort (4,807 people aged 12 to 65 who had used cannabis in the past year, 42.5% of them less than monthly, matched to 10,395 who had not; 73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoking tobacco; 12 months of follow-up, data before October 2018), respiratory emergency visits or admissions were 3.6% against 3.9% (odds ratio 0.91, 0.77–1.09), while emergency visits or admissions for any reason were 30.0% against 26.0% (1.22, 1.13–1.31). The respiratory odds ratio was 0.80 (0.65–0.99) among people who currently or formerly smoked tobacco and 1.23 (0.89–1.70) among people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record, uncorrected subgroup tests. Exposure was one question about any use in the past year; route, amount and strength were not collected.

Tobacco and the comparison. Tobacco was common in these groups (73.9% in the Ontario groups; a 2018 commentary cites about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoking tobacco and notes that cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes). Many symptom studies did not control for it (the committee), and NHANES and SPIROMICS reported FEV1 only for cannabis and tobacco smoking together, so a difference from people who smoke neither can partly reflect tobacco; the commentary adds that statistically controlling for tobacco may remove variance that belongs to cannabis use. Where tobacco was counted in the same model (CARDIA), tobacco alone showed the expected dose-related loss (FEV1 63 mL lower, −89 to −36, at more than 20 cigarettes a day) and no significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis was found for FEV1 or FVC; the committee notes no clear additive effect of smoking both on symptoms (one cross-sectional study). Whether tobacco was mixed into joints was not recorded in CARDIA or the Ontario data. In a Vancouver sample of 878 adults aged 40 or more (the 2024 review's account; the comparison group is not named there), people who had smoked at least 50 joints and no tobacco were not at significantly greater risk of COPD or breathing symptoms, while people who had smoked both had higher odds of COPD (2.90, 1.53–5.51) and of symptoms (2.39, 1.58–3.62).

Against tobacco. The committee's chapter summary says the respiratory risks of cannabis smoking appear relatively small and far lower than those of tobacco smoking, a judgment that is not one of its numbered conclusions. Its chapter also reports pieces that point the other way: in 15 volunteers one joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide and three to five times the tar deposition of one cigarette, and in the Wellington sample the authors estimated that each joint's association with a lower FEV1/FVC ratio was similar to that of 2.5 to 5 cigarettes (an analysis the committee criticises); it adds that people who smoke cannabis usually smoke fewer per day. No study in the parts read compared the two at matched exposure.

Not measured and limits. Cannabis use was self-reported; route and method of smoking (joint, pipe, bong), amount, product strength and tobacco mixed into joints were not recorded in CARDIA or the Ontario data, and the committee notes that a joint's strength varies widely between joints and between years. Cohorts were young, and the review's authors note that obstructive lung disease in people who smoke tobacco is usually identified after age 35 to 40. None of these studies can show cause. Comparisons with other ways of taking cannabis are few, small and second-hand. The vaporizer study without a control group enrolled 22 people who used cannabis often and had breathing symptoms; after a month, the 12 who had not developed a respiratory illness reported fewer symptoms and had a higher FVC, while FEV1 did not change significantly (the 2024 review's account; the committee described a 12-person study in which symptoms resolved). In a laboratory crossover (11 people who smoked cannabis often and 9 occasionally), smoked cannabis raised exhaled carbon monoxide more than vaporised cannabis, and breathing rate did not change with either; in another laboratory study blunts gave more carbon monoxide than joints; and Canadian medical cannabis patients (a survey of 364) rated vaporizing and eating as less harmful to breathing than smoking. The committee lists whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms as unknown, and the 2024 review calls its conclusions by route tentative. Funding as printed: the review, no project funding (two authors with federal support); the CARDIA analysis, the US National Institute on Drug Abuse (CARDIA's data collection is funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute); the Ontario study, a grant competition run by The Lung Association – Ontario with unrestricted funding from Tetra-Bio Pharma, a company developing cannabinoid drugs (the paper says the funders had no role); the committee's report, US federal agencies and health foundations, with no cannabis or tobacco industry sponsor listed; the 2024 review by route, no funding and no conflicts declared. The Ontario result (no extra respiratory visits) is paired with independent work: the 20-year CARDIA cohort found no sign of harm to lung function at light exposure, while the independent review found more symptoms. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed (the symptom finding alone would be replicated; the lung-function findings are mixed).
plain: In studies that compared people who smoke cannabis with people who do not, people who smoked cannabis more often had cough, phlegm and wheezing, and in two long-running studies these eased in people who stopped. Many of the people who smoked cannabis also smoked tobacco, so the studies cannot say how much of this comes from cannabis. In the longest study (5,115 adults followed for 20 years; those who smoked cannabis mostly did so lightly), lung function was not lower in people who smoked cannabis lightly, while tobacco smoking lowered it; too few people had smoked cannabis heavily for many years to know what that does. An Ontario study that followed about 15,000 people for a year found no difference in emergency visits or hospital stays for breathing problems between people who had used cannabis and people who had not, although it counted any use and most people used it infrequently. None of this shows what smoking cannabis itself does. Comparisons with other ways of taking cannabis are few and small: in a study with no comparison group, breathing symptoms eased after a month of using a vaporizer instead of smoking, among the people who did not catch a chest illness during that month; in a laboratory study, smoking put more carbon monoxide into the breath than vaporizing; and medical cannabis patients rated vaporizing and eating as easier on their breathing than smoking.
population: People aged 12 and older, mostly young to middle-aged adults, in New Zealand, the United States and Ontario (Canada); cannabis smoking self-reported, mostly light or infrequent in the long US cohort and the Ontario cohort and moderate to heavy in the pooled cross-sectional symptom studies and the Los Angeles cohort; many also smoked tobacco
exposure: Smoking cannabis, self-reported (joints, pipes or bongs; method, amount, strength and any tobacco mixed in mostly not recorded)
comparator: People who do not smoke cannabis: in the pooled symptom comparisons, people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco; in the 20-year US cohort, people with no cannabis exposure, with tobacco counted separately in the same model; in the Ontario cohort, matched people who had not used cannabis in the past year (73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoking tobacco). For tobacco: people who smoked tobacco only (CARDIA)
outcome: Cough, phlegm, wheeze and bronchitis episodes; lung function (FEV1 and FVC) over time; emergency visits and admissions for respiratory reasons
magnitude: Symptoms, people who smoked cannabis against people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco (2018 review; risk ratio, 95% CI; risk difference): 4 cross-sectional studies pooled: cough 4.37 (1.71–11.19; 0.18, 0.15–0.21), phlegm 3.40 (1.99–5.79; 0.14, 0.10–0.17), wheeze 2.83 (1.89–4.23; 0.22, 0.14–0.29), dyspnea 1.56 (1.33–1.83; 0.06, −0.01 to 0.13); the risk differences are weighted differently from the ratios and mostly reflect one or two large studies. 2 prospective cohorts pooled (Dunedin, Los Angeles): cough 2.04 (1.02–4.06; 0.07, 0.02–0.13) and phlegm 3.84 (1.62–9.07; 0.12, −0.02 to 0.25), not significant after the small-sample adjustment (P = 0.10, 0.20). Los Angeles cohort: bronchitis episodes OR 2.3 (1.2–4.4). Wellington sample of 339 (committee's account): cough 29% against 5%, wheeze 27% against 11%, chronic bronchitis symptoms 19% against 3%. Committee's grades (its wording): 'substantial' for the association of long-term smoking with worse symptoms and more bronchitis episodes; 'moderate' for improvement after stopping. Lung function (CARDIA, tobacco in the same model; net difference against no exposure): lifetime cannabis exposure FEV1 +53 mL (28 to 79) and FVC +64 mL (36 to 92) at 7 joint-years; FEV1 +27 mL (−10 to 64) at 20 and −39 mL (−141 to 64) at 50; currently smoking cannabis only against neither FEV1 +0.7 mL (−12 to 13), FVC +8.2 mL (−5 to 22); tobacco only FEV1 −24 mL (−38 to −11). Ontario, matched, 12 months: respiratory emergency visit or admission 3.6% against 3.9%, OR 0.91 (0.77–1.09); any reason 30.0% against 26.0%, OR 1.22 (1.13–1.31). 2024 review by route (second-hand): NHANES, cough, cold, phlegm or respiratory illness in the past 7 days 16.9% (no cannabis smoking in the past 30 days) against 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% (1 to 5, 6 to 20, more than 20 days), wheeze in the past year 12.4% against 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5% (unadjusted); Vancouver, both cannabis and tobacco, COPD OR 2.90 (1.53–5.51) and symptoms OR 2.39 (1.58–3.62), cannabis without tobacco not significantly raised; laboratory crossover, more exhaled carbon monoxide after smoking than after vaporising (0.25 to 6 hours), no route effect on breathing rate.

evidence.locator: Methods › Study Selection; Results › Literature Search; Results › Study Characteristics
evidence.extracted: Registered review (PROSPERO CRD42017059224): 22 studies (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional) out of 73 candidate articles; 3 rated high risk of bias. Five databases, 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018, English only; people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use (no restriction by route is stated). 13 distinct outcomes, 5 poolable. The review frames its exposure as marijuana use, says smoking remains the main method of consumption and words its conclusion for smoking marijuana, but does not say every study was of smoking; use was quantified in joints and joint-years among other ways (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years).

evidence.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
evidence.extracted: Prospective cohorts, 2 studies pooled (Dunedin cohort, n = 1037, mean follow-up 15 years, use about once a week for a year on average; Los Angeles cohort, 299 people, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years, 49% lost to follow-up), people who used cannabis against nonusers (the Methods define nonusers as people using neither cannabis nor tobacco; the Results call them nonsmokers): cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), RD 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); heterogeneity low. After the Knapp-Hartung adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20). Both studies found that stopping cannabis was followed by a significant fall in respiratory symptoms. The abstract and Results report the pooled intervals (which exclude 1) as showing an increased risk; the Figure 2 legend gives the Knapp-Hartung P values.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Results › Study Characteristics
evidence.extracted: The authors say the lung-function evidence is limited by low exposure and young cohorts: tobacco's effect on FEV1 becomes measurable only after about 5 to 10 pack-years; obstructive lung disease develops in about a third of people who smoke tobacco long term and is usually identified after age 35 to 40; large cohorts of middle-aged to older people with heavier cannabis exposure may be needed. They add, as a conjecture, that few people may use enough cannabis to change lung function, so lung function may not be among its most important long-term health outcomes. Across all prospective lung-function evaluations only 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years; the authors also count 756 people who smoked cannabis only with more than 20 joint-years across all outcomes and studies (a different scope).

evidence.locator: Comment, 1st paragraph; Comment, 6th to 8th paragraphs; final paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors conclude that up to about 7 joint-years of lifetime exposure (for example 1 joint a day for 7 years or 1 joint a week for 49 years) gave no evidence that more exposure harms lung function, that at higher exposure the pattern levelled off or reversed especially for FEV1, and that the sample contained too few people with heavy use to confirm a harmful effect of very heavy use. They propose a stretch or training effect (one version called a speculative possibility) and a short-lived airway widening, which they consider unlikely to explain the higher volumes. Limitations named by the authors: no plethysmography, diffusing capacity or imaging of emphysema; only a minority with very high cannabis exposure, fewer still without tobacco, so estimates at high exposure are imprecise; self-reported exposure with recall error and no record of smoking method; unmeasured confounding possible. The final paragraph says the findings suggest an accelerated decline with heavy use, but the net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years and the spline slope (−2.2 mL per joint-year, P = 0.079) were not significant; only the slope for current use at 20 episodes a month was (−3.2 mL per episode a month, P = 0.017).

evidence.extracted: The authors accept that the null respiratory result may be real but give reasons it may understate an effect (not adjustable): too little cannabis smoke exposure among people in the study (citing research that lung-function decline occurs only above 20 'joints per year'), some non-inhaled use, secondhand cannabis smoke in controls, and low power. They also say the large share of people in the cannabis group who used it infrequently may have contributed to the null result, that causation should not be inferred, and that unmeasured confounding might explain the positive findings. Limitations stated: self-report (recall and social-desirability bias); no dose-response (frequency categories too small); no quantity or potency data; about 25% of the cannabis group unmatched; data only before October 2018; no secondhand-smoke adjustment; too few people under 20 and aged 50 to 65 for age-group analyses; a single province. The Discussion's threshold of 20 joints per year for lung-function decline cites two papers (Tan 2019 and Pletcher 2012); it reads as a rate, whereas the CARDIA paper's measure is cumulative joint-years, and that paper did not establish a threshold at 20 joint-years (net FEV1 difference +27 mL, -10 to 64); the Tan paper was not read.

evidence.locator: Results › Literature reviews, 2nd paragraph; Table 3 (Russell 2017 row); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Respiratory effects, 2nd paragraph; Table 4 (Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016, Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning One study in this review

Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. The scoping review of Russell 2017 is reported as finding that vaping reduced respiratory symptoms. The text's list of vaping studies also names Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023, which Table 4 gives as edible studies in children. No included study examined THC oil cartridges, followed people who vape for longer than a month, or compared them with people who do not use cannabis; the authors call for research on long-term outcomes of vaping and on vaping-associated lung injury with THC-containing e-liquids. evidence.locator: Abstract (Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraphs beginning Nevertheless, Evidence on the cardiovascular (its First point), Second, Third and In addition; Strength and limitations; Conclusion; Disclosure statement; Funding
evidence.extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled and no appraisal is reported (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).

risk_of_bias.note: Symptoms: pooled studies of mostly moderate risk of bias (cross-sectional pools 1 low and 3 moderate; two prospective cohorts, one with 49% lost to follow-up); ratios extracted or calculated from counts, so some are probably crude; symptoms and use both self-reported; whether the cannabis groups included people who also smoked tobacco is not described. The review is AMSTAR 2 critically low (provisional), the Ontario cohort ROBINS-E high (one question on any past-year use; matching changed the cannabis group), CARDIA some concerns (physical activity and other co-exposures not measured).

inconsistency.note: Lung function only: CARDIA, Dunedin and Los Angeles found no fall in FEV1 while Tucson found lower FEV1 after 1 year, NHANES a lower FEV1/FVC ratio (partly the higher FVC) and four studies higher airway resistance; the review's authors attribute the heterogeneity to uneven exposure and definitions, which is not a resolution. The symptom findings point the same way in every study.

indirectness.note: The symptom findings are read through two reviews (the Dunedin, Tucson and Los Angeles cohorts and the cross-sectional studies were not read here); the longest cohort is young with light exposure, so it does not speak to heavy long-term smoking; hospital use is a proxy for lung disease.

imprecision.note: Not counted: the symptom intervals exclude 1 in the cross-sectional pools; the Ontario respiratory interval (0.77–1.09) is narrow; imprecision at heavy exposure is stated in the claim as not known.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review (two-study prospective pools); not counted.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the relative risks of 2 to 4 are not counted as a large effect because tobacco co-use and self-report bias run away from the null.

grade.reasoning: Observational (cohorts, cross-sectional surveys and reviews of them), so the claim starts low. Rated as worded: an association, not a cause, and the rating is that of the whole claim, set by its weakest parts. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 (lung function) and indirectness −1 (the symptom evidence is second-hand through two reviews, METHODS §6.3) take the rating below the floor, so the certainty is very low; any two of the three would give the same. The biases that remain could plausibly change the symptom estimates materially (tobacco co-use and reporting bias both run away from the null), so no upgrade for a large effect. The review's own rating for cough, phlegm and wheeze is low and the committee's is substantial; those are their judgments, not this rating. Read alone, the symptom finding is the best supported part (the same direction in every study, a fall in symptoms after stopping in two cohorts) and would be replicated; the lung-function findings are mixed and the Ontario finding rests on one study of high risk of bias, so the status is mixed. The review, the committee's report and CARDIA overlap (CARDIA, Dunedin and Los Angeles are in both), so they are not counted as independent confirmations of each other. The 2024 review by route (AMSTAR 2 critically low) shares these cohorts, adds no pooled estimate and does not change the rating.

statement: Children: calls to the 55 US poison centres about children younger than 6 who ate cannabis edibles rose every year, from 207 in 2017 to 590, 983, 2,209 and 3,054 in 2021 (7,043 in all), and from 0.2 to 3.6 in every 1,000 calls about children of that age, while those calls overall fell (956,871 in 2017, 846,296 in 2021). The children's median age was 3 years (2-year-olds were the largest group, 27.7%; under 1 year, 1.9%), about half were girls, and 90.7% had eaten the product in their own home (97.1% in a home, their own or another). In the poison centres' grading, 2.2% of all 7,043 had a major effect and 21.9% a moderate one (together 35.1% of the 4,827 followed to a known outcome, editors' arithmetic); 22.7% were admitted to hospital (8.1% to critical care), 35 children were intubated, and no deaths were reported. Among those followed up, reduced alertness (CNS depression) was recorded in 70.0%, a fast heart rate in 11.4%, vomiting in 9.5%, slowed breathing in 3.1% and seizures in 1.6%. These are reported calls only, which the authors call an underestimate, and 30.4% were not followed to a known outcome. The authors could not count cases by state; they write that the rise is believed to be associated with more states allowing adult recreational use, that quarantines and school or daycare closures during the pandemic may have played a part, and that it is unknown whether more reporting or less stigma contributed; their data cannot separate these. The shares graded moderate (15.9% against 23.8%) or major (1.6% against 2.4%), and the shares admitted, were higher in 2020 to 2021 than in 2017 to 2019; for the change in where children were treated the authors write that it is unknown why it occurred, suggesting among other things more THC per package or more products bought, more severe effects, or clinicians' comfort and bed availability, and a comparison of later with earlier years of a rising series cannot single out the pandemic. Which products were eaten, how much THC they held and where they came from were not reported. The overview's earlier, second-hand child figures (2005 to 2015) pointed the same way. Funding as printed: the poison-centre study, no external funding and no conflicts declared.
plain: Calls to US poison centres about children under 6 who ate cannabis edibles rose every year, from about 200 in 2017 to about 3,000 in 2021. Most of the children were 1 to 4 years old and ate the edible at home; more than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital, 35 needed a breathing tube, and no deaths were reported. These are only the calls that were made, and the study could not tell how much of the rise came from changes in the law, the pandemic or more people calling.
population: 7,043 calls to US poison centres, 2017 to 2021, about children younger than 6 who ate cannabis edibles (reported calls, not all children exposed; median age 3).
exposure: eating a cannabis edible, as reported by the caller and coded by poison-centre staff; product, amount and source not recorded.
comparator: no comparison group; years compared with one another (2017 to 2019 against 2020 to 2021), with all calls about children under 6 as the denominator for the yearly share.
outcome: yearly number and share of calls; age, sex and place of exposure; the poison centres' outcome grade (no, minor, moderate or major effect); clinical effects, treatments and level of care.
magnitude: Poison-centre series (Tweet 2023; reported calls, National Poison Data System, children under 6, edible code): 207, 590, 983, 2,209 and 3,054 calls in 2017 to 2021 (7,043); per 1,000 calls about children under 6, 0.2, 0.6, 1.1, 2.5 and 3.6 (Figure 1 labels); all such calls 956,871 (2017) and 846,296 (2021). statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; figures second-hand, no systematic search or appraisal), cannabis can make it easier to fall asleep with short-term use, but people who use it regularly become tolerant to this, and stopping regular use is followed by sleep problems: cited studies found sleep difficulties in 32 to 76% of people in cannabis withdrawal, strange or vivid dreams starting within days of stopping and sometimes lasting weeks, and in sleep-laboratory studies longer time to fall asleep, more waking, less total and deep sleep, and a rebound of REM sleep, more marked in people who had used heavily. Poor sleep during abstinence was linked with relapse; sleep improved again with THC or a return to cannabis, but the review notes that regular use itself worsens sleep over time, and going back to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to get to sleep was commonly observed. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of sleep research says that cannabis can help some people fall asleep at first, but people who use it every day get used to that effect. When they stop, many sleep badly and have strange dreams for days or weeks. Poor sleep was linked with going back to cannabis. These are second-hand findings from a review that did not check study quality.
population: People who use cannabis regularly and stop, in studies cited by a narrative review
exposure: Stopping regular cannabis use (withdrawal and abstinence)
comparator: Their own sleep at baseline or during use, or healthy sleepers, as in the cited studies
outcome: Self-reported sleep problems and dreams, polysomnographic sleep, relapse
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized: sleep difficulties in 32 to 76% of people experiencing withdrawal, in studies of up to 450 participants; strange dreams starting within days and lasting up to about six weeks in some studies; polysomnography in withdrawal with longer sleep onset, more waking, reduced total sleep, efficiency and slow-wave sleep, and REM rebound.

statement: In placebo-controlled laboratory and simulator studies of mostly healthy adults given a single dose of THC (80 studies, 155 trials, 3,454 participants, 71% men; McCartney et al., 2021; AMSTAR 2 critically low, provisional), THC compared with placebo is associated with impairment of most driving-related skills shortly after use, by small to medium amounts: lane weaving (standard deviation of lane position, Hedges' g -0.29, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.11), reaction time while driving (-0.47), tracking (-0.42), information processing (-0.38) and working memory (-0.36), among others, while driving speed was not worse (people tended to drive slightly slower). How long the impairment lasted depended on dose, route and how often people used cannabis. In people who used cannabis less than weekly, impairment grew with dose and faded with time, and, the authors say, may last longer after THC is eaten than after it is smoked or vaped: at the reference dose the authors modelled (amount in the study card), the average across skills was predicted to fall to the authors' chosen threshold of no meaningful impairment after about 5 hours when smoked, 6 when vaped and 8 when eaten, but information processing was predicted to take about 8 to 9 hours after inhaling, longer than the abstract's summary for cognitive skills says, and lane weaving, a driving measure, about 7 to 8 hours. People who used cannabis weekly or more were less impaired at the same dose, but their data were too uniform to model how long impairment lasts for them. These durations are predictions without confidence intervals from a model fitted mostly to tests within 4 hours of use; they assume steady recovery and say nothing about when any one person is safe to drive. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In lab and driving-simulator studies, THC made people worse at driving skills such as staying in lane and reacting, by a small to medium amount. The effect faded over several hours: faster after smoking or vaping than after eating THC, and more slowly after bigger doses. People who use cannabis often were less affected, but nobody worked out how long it lasts for them. These are averages from a computer model, not a safe time to drive for any one person.
population: Mostly healthy adults (71% men) in placebo-controlled experimental studies published 2000 to 2020; duration models in people who used cannabis less than weekly

comparator: Placebo, within or between participants
outcome: Driving performance in simulators or on the road, driving-related cognitive skills, and the predicted time for impairment to fall below a threshold
magnitude: Peak effects (Hedges' g, 95% CI): lane weaving -0.29 (-0.47 to -0.11); lateral control -0.24 (-0.41 to -0.08); driving reaction time -0.47 (-0.70 to -0.23); tracking -0.42 (-0.58 to -0.25); information processing -0.38 (-0.55 to -0.21); working memory -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20); divided attention -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.20); speed +0.14 (-0.01 to +0.29). Regular use against other use in the combined inhaled model +0.17 (+0.06 to +0.28). Predicted recovery to g = -0.25 at the reference dose in other use: aggregate 300 min smoked, 350 min vaporised, 480 min oral; lane weaving 427 and 472 min; information processing 486 and 530 min (smoked, vaporised); no intervals given.

statement: In sleep-laboratory studies of cannabis products taken by mouth, sleep did not detectably change on average: in six modern trials pooled in a 2025 meta-analysis (Velzeboer et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 178 participants, editors' sum from Table 1), mostly of CBD or low-dose THC medicines and four of six in people with sleep disorders (sleep apnea, insomnia, REM behaviour disorder in Parkinson's disease), total sleep time (standardized difference -0.02, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.21), time to fall asleep, waking during the night, sleep efficiency and deep sleep did not differ from placebo or baseline, while results for REM (dream) sleep were inconsistent (-0.04, -0.52 to 0.45; I-squared 77%). Small studies from 1972 to 1982, mostly with high oral THC doses, could not be pooled, and most of them found less REM sleep; and three comparisons (1973 to 2008) of people who smoke cannabis with people who do not mostly found no difference. All six pooled studies gave cannabis by mouth, and the authors note that clinical research has almost only studied oral use, so the result may not apply to smoked or vaped cannabis. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Many people use cannabis to help them sleep. In sleep labs, people who took cannabis products by mouth, mostly medicines with CBD or a little THC, slept about the same as when they took a dummy pill: no longer, no faster to fall asleep, no deeper. Dream sleep results did not agree. These studies did not test smoking or vaping, and most people in them had a sleep problem.
population: Adults in sleep-laboratory studies, mostly people with sleep apnea, insomnia or REM behaviour disorder with Parkinson's disease, and some healthy volunteers
exposure: Cannabis products taken by mouth (THC, dronabinol, CBD or combinations; doses are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Placebo or the same people's baseline nights
outcome: Polysomnographic sleep: total sleep time, time to fall asleep, waking after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, sleep stages, REM sleep
magnitude: Pooled standardized mean differences (95% CI), as printed in the forest plots: total sleep time -0.02 (-0.25 to 0.21); sleep onset latency -0.06 (-0.28 to 0.17); wake after sleep onset 0.11 (-0.13 to 0.34); sleep efficiency 0.01 (-0.25 to 0.27); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5%; REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1%.

evidence.locator: Figs. 2a, 3a, 4 and 5a (pp. 6-8); Results 3.2.1 to 3.2.4 (pp. 9-10)

Of 12 administration studies measuring total sleep time, one (n = 4) found an increase; of 12 measuring onset latency, one (n = 2) found an increase. The text prints +0.021, +0.056 and -0.009 for three of these, with intervals centred on the figures' values.

statement: In sleep-laboratory studies of people stopping after regular cannabis use or after daily high doses of THC, stopping is associated with worse sleep in the first week: pooling three small studies (about 38 people, editors' sum; Velzeboer et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low), sleep was shorter (standardized difference -0.79, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.42), took longer to start (1.21, 0.76 to 1.67) and was less efficient (-0.92, -1.38 to -0.46; two studies), with more REM (dream) sleep (1.61, 0.74 to 2.48) that began sooner (-1.09, -1.53 to -0.66), compared with sleep while still using. These are large standardized changes, but two of the three studies come from one 1970s laboratory that stopped high daily oral THC doses given in the study, the third is an uncontrolled before-and-after study of 20 people who were using cannabis and knew they had stopped, and the pooled data came from the first three days after stopping in two studies and days four to six in the third, so the review cannot say how long the changes last. The authors cite a suggestion that the very high oral THC doses in these studies may have made the REM rebound larger. Of all seven withdrawal studies reviewed, five found longer time to fall asleep, three shorter sleep (four found no change), three more waking in the night and three more REM sleep. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people who use cannabis a lot stop, their sleep gets worse for at least the first few nights. In sleep labs they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and woke more, and had more dream sleep, compared with when they were still using. These studies were small and old, and two of the three stopped very large lab doses. They did not check how long the bad sleep lasts after the first week.
population: Adults actively using cannabis (real-world use, one study of 20 people) or men with a history of daily use given high daily oral THC doses in a laboratory (two studies of 7 and 11 people)
exposure: Stopping cannabis or THC (doses are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's sleep while still using, or on THC before placebo substitution
outcome: Polysomnographic sleep in the first week after stopping
magnitude: Pooled standardized mean differences (95% CI): total sleep time -0.79 (-1.16 to -0.42), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency 1.21 (0.76 to 1.67), 6.4%; sleep efficiency -0.92 (-1.38 to -0.46), two studies; REM sleep 1.61 (0.74 to 2.48), 46.8%; REM latency -1.09 (-1.53 to -0.66), 0%. Individual total sleep time estimates -0.95, -0.89 and -0.70.

evidence.extracted: Withdrawal meta-analyses of three studies: total sleep time -0.794 (-1.163 to -0.424), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency 1.213 (0.757 to 1.669), 6.43%; REM sleep 1.609 (0.737 to 2.479), 46.8%; REM latency -1.092 (-1.527 to -0.657), 0%; sleep efficiency, two studies, -0.922 (-1.379 to -0.464), 0%. Individual studies for total sleep time: Feinberg 1975 -0.95, Feinberg 1976 -0.89, Vandrey 2011 -0.70.

statement: In adults treated in emergency departments for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (repeated bouts of vomiting with regular heavy cannabis use), the evidence is insufficient to say whether capsaicin cream rubbed on the belly helps, as described in a 2024 systematic review of five studies with 386 patients (Sabbineni et al., 2024; AMSTAR 2 critically low). In the one small randomized trial (about 30 patients), nausea 30 minutes after the cream did not differ from a placebo cream, though more people had complete relief (29% against none) and nausea was lower at 60 minutes; of four non-randomized studies, one found fewer extra medicines and faster discharge (55% against 21% needing at most one more drug), one fewer extra medicines without a shorter stay, one no change in pain, and one no difference in stay or returns, with more hospital admissions after capsaicin (8 against 1, not significant). No serious side effects were reported, but the studies were small, mostly retrospective and at moderate to high risk of bias. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome means bouts of being sick again and again in some people who use a lot of cannabis for a long time. In hospital emergency rooms, some doctors rub a hot-pepper cream (capsaicin) on the belly. In one small fair test, it did not ease sickness more than a dummy cream after half an hour, though a few more people felt fully better. Other studies disagreed, so it is not known whether the cream helps.
population: Adults (some studies from age 16) treated for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome in North American emergency departments
exposure: Topical capsaicin cream applied in the emergency department (strengths are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Placebo cream (one trial), patients not given capsaicin, the same patients' earlier visits, or symptoms before the cream
outcome: Nausea and pain scores, need for rescue medicines, time in the department, admissions, return visits
magnitude: Randomized trial: nausea at 30 min difference -2.0 cm (interval printed 0.2 to -4.2), not significant; complete resolution 29.4% against 0%. Non-randomized: 55% against 21% needing at most one more drug and 3.72 against 6.11 h to discharge (Kum et al.); 179 against 201 min stay, p = 0.33 (Wagner et al.); admissions 8 against 1 (Yusuf et al.); pain before and after not significantly changed (Lee and Coralic).

statement: In adults treated in emergency departments for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, dopamine-blocking medicines given by injection (haloperidol, droperidol) were associated with faster relief and shorter stays in both studies described in a 2024 systematic review (Sabbineni et al., 2024; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 106 patients). In one small randomized trial (30 patients; Ruberto et al., 2021, as described in the review), haloperidol reduced pain and nausea more than ondansetron, a standard anti-sickness medicine, after 2 hours (difference 2.3 cm on a 10 cm scale), with more treatment success (54% against 29%), less need for rescue medicines (31% against 59%) and earlier discharge (3.1 against 5.6 hours); in one chart review of 76 patients, those given droperidol had shorter hospital stays (6.7 against 13.9 hours). Both medicines caused acute dystonia (sudden muscle spasms) in a few people: two return visits after haloperidol and one case after droperidol; two people were drowsy after droperidol. The evidence is small and at high risk of bias. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Some hospital medicines that block dopamine, a brain chemical, are used for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. In one small fair test, haloperidol eased pain and sickness more than a usual anti-sickness medicine and people went home sooner. In another study, people given droperidol left hospital sooner. Both medicines gave a few people sudden muscle spasms. The studies were small, so we cannot be sure.
population: Adults treated for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome in emergency departments
exposure: Intravenous haloperidol or droperidol given in hospital (doses are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Intravenous ondansetron (randomized trial); patients not given droperidol (chart review)
outcome: Pain and nausea scores, treatment success, rescue medicines, time to discharge, length of stay, adverse events
magnitude: Haloperidol against ondansetron: mean difference 2.3 cm in combined pain and nausea at 2 h (p = 0.01); success 54% against 29%; rescue antiemetics 31% against 59%; any medicine 31% against 76%; discharge 3.1 (SD 1.7) against 5.6 (SD 4.5) h (p = 0.03). Droperidol: hospital stay 6.7 against 13.9 h (p = 0.014); discharge after last antiemetic 137 against 185 min (p = 0.002). Acute dystonia: 2 return visits after haloperidol, 1 after droperidol.

statement: In adolescents and young adults who use cannabis frequently or heavily, compared with people of similar age who use little or no cannabis, cannabis use is associated with slightly lower scores on memory and thinking tests in studies that did not give cannabis to participants (the hours after a single dose given in a laboratory are covered by the answer on how long impairment lasts). In a meta-analysis of 69 cross-sectional samples published 1973 to 2017 (2,152 people who used cannabis, mean age 20.6, and 6,575 comparison participants with minimal use; Scott et al., 2018; AMSTAR 2 confidence critically low), the average difference in mostly raw test scores, not adjusted for other drug use, education or ability before use, was about a quarter of a standard deviation (d −0.25, 95% CI −0.32 to −0.17): learning −0.33, executive shifting −0.30, delayed memory −0.26, speed of processing −0.26, inhibition −0.25, working memory −0.22 and attention −0.21, with no clear difference on verbal or language (−0.14, −0.27 to 0.001), visuospatial (−0.04, −0.16 to 0.08) or motor tests (−0.02, −0.22 to 0.18). Results varied widely between studies (editors' approximate 95% prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); 22 of the 69 studies required no abstinence before testing or did not say; samples of people seeking treatment differed more (−0.43, −0.62 to −0.24; 12 studies; uncorrected P = .04); and small studies reported larger differences: allowing for missing small studies shrank the estimate of a simpler model from −0.21 to −0.13. The difference was smaller in studies that required a longer time without cannabis before testing: −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies) where more than 72 hours was required, against −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22) where 72 hours or less was required or none was stated; this compares studies, not the same people over time (see the answer on stopping). A systematic review of 2004-2015 studies (Broyd et al., 2016; critically low; nothing pooled) rated the evidence of poorer verbal learning and memory and attention in people who use cannabis regularly as strong and largely consistent (20 and 14 studies), and the evidence for working memory, planning-type executive functions, inhibition and decision making as mixed (a narrative review of the same year calls the findings for working memory, attention and impulsivity mixed; Curran et al., 2016, second-hand); more than half of its studies did not report IQ or education, and its authors suggest that links with how often people use may reflect lingering effects of recent use. Two cohorts that measured IQ in childhood add to this: in a British twin cohort, the 84 of 1,989 18-year-olds with cannabis dependence performed worse than the others on 4 of 6 executive-function scores, 2 after allowing for IQ at 12, but did not differ from their co-twins in 57 pairs in which only one twin was dependent (Meier et al., 2018); in a New Zealand birth cohort, 9 of 16 test scores at 38 (executive function, memory, processing speed, and two WAIS-IV index scores for perceptual reasoning and verbal comprehension) were lower the more of five interviews from 18 to 38 at which people had met criteria for dependence, after allowing for childhood IQ and sex, without correction for testing many scores, and these tests had not been given in childhood (Meier et al., 2012). The two reviews share primary studies and are counted once. None of these comparisons can show that cannabis caused the differences. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: On average, young people who use cannabis often score a little lower on tests of learning, memory, attention and planning than people of the same age who use little or none: about a quarter of a standard deviation, which is a small difference. Tests of language, of shapes and space, and of movement showed no clear gap. The gap was smaller in studies that asked people to go more than 3 days without cannabis before the test, bigger in people seeking treatment, and small studies may have made it look bigger. These studies tested people after they had started using, so they cannot show that cannabis caused the gap; in one twin study, the gap on thinking tests at 18 was smaller and no longer clear when each twin was compared with their co-twin.
population: Adolescents and young adults (sample mean ages 26 or younger; mean age about 21) who use cannabis frequently or heavily, most with frequent use or a cannabis use disorder, in cross-sectional studies; members of two population cohorts (New Zealand, born 1972-73; England and Wales, twins born 1994-95)
exposure: Frequent, heavy or problematic cannabis use as each study defined it (amount, potency and route mostly not recorded); in the cohorts, DSM cannabis dependence in the past year at 18 (British twins) or at up to five interviews from 18 to 38 (New Zealand)
comparator: People of similar age with minimal or no cannabis use, as each study defined them; in the twin analysis, the co-twin without dependence
outcome: Scores on standardized memory, attention, processing-speed, executive, verbal, visuospatial and motor tests in studies that did not give cannabis, as group differences in standard-deviation units; abstinence before testing ranged from none to about 3 months
magnitude: Scott et al. 2018 (69 samples; 2,152 against 6,575; raw-score Hedges-corrected d, negative = lower in the cannabis groups): overall −0.247 (95% CI −0.32 to −0.17), between-study variance 0.070 (P < .001; editors' approximate prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); learning −0.33 (−0.42 to −0.24); executive abstraction/shifting −0.30 (−0.40 to −0.20); speed −0.26 (−0.38 to −0.15); delayed memory −0.26 (−0.35 to −0.16); inhibition −0.25 (−0.38 to −0.13); updating/working memory −0.22 (−0.31 to −0.12); attention −0.21 (−0.31 to −0.12); verbal/language −0.14 (−0.27 to 0.001); visuospatial −0.04 (−0.16 to 0.08); motor −0.02 (−0.22 to 0.18). Required abstinence more than 72 h −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies, n = 928) against 72 h or less −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22; 54 studies, n = 7,799), P = .01. Treatment-seeking −0.43 (−0.62 to −0.24; 12 studies) against others −0.22 (−0.29 to −0.14), uncorrected P = .04. Small-study effects: Egger t = 4.70, P < .001; trim-and-fill in a univariate model −0.206 to −0.128. Broyd et al. 2016 (qualitative ratings, chronic use): verbal learning and memory +++ (20 studies), attention +++ (14), working memory +– (16), planning-type executive functions +– (23), inhibition +– (9), decision making +– (17), psychomotor function + (10). Meier et al. 2018 (age 18; 84 with dependence among 1,989; sex-adjusted z-scores): 4 of 6 executive scores worse (Spatial Span Forward −0.48 against 0.02), 2 of 6 after IQ at 12; 57 discordant twin pairs, no significant difference (Spatial Span Forward −0.38 against −0.18, p = .20). risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional comparisons of raw scores, not adjusted for ability before use, education or other drug use, with no study-level appraisal in either review (AMSTAR 2 critically low: cards sc_scott_2018, sc_broyd_2016); more than half of the studies in one review did not report IQ or education. The cohort findings carry their own risks (sc_meier_2012, ROBINS-E high for confounding; sc_meier_2018, some concerns).

inconsistency.note: Wide spread between studies (between-study variance 0.070, P < .001; approximate prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); findings for working memory, executive functions and decision making are mixed. Part of the spread is explained by abstinence before testing and treatment seeking.

indirectness.note: Second-hand (METHODS §6.3): the primary studies inside both reviews were not read, and Broyd et al.'s ratings are its authors' consensus. Most samples used frequently or had a use disorder and were young, which the claim states; the estimates do not describe occasional use or older adults.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval is narrow (−0.32 to −0.17), and seven domain intervals exclude zero.

publication_bias.note: Funnel asymmetry and a significant Egger test (t = 4.70, P < .001); trim-and-fill shrank the estimate by about 38%; the search was limited to English-language peer-reviewed studies.

dose_response.note: Associations with frequency, duration and age of onset are reported by Broyd et al. but not pooled, and its authors read the frequency links as possible residual effects; Scott et al. found no moderation by age at first use. No upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Differences that predate use and other drug use would more plausibly enlarge than hide the differences; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational (cross-sectional) evidence starts low and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness (second-hand) and publication bias, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded, an association in young people who use cannabis frequently, tested when not intoxicated; whether differences remain after stopping, and whether cannabis lowers IQ, are separate answers. Status replicated: the direction is the same in most of the independent primary studies in both reviews (for verbal learning and memory, Broyd et al. cite 8 studies in adolescents and young adults that found poorer scores and 2 that did not), though the size varies widely. Overlap: Scott et al. (1973 to 2017) and Broyd et al. (2004 to 2015) share primary studies (Fried et al., 2005, for example, is in both), and Dunedin is among Broyd et al.'s studies, so the reviews are counted once and not as independent replication; the British twin cohort is independent of both pools.

statement: In people who used cannabis frequently, the evidence is insufficient to say whether differences in memory and thinking tests remain after they have stopped for days or weeks, and the question is disputed. Differences were smaller in studies that required longer abstinence: in a meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies of adolescents and young adults (Scott et al., 2018; AMSTAR 2 confidence critically low), the 15 studies that required more than 72 hours without cannabis before testing (928 participants; 7 to 90 days by the first reader's reading of the Table) found an average difference from comparison groups with minimal use of −0.08 standard deviations (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07), against −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22) in the 54 studies that required 72 hours or less or did not say (P = .01; the authors say the abstinence associations hold only at thresholds not corrected for multiple comparisons). This compares different studies, not the same people before and after stopping; the interval includes no difference and reaches −0.22, close to the overall difference of −0.25; only 14 of the 69 studies reported checking abstinence; at least 7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies come from papers sharing one author, and 11 of the 15 had age ranges ending at 20 or younger. A systematic review of 2004-2015 studies (Broyd et al., 2016; critically low) found eighteen studies of people abstinent for more than a day, most often 21 to 35 days and few for longer: some found poorer attention, verbal or working memory or psychomotor speed after 23 to 53 days of abstinence, or poorer executive function in older adults abstinent more than 28 days, while others found no difference from controls, including a prospective study in which adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls and a cohort in which people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months did not differ on any test from people who had not used. It rated persistence as mixed for verbal learning and memory, working memory, attention and planning-type executive functions, called recovery contentious and suggested that verbal learning and memory may recover with prolonged abstinence, while its summary table is firmer than these ratings (likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function, possible ones on verbal learning and memory). A narrative review of the same year (Curran et al., 2016) states that studies converge on no impairment beyond 4–6 weeks, citing two earlier sources, and adds that brain cannabinoid receptor levels return to normal after about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence, which is not a test of memory or thinking. In a New Zealand birth cohort, people with dependence at 2 or more of 5 interviews whose at least weekly use began before 18, and who used cannabis weekly or less in the year before testing at 38, had lower IQ at 38 than in childhood (17 people, p = .03 by a test the paper does not describe), but they had used on up to 52 days that year and were not compared with people who never used, so this is not a test of abstinence (Meier et al., 2012). The individual abstinence studies are known here only through the reviews' descriptions, and the reviews share studies. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: It is not clear. In studies that asked people to go more than 3 days without cannabis before the test, the average gap in scores was small and could be zero, though a gap nearly as big as the average across all studies is not ruled out; and these were different studies, not the same people before and after stopping. Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree: some found lower scores on some tests, others found none. Few studies followed people for longer; in one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not differ on any test from people who had not used. Reviews read this evidence in opposite ways.
population: People who used cannabis frequently or heavily, mostly adolescents and young adults (a few studies of older adults), tested after a period without cannabis
exposure: Stopping cannabis for more than 72 hours to about 3 months before testing (mostly 3 to 5 weeks; abstinence checked in a minority of studies), and in a few cohorts for 12 months or more
comparator: People who used little or no cannabis; people who continued using; or the same people tested before they stopped (prospective studies)
outcome: Memory, attention, processing-speed, psychomotor and executive test scores after abstinence, and in one cohort full-scale IQ
magnitude: Scott et al. 2018 (raw-score d against comparison groups): required abstinence more than 72 h −0.08 (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies, n = 928, P = .29) against 72 h or less −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22; 54 studies, n = 7,799); chi-square 6.36, P = .01 (abstinence associations described by the authors as holding at uncorrected thresholds); longer mean reported abstinence went with smaller differences (beta 0.059, P = .04 uncorrected; 28 studies); required abstinence mean 152.7 h (SD 335.2), none or unstated in 22 studies, 1 to 72 h in 32, more than 72 h in 15; monitored in 14. Broyd et al. 2016: eighteen abstinence studies (eleven cross-sectional, abstinent 7 days to more than 1 year; seven prospective, 21 days to 4–8 years); persistence rated +– for verbal learning and memory (9 studies), working memory (7), attention (10), planning-type executive functions (9) and verbal fluency (4), + for psychomotor function (6), – for other memory functions, time estimation and decision making. Meier et al. 2012: dependence at 2 or more waves, at least weekly use before 18, and weekly or less use in the year before testing (median 14 days, range 0 to 52; n = 17), childhood to adult IQ about 102 to 97.5, p = .03 (values read from a figure).

risk_of_bias.note: The abstinence contrast is between studies that also differ in laboratory, sample and protocol (at least 7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies from papers sharing one author; rows that apparently share a comparison group fall in opposite subgroups); abstinence was checked in 14 of 69 studies; the abstinence studies in the systematic review are mostly small and cross-sectional, and the prospective ones mostly lack retested comparison groups, so practice is not separated from recovery (AMSTAR 2 critically low: cards sc_scott_2018, sc_broyd_2016).

inconsistency.note: Studies disagree, some finding differences after 23 to 53 days and others none after 12 months or more, and the two reviews of the same years read them in opposite ways; length of abstinence alone does not explain the disagreement.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the individual abstinence studies are known only through the reviews' descriptions, some with misplaced citations (card sc_broyd_2016, reporting issues), and the narrative review's statement rests on two sources not read and on receptor imaging rather than tests; abstinence mostly lasted 3 to 5 weeks.

imprecision.note: The longer-abstinence estimate rests on 15 small studies (928 participants), and its interval (−0.22 to 0.07) includes no difference and reaches −0.22, close to the overall difference (−0.25); the between-study test (P = .01) is not corrected for the several study features tested.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed for the abstinence subgroup or the abstinence studies; not rated down separately.

large_effect.note: Not applicable to a claim of insufficient evidence.

dose_response.note: Longer mean reported abstinence went with smaller differences across 28 studies (P = .04, uncorrected), a between-study gradient that may reflect other study differences; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: People who manage to stop may differ from those who continue, in either direction; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence: differences are smaller after longer abstinence in a between-study comparison, but neither their disappearance nor their persistence after weeks can be shown with precision. Overlap: the abstinence studies in the systematic review and the longer-abstinence studies in the meta-analysis share studies (Fried et al., 2005, for example, is in both), and the narrative review adds no new data, so the sources are not independent replication. Status contested: credible studies point both ways, and two reviews of the same years draw opposite conclusions (one calls recovery contentious, the other says studies converge on no impairment beyond 4–6 weeks).

debate.question: After people who used cannabis often stop, do differences in memory and thinking go away within days or weeks, or do some remain?
debate.evidence_yes: The systematic review that describes the abstinence studies one by one (Broyd et al., 2016; sc_broyd_2016; funded by the Australian Research Council and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no conflicts declared) reports deficits after weeks without cannabis in several of them: some aspects of attention, verbal and working memory and psychomotor speed in adolescents abstinent 28 and 35 days; working memory and risk taking in adolescents abstinent 53 days; poorer verbal fluency in young adults abstinent up to 4 weeks; executive function and information processing in older adults abstinent more than 28 days; adults who improved on tracking and divided attention over 8 to 23 days but stayed below controls; visual search still impaired after 3 weeks in adolescents whose verbal learning had improved; and, in identical twins of whom one had used and had been abstinent more than 12 months, poorer Block Design with trends on delayed recall and finger tapping. Poorer performance after abstinence went with more lifetime use or earlier onset in two adolescent studies and predicted relapse within a year in one. Its authors conclude that evidence for persistent dysfunction continues to emerge, and cite an earlier study that used sensitive measures of brain function and found attention-processing deficits related to years of use in people abstinent 2 years. In the meta-analysis that found smaller differences after longer abstinence (Scott et al., 2018; sc_scott_2018), the interval for studies requiring more than 72 hours (−0.22 to 0.07) reaches −0.22, close to the overall difference of −0.25, so a difference of nearly that size is not ruled out. In the Dunedin cohort, people with dependence at 2 or more interviews whose at least weekly use began before 18, and who used weekly or less in the year before testing, still had lower IQ than in childhood (17 people, p = .03), which its authors read as incomplete recovery, although these people were not abstinent (Meier et al., 2012; sc_meier_2012).
debate.evidence_no: In a meta-analysis of 69 cross-sectional samples of young people (Scott et al., 2018; sc_scott_2018; funded by the US Department of Veterans Affairs, with no role for the funder; one author reports royalties from the Brain Resource Center), studies that required more than 72 hours without cannabis found an average difference of −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07), against −0.30 in studies requiring 72 hours or less (P = .01, at thresholds the authors describe as not corrected for multiple comparisons), and longer mean reported abstinence went with smaller differences (P = .04, uncorrected); the zero or unknown abstinence studies did not drive the contrast, as the authors report, and they read it as residual effects of recent use or withdrawal rather than lasting change. In the systematic review that lists persisting deficits, the two prospective studies that controlled for ability before use include one in which adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls on any measure, and in a cohort tested three times 4 years apart, people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months improved relative to people who continued on immediate verbal memory and did not differ from people who had not used on any test; several studies found no difference on broader attention measures between people who had stopped and controls, and verbal learning improved by 2 weeks in adolescents (Broyd et al., 2016; sc_broyd_2016). Its authors suggest that attention deficits may be residual effects that fade as cannabinoids are cleared, and that verbal learning and memory may recover with prolonged abstinence. A narrative review (Curran et al., 2016; sc_curran_2016; funded by the US National Institutes of Health and the UK Medical Research Council; competing interests declared, with details only in the web version) states that studies are converging on no impairment beyond 4–6 weeks, citing a study of people with long-term use and a meta-analysis of residual effects, and adds that brain cannabinoid receptor levels return to normal after about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence.
debate.neither_can_show: Most abstinence studies compare different people once, and people who manage to stop may differ from people who continue in ability, motivation or other drug use; apart from two prospective studies, none of the studies in these reviews tested people before they first used. Where the same people are retested without a retested comparison group, improvement from practice cannot be separated from recovery. Only 14 of the 69 studies in the meta-analysis reported checking abstinence, most abstinence periods were 3 to 5 weeks, and few studies went beyond a year. The between-study abstinence contrast is also a contrast of laboratories and samples: at least 7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies come from papers sharing one author, and 11 have age ranges ending at 20 or younger. A difference that remains after stopping need not have been caused by cannabis, and receptor imaging does not measure memory or thinking. Differences between group averages are not the same as problems in daily life. The individual abstinence studies, and the two sources behind the 4–6 weeks statement, are known here only through the reviews' descriptions.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Part of the small difference seen in people who use cannabis often is probably the after-effect of recent use: the difference is smaller in studies that required more than a few days without cannabis (Scott et al., 2018), and attention and verbal learning improved over days to weeks in the studies that retested people (Broyd et al., 2016). Whether a small difference remains after several weeks is open: the reports of persisting deficits come mainly from cross-sectional samples, mostly of adolescents and young adults (Broyd et al., 2016), and the reports of no difference from a between-study comparison and a few cohorts (Broyd et al., 2016; Scott et al., 2018), all known here through reviews. For a year or more without cannabis, the evidence is a handful of studies with mixed results (Broyd et al., 2016). The statement that impairment does not persist beyond 4–6 weeks (Curran et al., 2016) is firmer than the evidence these reviews describe, and so is the review's summary that effects on attention and psychomotor function are likely to persist (Broyd et al., 2016).
debate.what_would_settle_it: Studies that test the same people before they start using, while they use and repeatedly after they stop, with urine tests confirming abstinence at each visit, beside comparison groups retested on the same schedule to allow for practice; follow-up from days to years; enough people to analyse results by length of verified abstinence; and a pre-registered meta-analysis of individual participants' data stratified by verified abstinence. None of the sources read reports such a study.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether rates of schizophrenia or psychosis changed as cannabis use rose: the studies that narrative reviews cite disagree, all are ecological, and their figures are second-hand here. As described in two reviews, an Australian modelling study by the reviewers' own group found no clear rise in psychosis incidence after steep rises in cannabis use in the 1980s and 1990s; a British modelling study judged it too early to see any rise in England and Wales; case-register studies in Britain and Switzerland (south-east London and Zurich) reported rising incidence of psychoses in recent birth cohorts; and a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice found no increase, cited to a 2008 government advisory report (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015). Another review describes incidence of schizophrenia in south-east London as doubling between 1965 and 1999 while the share of patients who had used cannabis rose (Murray et al., 2016), and a third cites a 2009 paper on diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005 among studies finding no change or a decrease (Gage et al., 2016). A critical overview states that UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, citing a commentary for this, and that first admissions for schizophrenia did not rise and perhaps fell slightly, without a source for the admissions figures, and treats this as evidence against a causal effect (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Reviews that lean towards a causal reading call such evidence weak: it cannot show that the people who used cannabis are those who became ill, and it does not account for confounders or for other risk factors that may have fallen over the same period (Gage et al., 2016); even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly, and changes in diagnostic criteria and services, poor administrative data and possible falls in incidence from social improvements could hide a rise (Hall, 2015). The 2007 systematic review cites the same Australian and British modelling studies rather than new data (Moore et al., 2007), and a 2021 viewpoint calls for controlled before-and-after comparisons where cannabis use rose after decriminalization (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). Across places rather than over time, in one primary study of 10 sites in Europe and Brazil, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls reported daily use (r about 0.8) or high-potency use (about 0.7); this is an ecological correlation, and although the paper calls the two measures only modestly correlated (r = 0.2), its own site figures correlate at about 0.71 (editors' calculation), so the two correlations are not separate evidence (Di Forti et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: If cannabis causes psychosis, rates of schizophrenia might be expected to rise when more people use cannabis. The studies that reviews describe disagree: an Australian study found no clear rise after cannabis use went up, studies in south-east London and Zurich found psychosis becoming more common in people born more recently, and a review says that in the UK first hospital admissions for schizophrenia did not rise although cannabis use rose at least tenfold. These studies compare whole populations over time, so they cannot tell whether the people who used cannabis are the ones who became ill, and changes in how illness is diagnosed and recorded could hide a rise. They are known here only through reviews.
population: Whole populations over time in Australia, England and Wales, south-east London, Zurich and the UK, as described in narrative reviews; and 10 catchment areas in the UK, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy and Brazil compared with each other (2010 to 2015)
exposure: Rising cannabis use in the population over decades (as described in the reviews); across sites, the share of population controls reporting daily or high-potency use
comparator: Earlier periods or birth cohorts in the same populations; sites with less daily or high-potency use
outcome: Incidence of schizophrenia or psychotic disorder (treated or registered cases, first admissions, modelled incidence); across sites, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder per 100,000 person-years
magnitude: No pooled estimate. As described in reviews: no clear rise in Australia (modelling); too early to detect in England and Wales (modelling); rising incidence in recent birth cohorts in south-east London and Zurich (case registers), with schizophrenia incidence in south-east London described as doubling between 1965 and 1999 (one review); no rise in a British general-practice study (cited to a 2008 government report) and no change or a decrease in diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005 (a 2009 paper cited by another review); at least a tenfold rise in UK cannabis use since the 1970s (from a commentary) without a rise in first admissions (no source given). Across 10 sites: correlation of adjusted incidence with daily use among controls r = 0.8 (p = 0.0109) and with high-potency use r = 0.7 (p = 0.0286); the two exposures correlate across sites at about 0.71 by the editors' calculation from the site table, although the paper prints r = 0.2.
