statement: In two US national household surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever used cannabis had met, or were estimated to meet at some time in their life, criteria for cannabis dependence under older, narrower diagnostic definitions. In the National Comorbidity Survey (fieldwork 1990 to 1992; a probability sample of 8,098 people aged 15 to 54; response 82.4%; a standardized interview, the CIDI, given by lay interviewers), 46.3% of the population had ever used cannabis and 4.2% had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for cannabis dependence, so 9.1% (SE 0.7; about 7.7% to 10.5%, editors' calculation) of the people who had ever used it, even once, had ever been dependent by the time of the interview, against 23.1% for heroin, 16.7% for cocaine and 15.4% for alcohol in the same survey and 31.9% for tobacco (tobacco dependence was assessed, for daily smoking only, in a subsample of 4,414 and divided by tobacco use taken from another 1991 national survey, so it has no standard error); among people who had used cannabis, 12.0% of men and 5.5% of women had been dependent (Anthony et al., 1994). The dependence questions were asked only of people who reported at least several occasions of use, people who had started recently had had little time to become dependent, and the authors expect incomplete reporting, and the survey's leaving out people who had died, to lower the figures, while casual use that people forget or do not mention would push them the other way. In the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (interviews in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005; 7,389 adults who had ever used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence by a structured interview, the AUDADIS-IV), a survival analysis of recalled ages of first use and of onset estimated that 8.9% of people who used cannabis would become dependent at some time in their life (no interval given), 5.9% within 10 years of first use and about 2% within the first year, and half of the people who became dependent had done so within about 5 years of first use; the corresponding lifetime figures were 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol and 20.9% for cocaine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). The figure of about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used, or about 1 in 10, that narrative reviews repeat is cited to these surveys or matches them (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, cite a 2006 book chapter for it, with their comparison figures from the 1990-92 survey; Volkow et al., 2014, and Curran et al., 2016, cite the 2001-05 analysis; Connor et al., 2021, the 1990-92 survey); the reviews' figures are second-hand. Two of these reviews also give about 1 in 10 for other groups without data of their own: Connor et al. (2021), citing a UN report, for people who use cannabis worldwide and for people who use it regularly, and Hall (2015), in its abstract, for people who use it regularly. DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence are narrower than DSM-5 cannabis use disorder, which needs 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months and includes mild cases (Connor et al., 2021). Higher figures from more recent US national data use other definitions and denominators: Connor et al. (2021) cite about 30% of people who use cannabis as developing a use disorder, without giving the measure (Hasin et al., 2015, not read here), and a 2020 professional statement gives 3 in 10 people who had used cannabis in the past year as meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis of the 2012 to 2013 survey; second-hand); the pooled figures of a 2020 meta-analysis of general-population studies are given in the claim on cannabis strength and dependence. Both surveys are from the US, leave out people living in institutions, rely on what people recalled and reported, and predate legal markets and today's stronger products; figures by how often people use and by the age at which they started are in the claim on frequency and age of starting. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In two large US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever tried cannabis, even once, had been dependent on it or were expected to become dependent at some point in their life, using an older, narrower definition of dependence. In the 1990 to 1992 survey this was fewer than for tobacco (about 32 in 100), heroin (23), cocaine (17) or alcohol (15), and more men (12 in 100) than women (about 6 in 100) who had used cannabis had been dependent. The 2001 to 2005 survey estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime and about 6 in 100 within 10 years of first use; for half of the people who became dependent, it began within about 5 years. Today's diagnosis, cannabis use disorder, also counts milder cases, and newer US figures, such as 3 in 10 among people who used in the past year, count only people using recently. Both surveys are from the US, from 1990 to 2005, before today's stronger products.
population: People in US national household surveys who had ever used cannabis: ages 15 to 54 in 1990 to 1992 (National Comorbidity Survey; 46.3% of 8,098 had used) and adults interviewed in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005 (NESARC; 7,389 who had used)
exposure: Any lifetime use of cannabis, even once (in the 1990-92 survey the dependence questions were asked only after at least several occasions of use)
comparator: None for the main figure (a share of everyone who had used); other substances in the same surveys
outcome: Lifetime DSM-III-R cannabis dependence as a proportion at interview (1990-92); lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV cannabis dependence after first use, by years since first use (2001-05)
magnitude: NCS 1990-92 (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1), lifetime dependence 4.2% (0.3), dependence among people who had used 9.1% (0.7; editors' 95% CI about 7.7% to 10.5%); heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7); tobacco 31.9% (no SE: dependence assessed in a subsample of 4,414, use taken from the 1991 NHSDA); among people who had used cannabis, men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5). NESARC 2001-05 (7,389 who had used cannabis; actuarial survival estimates, no intervals): lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence 8.9% (nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%); 5.9% within 10 years of first use; about 2% within the first year; half of the cases of dependence about 5 years after first use (a median among people who became dependent). Second-hand: about 1 in 10 of people who use regularly (Connor et al., 2021, citing a UN report; Hall, 2015, abstract); about 30% developing a use disorder in more recent US data, measure not given (Connor et al., 2021, citing Hasin et al., 2015); 3 in 10 people who used in the past year meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis).

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded. The 1990-92 survey is at low risk as a description of what it measured (JBI on card sc_anthony_1994: probability sample, response 82.4% with a non-response survey and weights, one standardized interview for all drug classes, design-based standard errors); its exclusions (institutions, deaths) and self-report would lower the figure, as its authors say, but not plausibly by much. The 2001-05 analysis is at moderate risk (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011: recalled ages, sometimes decades later; deaths and people in institutions excluded; lifetime estimates projected without intervals), but its lifetime figure agrees with the first survey's.

inconsistency.note: The two surveys measure different quantities (a proportion at one interview among everyone who had ever used, against a projected lifetime probability) and agree closely (9.1% and 8.9%). The higher figures the reviews cite use other definitions and denominators and are reported as such, not pooled.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US household populations, 1990 to 2005, DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence, all stated in the claim; the gap to DSM-5 use disorder, to other countries and to today's products is stated, not assumed away.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to two national surveys.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions in survey populations): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Not downgraded: two independent national probability surveys, a decade apart and with different instruments and DSM versions, give about 9 in 100, and the claim states their measures, years and populations. Strict reading: the 2001-05 timing figures (5.9% within 10 years, about 2% in the first year, half of the cases within about 5 years) rest on recalled ages and an actuarial curve without intervals and on their own would be rated down one level for risk of bias, to very low. The narrative reviews and the 2020 professional statement are used only to trace the figure they repeat, to show the other denominators behind higher figures, and for the DSM-5 definition; they add no data, and the 30% and 3 in 10 they cite for newer data are second-hand and on other denominators and do not enter the rating. Overlap: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and Connor et al. (2021) take their 9% from the 1990-92 survey or a chapter by its first author (Connor's other 1 in 10 figures come from a UN report), and Volkow et al. (2014) and Curran et al. (2016) from the 2001-05 analysis, so the reviews are not further replication. Status replicated: the two surveys are independent and agree.

statement: In studies of pregnant women and their newborns published from 1982 to 2014 (24 articles from 19 studies, mostly cohorts; 15 of the 24 articles before 2000, editors' count; English only), any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (women using other illicit drugs left out, but not those who smoked tobacco or drank alcohol), compared with no cannabis use during pregnancy, is associated with somewhat smaller babies and more admissions to intensive care; whether it is linked to early birth is uncertain. In a 2016 meta-analysis whose pooled estimates are not stated to be adjusted for anything (the mean differences were pooled from raw group means, so they are unadjusted; Gunn et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low), exposed babies weighed on average about 109 g less at birth (95% CI 39 to 180 g; 10 studies, 4 of them finding lower weight; I2 63%), and had higher odds of weighing under 2,500 g (OR 1.77, 1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies, 2 of them positive; I2 89%) and of admission to neonatal or other intensive care (OR 2.02, 1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies, 3 positive; I2 78%); the estimate for preterm birth (before 37 weeks in most studies) fits both no difference and about twice the odds (OR 1.29, 0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies), and length of pregnancy, length and head size at birth, Apgar scores, birth defects and deaths around the time of birth showed no clear difference. No absolute risks were reported in the article, and the review does not discuss whether intensive-care admission reflects the babies' health or hospital practice toward babies of mothers known to use drugs (editors' observation). Mothers who used cannabis also had higher odds of anaemia (OR 1.36, 1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies), a result carried mainly by one large study. The review's authors say that, because most studies did not separate cannabis from tobacco and alcohol, and tobacco and heavy alcohol use are established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and babies small for their gestational age, they cannot tell whether the associations come from cannabis. As described second-hand in narrative reviews and a professional statement: an earlier meta-analysis linked regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy with lower birth weight, a smaller reduction than with tobacco smoking, and one large study found no rise in birth defects (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009); later large studies reported that the lower birth weight generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, although cigarette smoking has often been hard to adjust for fully, and self-reported use under-counts use, which Hall says probably weakens the associations (Hall, 2015); and in one US state with legal cannabis, prenatal use went with 1.5 times the odds of low birth weight after adjustment for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use (OR 1.5, 1.1 to 2.1; Crume et al., 2018, as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In studies mostly from before 2000, babies of women who used cannabis in pregnancy weighed on average about 109 grams less at birth than babies of women who did not, and more often went to newborn intensive care. Whether they were more often born early is not clear, and birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common. Many of the mothers also smoked tobacco or drank alcohol; smoking and heavy drinking can also make babies smaller, and most studies did not separate them from cannabis, so the studies cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.
population: Pregnant women and their babies up to 6 weeks after birth, in 19 mostly cohort studies published from 1982 to 2014 in the USA, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Iran, Jamaica, Spain and Brazil; one later US state study as relayed by a professional statement
exposure: Any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (the authors note reliance on self-report, which may under-count use), with use of other illicit drugs excluded but tobacco and alcohol use allowed; frequency, amount, timing and potency not analysed
comparator: Women who did not use cannabis during pregnancy, and their babies (their tobacco and alcohol use not reported)
outcome: Birth weight; low birth weight (under 2,500 g); admission to neonatal or other intensive care; preterm birth (before 37 weeks); gestational age, length and head circumference; Apgar scores; birth defects and perinatal death; maternal anaemia
magnitude: Gunn et al. 2016 (pooled, no adjustment stated; random effects unless noted): birth weight about 109 g lower in exposed babies (printed as a positive mean difference, 109.42 g, 95% CI 38.72 to 180.12; 10 studies; I2 63%); low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies; I2 89%); NICU or ICU admission OR 2.02 (1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies; I2 78%); preterm birth OR 1.29 (0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies; I2 85%); gestational age -0.20 weeks (-0.62 to 0.22; 5 studies; fixed effect); length -0.10 cm (-0.65 to 0.45; 6 studies; I2 59%); head circumference -0.31 cm (-0.74 to 0.13; 6 studies; I2 97%); maternal anaemia OR 1.36 (1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies; fixed effect). No absolute risks reported. As relayed by Page et al. 2020: one later US state study, low birth weight OR 1.5 (1.1 to 2.1) adjusted for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use.

risk_of_bias.note: Pooled estimates not stated to be adjusted for anything (continuous outcomes pooled from raw means and SDs, so unadjusted; whether any odds ratio taken from a paper was adjusted is not said), in which tobacco and alcohol use, both known causes of low birth weight and early birth, are not separated from cannabis; exposure largely self-reported and under-reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_gunn_2016). A stricter reading would rate down two levels; the floor is reached either way.

inconsistency.note: Unexplained heterogeneity in the significant pools (I2 63% to 89%); most single studies found no association (6 of 10 for birth weight, 5 of 7 for low birth weight).

indirectness.note: Worded for the exposure as studied (any use, in articles mostly published before 2000); the second-hand reports only qualify.

imprecision.note: Wide intervals for low birth weight (1.04 to 3.01) and intensive-care admission (1.27 to 3.21); the preterm interval (0.80 to 2.08) fits both no difference and a doubling, so the absence of a link is not shown; pooled numbers of participants are not reported.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not downgraded separately.

large_effect.note: The intensive-care odds ratio (2.02) is not stated to be adjusted and is open to confounding by tobacco and alcohol; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding by tobacco and alcohol would more plausibly inflate than hide the associations; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low, the floor. Rated for the crude association as worded; these sources do not establish that cannabis causes the differences, and the review's authors say so. The narrative reviews and the professional statement are second-hand and overlap with the meta-analysis (Hayatbakhsh et al., 2012, is among its positive studies and among the later studies Hall, 2015, cites), so they qualify and are not counted as independent replication. Status mixed: the pooled estimates point to lower birth weight and more intensive-care admission, but most single studies found no association and the heterogeneity is unexplained.

statement: In prospective population cohorts from the USA (one with Puerto Rico), Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand that measured cannabis use before age 18 and depression or anxiety later, adolescents in the highest category of use each study reported (mostly self-reported frequency in the past year or 6 months, such as weekly or daily use; in one study a cannabis use disorder by 17, whose comparison group the review does not state), compared with adolescents who did not use cannabis, had modestly higher odds of depression in young adulthood after adjustment for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety and other covariates chosen by each study: in a 2019 meta-analysis (Gobbi et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low) the pooled adjusted OR was 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62; 7 studies; I2 0%), with every study's estimate above 1 (1.02 to 2.62) but only 2 of the 7 significant on their own, and 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67) without a cohort that overlaps with another. Anxiety did not clearly differ (OR 1.18, 0.84 to 1.67; 3 studies; I2 42%). No absolute risks were reported. The review's figure of 7.2% of young-adult depression attributable to cannabis is given without a method and assumes that the link is causal; it matches the pooled odds ratio, taken as a relative risk, applied to the share of US adolescents reporting any past-month use (editors' reconstruction), although that odds ratio compares the highest level of use with none. Which pooled estimates were adjusted for tobacco and other drugs cannot be checked from the article, and the authors say a strong causal inference cannot be made; they cite another team's propensity-score analysis in which the association became non-significant, while their own reanalysis of the cohort with the largest estimate (a cannabis use disorder by 17) gave odds ratios of 2.5 (1.1 to 5.5) with conventional adjustment and 2.6 (1.2 to 5.5) with propensity scores; of 24 studies they could not pool, they describe most as finding a positive association and six as finding none, one of them finding that males with more depressive symptoms went on to use more cannabis and linking later depression to tobacco rather than cannabis. Narrative reviews describe the link with depression as inconsistent and weaker than that with psychosis, with a dose–response relation in one birth cohort (frequency of use by 16) and a 1.5-fold difference between the heaviest use at 18 and no use in the Swedish conscript cohort, both no longer significant after adjustment, and relay an earlier meta-analysis of longitudinal studies with OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94) and weak support for a causal explanation (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; second-hand); another links regular use with anxiety and depression without established causality (Volkow et al., 2014). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Teenagers who used cannabis most often were a little more likely to be depressed as young adults than teenagers who did not use it (about 1.4 times the odds, in 7 long-term studies), even after taking into account how they felt at the start. Anxiety did not clearly differ, but only 3 studies measured it. These studies cannot show that cannabis caused the depression: other differences between the teenagers may explain it, and in some studies the link disappeared after more careful adjustment.
population: Adolescents in prospective population cohorts in the USA (one with Puerto Rico), Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand, followed into young adulthood (the studies pooled in one 2019 meta-analysis)
exposure: Cannabis use before 18, mostly self-reported frequency in the past year or 6 months; the highest category each study reported (in one study a cannabis use disorder by 17)
comparator: Adolescents in the same cohorts who did not use cannabis (who could use alcohol, tobacco or other drugs), by the review's rule for studies that reported several levels of use; for the one study of a cannabis use disorder by 17, the review does not state the comparison group
outcome: Depression and anxiety in young adulthood (diagnostic criteria or scale cut-offs), adjusted at least for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety
magnitude: Gobbi et al. 2019, pooled adjusted odds ratios (random effects), highest reported use category against no use: depression 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62; 7 studies; I2 0%; study estimates 1.44, 1.50, 1.10, 1.30, 1.48, 2.62 and 1.02); without the overlapping Victorian cohort 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67); by measure, structured diagnosis 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) and scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97); by country, USA 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) and other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56); anxiety 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67; 3 studies; I2 42%). Review's own reanalysis of the use-disorder cohort: 2.5 (1.1 to 5.5) by multivariable regression and 2.6 (1.2 to 5.5) with propensity scores. No absolute risks. Second-hand: an earlier meta-analysis of longitudinal studies, depressive disorders OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94), as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009 and Hall 2015.

risk_of_bias.note: Adjusted for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety, but adjustment for tobacco, other drugs, childhood adversity, family history and peer factors varies by study and cannot be checked from the article; another team's propensity-score analysis found no significant association, while the review's own propensity-score reanalysis of one cohort did; exposure self-reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_gobbi_2019). Residual confounding, or depression leading to cannabis use, could change an odds ratio of this size materially.

inconsistency.note: No detectable heterogeneity in the depression pool (I2 0%); all seven estimates above 1.

indirectness.note: Worded for the contrast pooled (highest reported use category against none) and the outcomes measured.

imprecision.note: The depression interval is reasonably narrow, but the anxiety estimate rests on 3 studies with an interval from 16% lower to 67% higher odds, so the absence of a link with anxiety is not shown; only 2 of the 7 depression studies were significant on their own.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; not downgraded separately.

dose_response.note: Not analysed: only the highest category was pooled; the narrative reviews relay dose–response relations that lost significance after adjustment.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: very low, the floor; the depression association alone would also be very low because of the risk-of-bias downgrade. Rated for the adjusted association as worded; whether cannabis use causes depression is not established by these sources, and the review's attributable-case figure is not used. Status replicated: seven cohorts, at least six of them independent (the Victorian cohort overlaps with the Australasian consortium), point the same way. The earlier meta-analysis relayed by both Hall reviews covers adolescents and adults and may share cohorts with this one; it is second-hand and not counted as independent replication, and the two Hall reviews, by the same author, describe the same studies.

statement: In prospective population cohorts in the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, adolescents in the highest category of cannabis use each study reported, compared with adolescents who did not use cannabis, had higher odds of suicidal thoughts and suicide attempts after adjustment at least for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety, but each pooled estimate rests on three studies, two of which in each pool measured the outcome during adolescence rather than in young adulthood as the review intended (Gobbi et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low): suicidal ideation OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.11 to 2.03; I2 0%; only one of the three study estimates, 1.74, 1.16 to 2.60, excluded no difference on its own, and the one young-adult estimate was 1.10, 0.58 to 2.07) and suicide attempts OR 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84; I2 61%; study estimates 4.81, 6.83 and 1.87, the young-adult one 6.83, 2.04 to 22.90, and the most precise 1.87, 1.09 to 3.22, from a Canadian study that is also in the ideation pool). No absolute risks were reported. As described second-hand in two narrative reviews by the same first author (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015), the wider evidence is mixed: in a New Zealand case–control study of suicide attempts needing hospital care, 16% of 302 people who attempted suicide met criteria for cannabis dependence or abuse against 2% of 1,028 community controls, and adjustment for social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence reduced the odds ratio to about 2 (about 9 before adjustment, editors' calculation from the rounded percentages); in prospective studies, a dose–response between frequency of use by 16 and suicide attempts did not survive adjustment, a re-analysis of the same cohort found more than weekly use linked to reported suicidal ideation in males only, cannabis went with self-harm in females only in another study, heavy use raised the risk of depression but not of suicide in a third, and an earlier meta-analysis found the studies too varied to pool. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Teenagers who used cannabis most often were more likely to report thinking about suicide (about 1.5 times the odds) and attempting it (about 3.5 times the odds) than teenagers who did not use it, in a review that combined three studies for each. In most of these studies this was measured while they were still teenagers. In other studies described in reviews, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard life circumstances were taken into account. These studies cannot show that cannabis caused suicidal thoughts or attempts.

statement: As described in an American Heart Association scientific statement and in narrative reviews (all figures second-hand; no primary study was read here, and the statement gives no search or appraisal method), studies of adults who use cannabis point in different directions on heart attack, stroke and other heart and blood-vessel disease, and the AHA writing group judged the evidence still inconclusive (Page et al., 2020). In the hour after use, the risk of a heart attack starting was 4.8 times that at other times in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, an estimate printed without an interval that rests on few exposed people (9 had smoked cannabis within an hour of presenting with the heart attack, by the statement's account) (Mittleman et al., 2001, as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015, calls it a quadrupling). Two surveys found more stroke: past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, 2.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related factors including tobacco smoking, with the excess confined to weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7; adjustment not stated) (Hemachandra et al., 2016); and among adults aged 18 to 44, use went with an adjusted OR for stroke of 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Parekh et al., 2020; adjustment set not stated). Health-record and hospital databases report more heart attacks where cannabis use is recorded, for example 1.37% against 0.54% over 3 years (about 14 against 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion; RR 2.53, adjustment not stated; Chami & Kim, 2019), but the statement warns that samples of hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias. Against these, in the CARDIA cohort (5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start, followed for more than 25 years) cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., 2017; no estimates printed). After a heart attack the findings run both ways: long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; adjustment not stated; Frost et al., 2013), while among 2,097 young adults treated for a heart attack at two academic hospitals, all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were higher (adjusted HR 1.99 and 2.22; no intervals printed) in people who used cocaine and marijuana, as the statement's table words it, which does not isolate cannabis (DeFilippis et al., 2018). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate, to which healthy young adults quickly become tolerant, and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; the angina finding also in Page et al., 2020). The statement names short-term, observational and retrospective designs, poorly measured exposure, recall bias, low-risk cohorts and confounding by tobacco as the main weaknesses, and judges the evidence for people with cardiac risk factors insufficient; Hall (2015) concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does cannabis cause heart attacks or strokes? This has not been shown. In one study, a heart attack was more likely to start in the hour after using cannabis, and two surveys found more strokes, mostly in people who used cannabis every week or more. Hospital records also show more heart attacks in people who use cannabis, but these records are hard to interpret. A study that followed young adults for over 25 years found no link with heart disease or stroke. In lab studies, cannabis raised heart rate and brought on chest pain (angina) in people with heart disease. The American Heart Association called the evidence inconclusive. These figures come from reviews, not from the studies themselves, and the studies could not fully separate cannabis from tobacco. See the contested question.
population: Adults in studies relayed by an American Heart Association statement and narrative reviews: people with a heart attack (a US case-crossover study and its follow-up), population survey samples, US hospital and health-record databases, and young US adults in the CARDIA cohort
exposure: Cannabis use as each relayed study recorded it: use in the hour before a heart attack (case-crossover); past-year use, weekly or more, or more than 10 days a month (stroke surveys); recorded use or diagnosis codes (hospital databases); cumulative lifetime and recent use (CARDIA)
comparator: The same people at other times (case-crossover); people without reported or recorded use in the same survey, cohort or database; placebo in laboratory studies
outcome: Onset of heart attack; stroke or transient ischaemic attack; heart attacks in hospital records; new cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease and cardiac death; death after a heart attack; heart rate and angina
magnitude: All second-hand. Case-crossover (Mittleman et al. 2001, 3,882 people with a heart attack): onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use (no interval; 9 people had smoked cannabis within 1 hour of presentation); follow-up of 1,913: mortality over 3.8 years 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009, without intervals; the AHA statement says many mortality findings of these smaller follow-up studies did not reach statistical significance). Stroke: Hemachandra et al. 2016, past-year use, rate ratio 3.3 (1.8 to 6.3) before and 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1 to 10.7) for weekly or more frequent use; Parekh et al. 2020, adults aged 18 to 44, adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, and, for that frequent use together with combustible-cigarette use, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97), and with e-cigarette use, 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46), each against people who did not use cannabis. Databases: Chami & Kim 2019, 3-year heart-attack incidence 1.37% vs 0.54% (about 14 vs 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion), RR 2.53 (2.45 to 2.61); Desai et al. 2019, heart-attack admissions of young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%. CARDIA (Reis et al. 2017, 5,113 adults, over 25 years): no association, no estimates printed. After a heart attack: Frost et al. 2013, mortality 29% higher, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.05, P = 0.28; DeFilippis et al. 2018, 2,097 young adults, adjusted HR 1.99 (all-cause) and 2.22 (cardiovascular) among people who used cocaine and marijuana, no intervals; Johnson-Sasso et al. 2018, mortality OR 0.79 (short-term outcomes by the reference title; no interval or adjustment printed). Laboratory: exercise time to angina 48% shorter after one cannabis cigarette than after placebo.

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable at the level of the primary studies: the AHA statement gives no search, selection rule or appraisal (card sc_page_2020: overall high) and the narrative reviews are unsystematic (cards sc_hall_2009, sc_hall_2015, sc_volkow_2014). The relayed studies are mostly hospital databases with selection bias, surveys with self-reported use and case reports, with adjustment unstated in most and tobacco use inadequately handled, as the statement itself says.

inconsistency.note: The long prospective cohort found no association while the case-crossover, survey and database studies did; outcomes after a heart attack run both ways (non-significantly higher long-term mortality, lower in-hospital mortality); one case-crossover estimate is given as 4.8 times, a quadrupling and 3–4-fold by the reviews.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: every figure is a review's account of studies not read here (METHODS §6.3), and several rows of the statement's table cannot be right as printed (card sc_page_2020, reporting issues).

imprecision.note: The trigger estimate rests on few exposed people (9 had used within an hour of presentation, by the statement's account) and has no interval; stroke intervals are wide (2.1 to 10.7; 1.08 to 3.10); the CARDIA null is printed without estimates, so its precision is unknown; the mortality hazard ratios after a heart attack have no intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources.

large_effect.note: The 4.8-fold trigger estimate rests on few exposed people, without an interval or adjustment; no upgrade.

dose_response.note: Gradients by frequency (mortality after a heart attack; stroke with weekly or more frequent use) come second-hand from single studies without stated adjustment, and the AHA statement says many of the mortality findings did not reach statistical significance; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence seen only through reviews starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision: very low, the floor. Overlapping sources are counted once: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and the AHA statement relay the same case-crossover study, and its mortality follow-ups (the 1,913-person study and Frost et al., 2013) come from the same onset study, so the trigger, the mortality gradient and the non-significant long-term mortality are not independent; the statement's inpatient analyses largely share one database. Contested because credible designs disagree (the long cohort against the trigger, survey and database studies; after a heart attack, a non-significant excess, a lower short-term mortality and a higher mortality in people who used cocaine and marijuana) and the reviews read the same evidence differently (still inconclusive for the AHA; probable for middle-aged adults in Hall, 2015). The claim rests only on second-hand sources (a professional statement without a stated search, and narrative reviews), so it stays at draft and says so (METHODS §6.3).

debate.question: Does using cannabis raise the risk of heart attack, stroke or other heart and blood-vessel disease?
debate.evidence_yes: In a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, the risk of onset in the 60 minutes after cannabis use was 4.8 times baseline; 37 had smoked cannabis within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of presentation (Mittleman et al., 2001, as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), and in a follow-up of 1,913 of them mortality over 3.8 years rose with frequency of use, 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, without intervals; the AHA statement says many mortality findings of these smaller follow-up studies did not reach statistical significance). Among 2,097 young adults treated for a heart attack at two academic hospitals, adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause and cardiovascular death were 1.99 and 2.22 among people who used cocaine and marijuana, as the statement's table words it (DeFilippis et al., 2018, as relayed by Page et al., 2020). In a population survey, past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack and a rate ratio of 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment that included tobacco, the excess lying in weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7); in a US survey of adults aged 18 to 44 the adjusted OR for stroke was 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Hemachandra et al., 2016, and Parekh et al., 2020, both as relayed by Page et al., 2020). A health-record database found a 3-year incidence of heart attack of 1.37% against 0.54% (RR 2.53, 2.45 to 2.61), an inpatient database found heart-attack admissions of young adults of 0.23% against 0.14% among people using cannabis without other substances, and a systematic review of studies and case reports found that 28 of 33 studies suggested a higher risk of both acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease (all as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease, exercise time to angina falling by 48% against placebo in one. Hall (2015) reads the evidence as consistent with adverse cardiovascular effects in middle-aged and older adults, adds a French series of cannabis-related hospitalisations that included heart attacks and a fatal stroke in young adults with no other known risk factors, and concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack; Volkow et al. (2014) describe use as associated with vascular conditions that raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication.
debate.evidence_no: In the CARDIA cohort, 5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the 1985–1986 baseline and followed for more than 25 years, cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020), and in the same cohort higher aortic and coronary calcium went with cannabis only in people who had ever smoked tobacco (Auer et al., 3,498 participants). After a heart attack, long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; 3,886 patients; Frost et al.), and in hospital records of more than 1.2 million heart-attack patients a composite outcome (death, balloon pump, ventilation, cardiac arrest or shock) was not associated with cannabis use and mortality was lower (OR 0.79, no interval; short-term outcomes by the reference title; Johnson-Sasso et al.). The AHA statement warns that studies restricted to hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias, so cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation is uncertain; that most data are short-term, observational and retrospective, with poorly determined exposure, recall bias and low-risk cohorts; and that tobacco and other drug use are inadequately handled in data collection and adjustment; citing a review of cannabis arteritis, it gives 97% as the share of people who smoke cannabis who also smoke tobacco. The 4.8-fold trigger estimate has no printed interval and rests on few exposed people, the 4.7 estimate for weekly use has no stated adjustment, the higher mortality after a heart attack in young adults is given for cocaine and marijuana use together, and the database estimates are crude or silent on adjustment (Page et al., 2020). The AHA writing group judges the evidence still inconclusive overall and insufficient for people with cardiac risk factors.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether cannabis itself causes any of these events: none of the relayed studies convincingly separates cannabis from tobacco, which most people who smoke cannabis also use, or from other drugs, and none is a sibling comparison or a genetically informed design. The case-crossover design removes stable differences between people, but it concerns the minutes to hours after use and rests on few exposed people and on their recall of timing, while CARDIA concerns decades of use in young adults with few events, so the two results need not conflict. Whether results from smoked cannabis apply to eating or vaping it, and whether older studies apply to today's stronger products, which the statement itself questions. How large any risk is for a given person: no source gives absolute rates by age and baseline risk. All figures here are second-hand, and several rows of the statement's own table cannot be right as printed (card sc_page_2020).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From second-hand sources only: the clearest signal is short-lived, a higher chance of a heart attack starting in the hour after use, from one case-crossover study with few exposed people (Mittleman et al., 2001, as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015), together with laboratory evidence that cannabis raises heart rate and can bring on angina in people with heart disease (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Page et al., 2020). Signals for stroke come from two surveys and lie mainly in frequent use (Page et al., 2020); the hospital-database associations are hard to read because of selection bias, unstated adjustment and tobacco (Page et al., 2020). The one long cohort of young adults found no association with new heart disease or stroke over 25 years (Page et al., 2020), which fits a short-lived trigger as well as no effect, because such a cohort has few events. After a heart attack the relayed findings run both ways: the higher-mortality estimate in young adults does not separate cannabis from cocaine (Page et al., 2020), and a rise in mortality with frequency of use in a smaller follow-up is relayed without intervals (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015). The AHA judges the evidence inconclusive and, for people with cardiac risk factors, insufficient (Page et al., 2020), and the editors agree that no long-term risk figure can be given from these sources. The primary studies themselves have not been read for this page.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Large prospective cohorts, or a pooled analysis of existing ones, with repeated measures of how often, by which route and how strong the cannabis used is, and of tobacco, analysed separately in people who have never smoked tobacco, with confirmed heart attacks, strokes, rhythm problems and cardiac deaths and absolute risks by age and baseline risk; case-crossover studies with objectively timed use; sibling or genetically informed designs; and a systematic review with a stated search and risk-of-bias appraisal to bring them together (the AHA statement calls for carefully designed prospective short- and long-term studies).

statement: In people who use cannabis, using it more often and starting younger are associated with a higher share meeting criteria for dependence in the figures that narrative reviews cite, but most of these figures are second-hand and rest on different designs and definitions, and in the one national survey analysis read that adjusted for other disorders, starting early went with a lower, not a higher, hazard of dependence. By frequency of use (second-hand): 17.0% of people who smoked cannabis weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021, which also calls this almost 1 in 19, although 9.7% is about 1 in 10); about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people who use daily (a UN report cited by Connor et al., 2021); 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (two reviews cited by the same review); half of people who use daily, from a 3-year prospective study (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015; its title refers to frequent use); and 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily, cited to a review that does not contain the figure (Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), so it cannot be traced, and repeated without a citation in a 2020 professional statement (Page et al., 2020). No definitions or adjustment are given with these figures. By age of first use (second-hand): one in six of people who start in adolescence, against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, citing a 2006 book chapter for both figures; Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt for one in six, with 17% in its table, and the 2001-05 survey analysis for 9%); people who start in adolescence about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start as adults to have dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014); and first use before 16 linked to a higher risk and faster progression (Connor et al., 2021, citing three sources). In the 1990-92 US National Comorbidity Survey, by age at interview rather than age at first use, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of people aged 15 to 24 who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), against 8.1% at 25 to 34, 8.5% at 35 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years in which to become dependent; the authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used, and note that differences between age groups may also reflect birth cohort, period and drug availability, and that deaths linked to dependence remove dependent people from older groups (Anthony et al., 1994). In the 2001-05 US NESARC (7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence; recalled ages), first use before 14, compared with first use at 14 or later, went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (hazard ratio 2.47) and a lower one in the adjusted model (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), a model that stepwise selection built from sex, age, race or ethnicity, mood, anxiety and personality disorders, and dependence on nicotine, alcohol and cocaine (mood disorders, 2.69, and cocaine dependence, 4.14, among others, went with higher hazards); the authors suggest that the transition may come less from early onset itself than from the psychiatric and substance use disorders that go with it, and that people who start later may use more intensely and find cannabis easier to get (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). Because that model also adjusted for disorders that may have begun after first use, the reversal does not show that starting early protects against dependence (editors' reading). In a 3-year prospective study, measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016, which calls its sample people who used daily; its title refers to frequent use), and twin studies find shared genetic and environmental influences on starting early (Connor et al., 2021). None of the sources measured how much THC people took, and, in the editors' reading, frequent use is partly built into what dependence means (its criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using), so the two are hard to separate. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Reviews report that people who use cannabis more often are more likely to be dependent: figures for people who use daily run from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2, depending on the study, and one often-quoted figure (25 to 50 in 100) cannot be traced to any study. Reviews also say about 1 in 6 people who start as teenagers become dependent, against about 1 in 10 of everyone who has used. But in a large US survey, starting before age 14 went with more dependence only until other mental health and drug problems were taken into account; after that, it went with less. That does not mean starting early protects: some of those problems may have come after people started. So it is not clear whether starting young itself raises the risk or whether people who start young are at higher risk for other reasons. Most of these numbers are second-hand, and none of these studies can show cause. See the contested question.
population: People who use cannabis: US national survey samples (1990-92, ages 15 to 54; 2001-05, adults who had used) and the cohorts and surveys cited by narrative reviews for frequency and age of onset (definitions often not given)
exposure: Frequency of use (weekly, daily, regular, a history of daily use, frequent use, as each source defined it) and age at first use (adolescence, before 16, before 14); in one survey, age at interview
comparator: People who use less often or started later; in the 1990-92 survey, older age groups at interview
outcome: Cannabis dependence (DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, or as the cited studies defined it; dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use in one study)
magnitude: Second-hand frequency figures: 17.0% weekly and 19.0% daily meeting dependence criteria; 9.7% of weekly smokers without dependence dependent within a year (Cougle 2016 via Connor 2021); about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people using daily (UN report via Connor 2021); 30-40% with a history of daily use (two reviews via Connor 2021); half of people using daily (van der Pol 2013 via Hall 2015); 25-50% of daily smokers (Volkow 2014, not traceable; repeated without a citation by Page 2020). Second-hand age figures: one in six with adolescent onset (book chapter via Hall 2009 and Hall 2015; 17% in Volkow 2014 Table 1); 2-4 times dependence symptoms within 2 years, adolescent against adult onset (Chen 2009 via Volkow 2014). NCS 1990-92 by age at interview, DSM-III-R dependence among people who had used: 15-24, 15.3% (SE 2.3); 25-34, 8.1% (0.7); 35-44, 8.5% (1.3); 45-54, 3.1% (1.5). NESARC 2001-05, first use before 14 (1,051 people, unweighted) against 14 or later (6,339): unadjusted HR 2.47 (95% CI 2.0 to 3.1); adjusted 0.63 (0.5 to 0.9); in the adjusted model male sex 1.44, age 18-29 3.09 and 30-44 2.46 (against 45 or older), mood disorder 2.69, anxiety disorder 2.31, personality disorder 2.30, nicotine dependence 2.06, alcohol dependence 2.55, cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3 to 7.6).

indirectness.note: Most figures are second-hand (narrative reviews; the studies behind them not read here, one a book chapter and one figure untraceable); the 1990-92 age groups are ages at interview, not at first use; DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence, not DSM-5 use disorder; frequency categories undefined.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately: most figures carry no interval, which is part of the second-hand problem; the one adjusted estimate (0.63, 0.5 to 0.9) excludes 1.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. Not upgraded for a dose-response gradient: the frequency gradient is second-hand, mostly cross-sectional and partly built into the outcome. Rated as worded, an association; whether frequent or early use causes dependence is the question in the debate box. Overlap: the one-in-six figure reaches three reviews from one source (a 2006 book chapter by the first author of the 1990-92 survey), Hall (2015) repeats Hall & Degenhardt (2009), and one 3-year study (van der Pol et al., 2013) is cited by two reviews for different findings (half of people using daily became dependent, Hall 2015; measures of use did not predict transition, Curran et al. 2016), so these are not independent replications. Status contested: for age of first use, crude figures and an adjusted national analysis point in opposite directions.

debate.question: Does using cannabis more often, or starting it younger, make dependence more likely, or do the people who use often or start young differ in other ways that explain the link?
debate.evidence_yes: Every source that reports dependence by frequency finds more in people who use more often: 17.0% of people who smoked weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021); a UN report gives about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people who use daily, and two reviews 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (all as cited by Connor et al., 2021); and a 3-year prospective study is cited for half of people using daily (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015), against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (see the claim on how many people become dependent). For age of starting, reviews give one in six of people who start in adolescence (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Volkow et al., 2014), describe people who start in adolescence as 2 to 4 times as likely as adult starters to show dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014), and cite first use before 16 as raising the risk and speeding progression (Connor et al., 2021). In the 1990-92 US survey, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of 15- to 24-year-olds who had used cannabis had ever been dependent, against 8.1% to 8.5% at 25 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years at risk, and its authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used (Anthony et al., 1994). Reviews also name concurrent tobacco use and male sex as risk factors (Curran et al., 2016).
debate.evidence_no: In the one national analysis read that modelled age of first use together with other risk factors (NESARC, 2001-05; 7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence), first use before 14 went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (2.47) but a lower one in a model chosen by stepwise selection that kept sex, age, race or ethnicity, mood, anxiety and personality disorders and dependence on nicotine, alcohol and cocaine (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), while mood disorders (2.69) and cocaine dependence (4.14) went with higher hazards; the authors suggest that the transition may come less from early onset itself than from the disorders that go with it, and that later starters may use more intensely and find cannabis easier to get (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). A 3-year prospective study found that measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016). Twin studies show genetic influence on starting early after allowing for other substance use, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety, and shared genetic or environmental factors contribute to early onset (Connor et al., 2021); a review names poor school achievement, deviant behaviour, rebelliousness, poor relationships with parents and parents' drug and alcohol problems as marking higher risk (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). The widely quoted 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily is cited to a review that does not contain it (Volkow et al., 2014) and is repeated without a citation in a 2020 professional statement (Page et al., 2020), and the age-group figures from the 1990-92 survey are by age at interview, not age at first use, and may also reflect birth cohort, period, availability and deaths in older groups (Anthony et al., 1994).
debate.neither_can_show: Whether frequent or early use causes dependence: in every source people chose how often to use and when to start, most figures reach us through narrative reviews, and the sources behind one in six (a book chapter) and 25 to 50% (untraceable) cannot be checked here. Frequency and dependence are entangled: the dependence criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using (Curran et al., 2016, Box 3), so people may use more often because they are dependent. Ages of first use and of onset were recalled, sometimes decades later. Adjusting for other psychiatric and substance use disorders removes confounding where those disorders came first, but where they followed cannabis use it may also remove part of a real effect (editors' point; the NESARC models entered mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders as time-varying). None of the sources measured how much THC people took (Connor et al., 2021).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). More frequent use goes with more dependence in every source that reports it, but the size depends on design and definition (from about 1 in 5 to about 1 in 2 of people using daily; Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021; van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015), most figures are second-hand, and one widely quoted figure cannot be traced (Page et al., 2020; Volkow et al., 2014). For age of starting, the crude figures point to more dependence in early starters (Connor et al., 2021; Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011; Volkow et al., 2014), but the one national analysis that adjusted for other disorders found the opposite (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011), which fits early starting being a marker of other risks at least as well as a cause; because that analysis also adjusted for disorders that may follow early use, it does not show that early starting protects, and the evidence read here does not settle which reading is right.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that follow people from before first use, with repeated DSM-5 assessments and measured THC exposure (standard units and product strength), reporting the cumulative probability of use disorder by frequency, age of first use and product, with psychiatric problems dated before and after first use; and sibling or co-twin comparisons of early and late starters.

statement: In published cases of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, again and again, in people who use cannabis regularly), pooled descriptively in a systematic review of reports from 2000 to September 2015 (Sorensen et al., 2017; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 211 patients from 80 case reports and 7 case series, 98 of them from one series entered as summary figures; no randomized trials, no comparison groups and no count of how many people who use cannabis develop the syndrome), all patients had recurrent vomiting with severe nausea and 85.1% had abdominal pain; 154 of 211 (72.9%) were men; among the 113 patients with individual data, the median age was 16 at first cannabis use (IQR 14 to 18; 84 patients), 24 at the start of symptoms (19 to 29; 101) and 28 at diagnosis (22 to 34; 111). Of the 197 whose frequency of use was reported, 76.6% used cannabis daily or more often and 97.4% at least weekly (the reviewers counted reports of heavy use as daily and of frequent use as weekly), and 45 of 179 (25.1%) had used for a year or less before symptoms began. Of the patients whose bathing was reported, 157 of 170 (92.3%) found that hot baths or showers relieved their symptoms. Of the 64 patients whose stopping was documented, 62 (96.8%) had complete resolution of symptoms; the two without resolution had no urine test to confirm that they had stopped, and all 21 patients who kept using still had symptoms. The review's tables differ on the details: its main table counts relief after abstinence or reduction and places one of the two patients without resolution in a case series rather than in the case reports the text cites, and another table describes a patient in the 98-patient series who did not improve despite reported abstinence, a patient the main table leaves out of the count. Follow-up was documented for only 85 of the 211 patients (40.2%), no time to resolution is reported although it was among the data to be collected, and whether symptoms returned when people started again was too inconsistently documented to count, although in one series all 3 patients who used cannabis again after a period without it became ill again. The review proposes recognising the syndrome by severe cyclic vomiting, usually with abdominal pain, at least weekly cannabis use before symptoms began, temporary relief with hot bathing and resolution after stopping, with male sex, starting cannabis in the teenage years and symptoms beginning in the twenties as supporting features; these features come from cases diagnosed by them, so their frequencies do not show how well they separate the syndrome from other causes of repeated vomiting, which no study in the review tested. In second-hand surveys of patients diagnosed with cyclic vomiting syndrome, 72% of 31 and 67% of 437 also used hot showers for relief, although many of them used cannabis (42% daily to weekly in the first; 81% in the second). Diagnosis came on average 4.1 years (SD 4.6) after symptoms began, and in four case reports patients first diagnosed with severe vomiting of pregnancy, whose cyclic vomiting had begun before the pregnancy, were later diagnosed with the syndrome. A 2021 review says the distinction from other cyclic vomiting disorders is underdeveloped and gives 90% of patients as reporting that hot baths and stopping cannabis relieve their symptoms, citing a 2019 clinical review and Sorensen et al. (2017) itself and merging two features that the systematic review counts separately (Connor et al., 2021; second-hand), and a 2014 review links repeated use with increased vomiting without a citation (Volkow et al., 2014). All nine proposed mechanisms were rated very low, and three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids; acute hospital treatments are covered in the claims on capsaicin cream and on dopamine-blocking medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome means bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, usually with belly pain, in people who use cannabis regularly. In 211 published cases, about three in four used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before the bouts began, and most found that hot baths or showers eased the symptoms for a while, though many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too. Of the 64 cases where stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better, and the 21 people who kept using did not. These are published cases only: nobody knows from them how common the syndrome is, fewer than half of the cases had any follow-up written down, and the signs used to recognise it come from the same cases, so how well they tell it apart from other vomiting illnesses has not been tested. On average it took about 4 years from the first symptoms to the diagnosis.
population: Patients with a clinician's diagnosis of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome described in published case reports and case series, 2000 to 2015 (211 patients; 72.9% men; median age at diagnosis 28)
exposure: Regular cannabis use as reported in each case (frequency known for 197, duration for 179); three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids
comparator: None (case descriptions); for resolution, patients who stopped compared with those who kept using
outcome: Features of the syndrome as recorded; relief with hot bathing; resolution of symptoms after stopping cannabis
magnitude: Sorensen 2017 cumulative synthesis (211 patients; each share is of the patients in whom the feature was reported): recurrent vomiting 100% (211); severe nausea and vomiting 100% (211); abdominal pain 85.1% (202); relief with hot bathing 92.3% (157 of 170); resolution after stopping 96.8% (62 of 64; all 21 who kept using had ongoing symptoms); at least weekly use 97.4% (197); daily or more 76.6% (197); regular use for more than a year 74.8% (179); men 72.9% (154 of 211). Duration of use before onset (179): 1 year or less 25.1%, 2-5 years 36.3%, 6-10 years 16.8%, 11 years or more 21.8%. Median ages, from the 113 patients with individual data: first use 16 (IQR 14-18; 84), onset 24 (19-29; 101), diagnosis 28 (22-34; 111). Mean delay to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6). Follow-up documented for 85 of 211 (40.2%). One series: all 3 patients who resumed after abstinence relapsed. Second-hand, cyclic vomiting syndrome surveys: hot showers used by 72% of 31 (42% using cannabis daily to weekly) and 67% of 437 (81% using cannabis).

risk_of_bias.note: Published case reports and series chosen by clinicians who decided to report them, often cases resembling the first description; the features counted are those used to make the diagnosis; outcomes documented for a minority (stopping for 64, any follow-up for 85 of 211) and abstinence not verified; no risk-of-bias tool applied by the review (card sc_sorensen_2017, AMSTAR 2 critically low).

inconsistency.note: The case reports and series describe the same features; some series' numbers differ between the review's text and tables (card reporting issues), which does not change the picture.

indirectness.note: Published, mostly hospital-diagnosed cases cannot stand for everyone who develops the syndrome, and the case features answer how it is recognised only as descriptions, not as tested diagnostic criteria.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately; the floor is reached.

publication_bias.note: Selection into publication is counted under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Case reports and series are observational and start low; down two levels for risk of bias (selection, circular diagnosis, incomplete follow-up) and one for indirectness: very low, the floor. Status replicated: the same picture (recurrent vomiting with regular use, relief with hot water, resolution after stopping) comes from many case reports and several series by different teams, though they reach the claim through one review and the series inside it are not counted again (card sc_sorensen_2017). Connor et al. (2021) take their 90% from a 2019 clinical review and from Sorensen et al. (2017) itself, so it is not separate evidence. The resolution figure describes documented cases, not what happens to everyone who stops, and the review's own tables differ on its details.

statement: As summarised in a 2007 narrative review of controlled-administration studies, most of them small, often with single doses of low-THC cigarettes or of oral THC given by researchers, many from the author's own laboratory and with participants' sex given for only a few of them (Huestis, 2007; figures second-hand; no systematic search), smoked THC, compared with THC taken by mouth, is associated with THC reaching the blood within minutes rather than hours, with higher and earlier peaks, and after frequent or heavy use THC and its breakdown products remained detectable for days to weeks. Smoked: in 6 people (the review does not give their sex) who smoked single cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC (about 16 and 34 mg; study conditions), THC appeared in plasma with the first puff, peaked at a mean of 84.3 and 162.2 ng/ml at 9.0 minutes, fell to about 60% and 20% of the peak 15 and 30 minutes after smoking, and was 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours, staying detectable (at 0.5 ng/ml) for 3 to 12 hours after the lower and 6 to 27 hours after the higher dose; the strongest effects came later, 30 to 45 minutes after smoking began, when blood levels were already falling. How much of the THC in a cigarette reached the blood varied with how people smoked, from 2% to 56% across studies (about 8% to 24% in others, depending strongly on experience with smoking cannabis). By mouth: THC was absorbed more slowly, with lower, later and more irregular peaks; after 20 mg of THC in a chocolate cookie, plasma peaks of 4.4 to 11 ng/ml came 1 to 5 hours after eating, with about 6% of the dose reaching the blood, and a study using a radiolabel method, which the author says overestimated THC, found peaks about 4 to 6 hours after 15 to 20 mg in oil; the review puts oral bioavailability at 4% to 20%, because THC is partly broken down in the stomach and much of it is converted in the liver, among other products into 11-OH-THC, which is active and reaches levels similar to or higher than those of THC after oral intake, against about a tenth of THC after smoking. In the studies described, effects after oral THC began later and lasted longer than after smoking. THC is almost entirely bound to lipoproteins in the blood (95% to 99%) and is stored in body fat; in people who use frequently, its final plasma half-life was about 4.1 days in a study with long sampling (24 to 36 hours in studies with shorter sampling), which the review attributes to storage in and slow release from fat, and THC-COOH, the breakdown product that urine tests measure, had a plasma half-life of up to 12.6 days in one person; the review notes that no pharmacokinetic differences between frequent and occasional use have been substantiated. Plasma: in people who use frequently, low levels remained at least 12 hours after last use (THC 0.86 ng/ml on average in one study; whole-blood levels are about half those in plasma), and after people who used chronically smoked four cigarettes containing labelled THC, a very sensitive method detected it in blood for up to 13 days. Urine: after one smoked cigarette (6 people), the last positive sample for THC-COOH at a cut-off of 15 ng/ml came an average of 33.7 hours (8 to 68.5) after the 1.75% and 88.6 hours (57 to 122.3) after the 3.55% cigarette, with positive and negative samples alternating near the cut-off, while the urine of a person new to cannabis may test negative within a few hours of one cigarette; one person who had used heavily for more than 10 years still tested positive (above 20 ng/ml) 67 days after last use, a case the review calls extreme, and in another person with heavy use cannabinoids were detectable in urine for 93 days (no cut-off given). A positive urine test shows that a person was exposed, not when, how much, by which route or whether they were impaired. These studies predate today's stronger products, edibles, vaporizers and concentrates, gave fixed doses and, where the review gives participants' sex, mostly involved men, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small lab studies from before 2007, in which people smoked weak cannabis cigarettes, THC in the blood was highest within minutes of smoking (at about 9 minutes) and fell to low levels within 2 hours, while the felt effects were strongest a little later, at 30 to 45 minutes. When THC was taken by mouth, it entered the blood slowly and at lower levels, peaking 1 to 6 hours later, and the effects began later and lasted longer. THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly; in people who use often, it could still be found for days to weeks. After one cigarette, the last positive urine test came about 1 to 4 days later on average, and the urine of someone new to cannabis may test negative within hours; in one person who had used heavily for years, urine was still positive after 67 days, and in another, cannabis could be found for 93 days. A positive test shows use, not when, how much or whether someone was impaired. The studies gave set doses, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more.
population: People given cannabis or THC in small controlled-administration studies summarised by a 2007 narrative review (6 people, sex not given, in the main smoking and urine studies; 17 volunteers in a capsule study; where the review gives participants' sex, mostly men), and single case reports of heavy long-term use
exposure: Single smoked cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC (about 16 and 34 mg) or oral THC (20 mg in a cookie; 15 to 20 mg in oil; a 10 mg dronabinol capsule), given by researchers (study conditions only); frequent or heavy long-term use for elimination and detection windows
