statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how much, cannabis use causes psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. The association with later psychosis is consistent and stronger with frequent use (see the answer on how often people use), but in the studies read a substantial part of it shrinks when measured confounders are taken into account, and genetically informed studies suggest that a further part reflects shared family or genetic liability, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely; none of these designs excludes a causal contribution, and none measures the effect of daily or high-potency use (the genetic studies concern ever trying cannabis, the co-relative study cannabis misuse). Adjustment for each cohort's measured confounders removed on average about 45% (10% to 80%) of the crude excess odds in seven cohorts, for exposure contrasts the review does not state (Moore et al., 2007). In the one co-relative study, a Swedish national registry study (as Ksir & Hart, 2016, describe it) described in a viewpoint whose second author co-wrote it (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), the odds ratio for schizophrenia with cannabis misuse fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and to 3.52 (3.92 in the viewpoint's table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, with no significance test at the twin level and the adjustment set not stated; an earlier cross-sectional sibling-pair study, by contrast, is described as arguing against stable family confounding (Gage et al., 2016). Three two-sample Mendelian randomization studies used genetic variants for having ever used cannabis, which explain about 1% or less of the variation in ever use where this is reported and, in two of the studies, did not reach genome-wide significance, with no adjustment beyond the source studies in the main analyses. The odds ratio for schizophrenia by genetic liability to ever use was 1.04 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.07) per doubling of the odds of ever use, a smaller step than one unit of log odds, and 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by the pleiotropy-robust MR-Egger method (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, which its authors rescale to 1.37 for ever against never use (Vaucher et al., 2018); and, per unit of log odds, 1.04 (p = 0.81) with five genome-wide significant variants or 1.10 (0.99 to 1.21) with 69 variants below that threshold, whose inverse-variance and weighted-median estimates did not reach significance (p = 0.074 and 0.156) while the outlier-filtered GSMR estimate, with 74 variants, did (1.21, p = 0.017) (Pasman et al., 2018). In the reverse direction, genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, Pasman et al., 2018), although the MR-Egger estimates in this direction were imprecise and included no effect (1.17, 0.96 to 1.43; 1.07, p = 0.81), and the genetic correlation between ever use and schizophrenia was 0.25 (Pasman et al., 2018, as corrected). These three studies share consortium data and are not independent, and their authors read them differently: one as strongly supporting a causal role of cannabis use (Vaucher et al., 2018), the other two as weak evidence in that direction and stronger evidence for the reverse (Gage et al., 2017; Pasman et al., 2018). The 2007 systematic review read its cohorts as consistent with an increased risk independent of the confounders measured and as enough to warn young people (Moore et al., 2007); later reviews and a viewpoint read the evidence available to them as shared vulnerability (Ksir & Hart, 2016), as partly causal with an appreciable non-causal share (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), or as strong enough for public-health messages that cannabis can increase the risk (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016, which calls cannabis a component cause). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does cannabis cause psychosis? This has not been shown either way. People who use cannabis, especially often, are more likely to develop psychosis, but about half of that link shrank, on average, once other differences between people were taken into account. In a Swedish study of relatives, the link got smaller the more closely related two people were, but it was still there between identical twins, though nobody checked whether that could be chance. Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia go with a higher chance of trying cannabis; evidence that genes linked to trying cannabis go with schizophrenia was weaker. None of the gene studies looked at daily or strong cannabis. The researchers who did these studies, and experts reading them, disagree. See the contested question.
population: People in general-population cohorts, a national registry and first-episode case-control samples, and people of mostly European ancestry in genome-wide consortium data (International Cannabis Consortium, UK Biobank and 23andMe for cannabis use; Psychiatric Genomics Consortium schizophrenia cases and controls)
exposure: Cannabis use (self-reported ever or frequent use; cannabis misuse in the co-relative study, a national registry study); in Mendelian randomization, genetic liability to having ever used cannabis
comparator: People who had not used cannabis; full siblings and identical co-twins discordant for misuse; people with lower genetic liability
outcome: Psychotic disorder or schizophrenia caused by cannabis use; and, in the reverse direction, ever using cannabis predicted by genetic liability to schizophrenia
magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Attenuation of the crude association by each cohort's adjustment: about 45% on average (10% to 80%; exposure contrasts not stated) (Moore et al., 2007). Co-relative (one registry study, misuse): OR 10.44 in the general population, 5.07 in full siblings, 3.52 or 3.92 in discordant identical twins (untested). Mendelian randomization, liability to ever use on schizophrenia: 1.04 (1.01–1.07) per doubling of the odds, MR-Egger 1.01 (0.93–1.10), 12 variants 1.03 (0.99–1.08) (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02–1.14) per unit of log odds, rescaled 1.37 (1.09–1.67) ever vs never, 1.41 (1.09–1.83) adjusted for the variants' associations with ever smoking (Vaucher et al., 2018); per unit of log odds, 1.04 (p = 0.81) with 5 genome-wide significant variants, 1.10 (0.99–1.21) with 69 variants at p < 10^-5, GSMR after outlier filtering (74 variants) 1.21 (p = 0.017) (Pasman et al., 2018). Liability to schizophrenia on ever use: 1.10 (1.05–1.14) per doubling, MR-Egger 1.17 (0.96–1.43) (Gage et al., 2017); 1.16 (1.06–1.27) per unit, MR-Egger SIMEX 1.07 (p = 0.81) (Pasman et al., 2018). Genetic correlation rg 0.25 (SE 0.03).

risk_of_bias.note: Cohort and case-control estimates remain open to residual confounding (family history, genetic liability and childhood adversity were rarely measured) and to use during an unrecognized early phase of the illness (cards sc_moore_2007, sc_di_forti_2019, sc_di_forti_2015). Mendelian randomization is observational too: the genetic design addresses confounding by environmental and social factors and, for the forward estimate, reverse causation, but its instruments are weak (0.15% to about 1% of the variance in ever use), may reach schizophrenia through other paths (risk-taking and impulsivity; only ever smoking was tested, in one study) and come from overlapping samples (cards sc_gage_2017, sc_vaucher_2018, sc_pasman_2018: ROBINS-E high for the forward estimates; the reverse estimates, from instruments for schizophrenia liability, were judged some concerns on cards sc_gage_2017 and sc_pasman_2018). The sensitivity analyses reported (MR-Egger intercepts near zero but with little power, I² 67% in one study; similar weighted-median estimates; stable leave-one-out results; no change after adjusting for ever smoking) do not justify leaving confounding unrated.

inconsistency.note: The designs point in different directions: the forward genetic estimates are positive in one study, small and method-dependent in a second and inconclusive in a third, while both studies that tested the reverse direction found it; the co-relative decline and the persistence of the cohort associations after adjustment are read in opposite ways by the critical reviews.

indirectness.note: The genetic instruments index liability to ever trying cannabis, not frequent, heavy or high-potency use, where the observational associations are largest; the co-relative study concerns registry-recorded misuse; most cohort outcomes are symptoms rather than diagnosed disorder; several figures are known only through narrative reviews.

imprecision.note: The identical-twin odds ratio was not tested for significance, and the forward genetic estimates have intervals from no effect to small effects (MR-Egger 0.93 to 1.10; 69 variants 0.99 to 1.21).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for the genetic studies; the cohort pools showed no small-study signal, with little power (card sc_moore_2007).

dose_response.note: The gradient with frequency is reported in the answer on how often people use; it is not used to upgrade a causal claim because a gradient of use carries gradients of confounders and the genetic designs do not address frequency.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence, Mendelian randomization included, starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Counted once: the three Mendelian randomization studies share the International Cannabis Consortium exposure data (Pasman et al.'s genome-wide study includes it) and Psychiatric Genomics Consortium outcome data, so their agreement in the reverse direction is not independent replication; the co-relative figures are one registry study seen through a viewpoint by one of its authors, and the same study is read differently by Ksir & Hart (2016) and Gage et al. (2016); Hall & Degenhardt (2009) and Gage et al. (2016) restate Moore et al. (2007). A genome-wide association study shows genetic overlap, not cause; co-twin comparisons remove shared family factors, not others. The authors of the three genetic studies read their results in different directions, and the 2007 review read its cohorts as consistent with an increased risk; these readings are reported, not used as evidence. Status contested: credible evidence and credible critiques point both ways, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does using cannabis cause psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, or do other differences between people, early illness leading to cannabis use, or shared genes explain the link?
debate.evidence_yes: In seven general-population cohorts the association remained after each cohort's own adjustment for measured confounders (about 60 across the studies, among them other substance use, personality traits, intellectual ability and other mental health problems), was larger for each cohort's most frequent use (pooled odds ratio 2.09) than for ever use (1.41), and was found for psychotic disorder (2.58) as well as for symptoms; the review's authors read this as consistent with an increased risk independent of the confounders measured (Moore et al., 2007; see the answer on how often people use). Most of these cohorts excluded people with psychosis at the start; in the Swedish conscripts, counting only admissions at least five years after conscription gave similar results; in the Christchurch cohort, modelling suggested that cannabis predicted later symptoms rather than the reverse, and fixed-effects regression for unmeasured confounders that do not change over time made little difference (Moore et al., 2007). A cross-sectional sibling-pair study is also described as arguing against stable family confounding, and one review judged shared genetic effects unlikely to explain the association because schizophrenia risk variants explain little of the variation in cannabis use (Gage et al., 2016). The review by the group that produced the potency studies adds that the Dunedin association remained after adjustment for psychotic symptoms at age 11 and that in the Christchurch cohort people tended to use less once minor psychotic symptoms appeared, which argues against self-medication (as described by Murray et al., 2016). In the one co-relative study the odds ratio was still 3.52 (3.92 in the table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, which by the viewpoint's own criteria favours a partly causal over an entirely non-causal reading (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). Genetic liability to ever using cannabis was associated with schizophrenia in the main analysis of two Mendelian randomization studies, at 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, stable when any single variant was left out and after adjustment for the variants' associations with ever smoking, which its authors read as strongly supporting a causal role (Vaucher et al., 2018), and at 1.04 (1.01 to 1.07) per doubling (Gage et al., 2017), and in the third only by the outlier-filtered GSMR method with 74 variants (1.21, p = 0.017; Pasman et al., 2018). In the 11-site case-control study the odds rose from occasional to daily use and were highest for daily use of high-potency types (4.78 against 2.19 for daily use of low-potency types, although a difference between types was not statistically shown, interaction p = 0.25), and across 10 sites the incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls used daily (r about 0.8) (Di Forti et al., 2019; see the answer on strong cannabis). As described in narrative reviews, high intravenous doses of THC can bring on brief psychotic symptoms in healthy volunteers (Murray et al., 2016; Gage et al., 2016; laboratory studies not read here), and two reviews judge the evidence strong enough for public-health messages that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016).
debate.evidence_no: Adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort, for exposure contrasts the review does not state), 60% to 80% in the three most comprehensively adjusted cohorts, and no study adjusted for all major confounders: early-life adversity and shared genetic effects were rarely measured (Moore et al., 2007; Gage et al., 2016; Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). Of the cohorts reported after 2007, the association did not survive adjustment in Zurich, and in ALSPAC it fell to the null after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drug use (1.12, 0.76 to 1.65) (Gage et al., 2016). In the one co-relative study the odds ratio fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and 3.52 in identical twins, a 66% decline that the viewpoint reads as familial confounding accounting for more than half of the association (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). In Mendelian randomization the evidence ran more strongly the other way: genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, p = 2.64×10^-5, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, with similar weighted-median and GSMR estimates, Pasman et al., 2018), and both teams read their results as weak evidence for an effect of cannabis use on schizophrenia and stronger evidence for the reverse, one suggesting that early symptoms or negative feelings might lead people at risk to use cannabis to cope (Gage et al., 2017; Pasman et al., 2018); the forward estimates shrank to 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by MR-Egger and 1.03 (0.99 to 1.08) with 12 variants (Gage et al., 2017) and were not significant with five genome-wide significant variants (1.04, p = 0.81; weighted median 0.95) or with 69 (1.10, 0.99 to 1.21) (Pasman et al., 2018). Lifetime cannabis use is genetically correlated with schizophrenia (0.25) and also with ever smoking, alcohol use, ADHD and risk-taking (Pasman et al., 2018). Specificity is doubtful: in one comparison of 9131 people with severe psychotic illness and 10,311 controls, daily tobacco smoking (odds ratio 5.11), recreational drug use (4.62) and heavy drinking (3.96) had odds ratios as large as cannabis use more than 21 times a year (3.47) (as reported by Ksir & Hart, 2016, without the adjustment set), and another review finds specificity of exposure in some studies but not all (Gage et al., 2016). The critical overview reads the family studies (most of the association disappearing after controlling for familial relationships in the Swedish registry; raised risk of schizophrenia in families of people with psychosis whether or not they used cannabis in a US family study) and the non-specificity as evidence of shared vulnerability, argues that a naturally occurring gradient of use carries a gradient of confounders, and concludes that "cannabis does not in itself cause a psychosis disorder" (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Rates of schizophrenia have not clearly followed rising cannabis use (see the answer on whether rates changed).
debate.neither_can_show: Cohort and case-control studies cannot rule out confounding by what they did not measure (family history, genetic liability, childhood adversity, premorbid functioning) or cannabis use that began during an unrecognized early phase of the illness, and adjusting for education or employment, which the illness itself may affect, can remove part of a real effect or add bias. Mendelian randomization protects against confounding by environmental and social factors that do not change genotype and, for the forward estimate, against reverse causation, but here its instruments index genetic liability to having ever tried cannabis and explain 0.15% to about 1% of its variation, so a small forward estimate says nothing about the risk with daily or high-potency use; the variants may act through traits such as impulsivity or risk-taking rather than through cannabis (only ever smoking was tested, in one study); the three studies draw on the same consortium data, with about 1500 people in both the exposure and the outcome samples of one; and the reverse estimate concerns genetic liability to schizophrenia, not diagnosed illness or its early symptoms, and assumes that schizophrenia risk variants act in the general population, most of whom never develop the illness (Gage et al., 2017). Weak instruments in two-sample designs bias estimates towards no effect, while overlapping samples bias them towards the observational association. A co-relative comparison removes family factors that relatives share but not those that differ between twins, and error in recording use weakens within-pair estimates more than population ones, so a decline with relatedness can overstate confounding; here it rests on one study whose twin estimate is printed two ways and was not tested. A genetic correlation above zero is expected under a causal effect as well as under confounding, so it cannot separate them on its own. Attributable fractions in these studies assume the associations are causal, and comparisons of rates across sites or over time are ecological.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the studies read, people who use cannabis, and especially those who use it often, are more likely to develop psychotic symptoms and disorders, and this is found in many independent cohorts (Moore et al., 2007). How much of that link cannabis itself causes is not known. A large part shrinks when measured differences between people are allowed for (Gage et al., 2016; Moore et al., 2007), and the one co-relative study and the genetic studies suggest that a further part reflects family background and shared genes, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely (Gage et al., 2017; Gillespie & Kendler, 2021; Pasman et al., 2018), so the evidence read here suggests the link is not wholly caused by cannabis. Whether part of it is, and how large that part is for daily or high-potency use, these designs cannot say: the identical-twin estimate stayed above 1 but was not tested (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), the forward genetic estimates are small, vary by method and concern only ever trying cannabis (Gage et al., 2017; Pasman et al., 2018; Vaucher et al., 2018), and the case-control study that shows the largest associations with daily and high-potency use (Di Forti et al., 2019) cannot rule out confounding or reverse causation. The critical reviews read here reach opposite conclusions, mostly shared vulnerability (Ksir & Hart, 2016) and partly causal (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), from overlapping evidence, the authors of the three genetic studies read their own results in different directions (Gage et al., 2017; Pasman et al., 2018; Vaucher et al., 2018), and neither conclusion follows from these data alone.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Mendelian randomization with genetic instruments for frequency of use or cannabis use disorder from larger genome-wide studies, tested in schizophrenia samples that record cannabis use so that the variants' effects can be compared between people who have and have not used cannabis (a causal effect should appear only in people exposed), with multivariable adjustment for smoking, risk-taking and education; co-relative analyses in several registries reporting the numbers of discordant pairs and intervals at each level of relatedness, with use recorded before any early symptoms; prospective cohorts that record frequency and the THC and cannabidiol content of what people actually use, by product testing or biomarkers, before any psychotic symptoms, with family history and polygenic scores; and controlled before-and-after studies of the incidence of psychotic disorder where cannabis use or potency changed sharply.

statement: In observational samples of people who used cannabis regularly or had a cannabis use disorder, the share with cannabis withdrawal, as each study defined it, differed greatly by where the samples came from, in a 2020 meta-analysis of 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants (searched to June 2019; Bahji et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low; English only; no group of people who did not cut down for comparison): 17 in 100 (95% CI 13 to 22) in 15 general-population samples holding 17,475 people, 54 in 100 (48 to 59) in 28 outpatient samples (5,684 people) and 87 in 100 (79 to 94) in 7 inpatient or residential samples (357 people). Withdrawal at any time in life was reported far more often than withdrawal in the past year (76 in 100, 70 to 82, in 18 cohorts, against 31 in 100, 27 to 36, in 32); like the differences by setting, these are comparisons between groups of studies, not within the same people. The one general-population sample assessed with DSM-5 criteria found it in 12.1% of 1,527 people. The review's headline figure, 47 in 100 (41 to 52; I2 99.2%; cohorts from 8% to 100%), is close to the plain average of the cohort estimates and is driven by small clinical samples; counted by participants it is about 28 in 100 (the review's own count, 6,469 of 23,518, is 27.5%, editors' calculation, and its forest plot's fixed-effect total, which gives larger cohorts more weight, is 0.28). Men and women did not differ (27 and 26 in 100, 15 studies), although the review's conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men. In DSM-5, as two reviews summarise it, cannabis withdrawal means at least three of seven symptoms developing within about a week after heavy and prolonged use stops (Bahji et al., 2020, which also word it as within 7 days of reduced use; Connor et al., 2021): irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; less appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and a physical symptom such as headache, sweating or stomach pain, with distress or impairment that Connor et al. describe as clinically severe. Many of these symptoms also occur in withdrawal from other substances and in other mental disorders (Connor et al., 2021). As described in narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand, symptoms typically begin 1 to 2 days after stopping, peak within the first week (at 2 to 6 days in one account) and fade within 1 to 2 weeks (Curran et al., 2016; Connor et al., 2021), while a 2020 professional statement describes a longer course, beginning a few days after stopping or cutting down, peaking at about 10 days and ending after 30 days (Page et al., 2020); craving, nightmares and nausea are also prominent (Curran et al., 2016), and irritability, sleep difficulty, low mood, craving and anxiety are listed by Volkow et al. (2014); people seeking help to stop report symptoms that include anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), which a later review by the same first author calls the most common symptoms, often severe enough to impair everyday life (Hall, 2015); one review gives around half of people who use daily as having withdrawal when they stop, citing an earlier review (Curran et al., 2016). On medical risk the sources disagree without evidence: one review says that, in people without other medical or psychiatric illness, withdrawal does not pose serious risks and usually needs only supportive care (Connor et al., 2021), while the 2020 professional statement advises clinicians to tell people who use heavily over the long term not to stop suddenly because of the risk of withdrawal (Page et al., 2020); neither cites a study for this. In one laboratory study, oral THC given by the researchers eased the symptoms (Budney et al., 2007, as cited by Curran et al., 2016), and in trials the THC medicines dronabinol and nabiximols reduced withdrawal symptoms but did not reduce cannabis use compared with a placebo (Curran et al., 2016). Sleep after stopping is covered in more detail in the claims on sleep. The cohorts defined regular use differently, most predate DSM-5, the review took the lowest threshold where studies offered several, cohorts with more tobacco use reported more withdrawal (a comparison between studies), and in people who use both daily, stopping both gives stronger symptoms than stopping either alone (Curran et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people who use cannabis regularly stop or cut down, some get withdrawal: irritability or anger, nervousness, poor sleep, less appetite, restlessness, low mood, or physical symptoms such as headaches. A 2020 review found it in about 17 in 100 people with regular use in general-population surveys, 54 in 100 in outpatient groups and 87 in 100 in inpatient groups; withdrawal at any time in life was reported much more often than in the past year. Reviews say it usually starts 1 to 2 days after stopping, is worst in the first week and fades within 1 to 2 weeks, though one professional statement says it can last about a month. Expert sources disagree on whether it carries any medical risk, and none gives evidence for its view. The studies defined regular use and withdrawal in different ways, many of the same feelings also come with other conditions, and none checked how often they occur in people who do not cut down.
population: People with regular cannabis use or a cannabis use disorder in 50 observational cohorts (15 general-population, 28 outpatient, 7 inpatient or residential; 38 from North America), and people seeking help to stop, as described in narrative reviews
exposure: Stopping or cutting down after regular use (regular use as each cohort defined it; the review gives no common definition)
comparator: None (prevalence without a comparison group); settings and timeframes compared with each other
outcome: Cannabis withdrawal syndrome as each study defined and measured it (rating scales, checklists and diagnostic interviews; most cohorts used DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria for the use disorder), at any time in life or in the past year; symptoms and time course as described in reviews
magnitude: Bahji 2020, random-effects pooled prevalence: general population 17% (95% CI 13 to 22 in Table 2; 13 to 21 in the text; 15 cohorts; 17,475 people; I2 98%); outpatient 54% (48 to 59; 28; 5,684); inpatient 87% (79 to 94; 7; 357 in the text, 359 in Figure 2); past year 31% (27 to 36; 32 cohorts); lifetime 76% (70 to 82; 18); overall 47% (41 to 52 in the abstract, 27 to 37 in the Results text; I2 99.2%; range 8% to 100%); Figure 2 totals: random effects 0.46 (0.37 to 0.55), fixed effect 0.28 (0.27 to 0.28); men 27% (21 to 34), women 26% (19 to 33), P = .99; one DSM-5 population cohort 12.1% of 1,527. Participant count: 6,469 of 23,518 in the abstract (27.5%, editors' calculation; cohort sizes times prevalences in Table 1 sum to 6,470). Time course as described in reviews: onset 1-2 days (24-48 hours), peak within the first week (2-6 days), resolution within 1-2 weeks; in one professional statement, onset after a few days, peak at about 10 days, end after 30 days.

risk_of_bias.note: Cohorts mostly rated fair (36 of 50) or poor (12) on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; clinical and residential samples selected for heavy use; lifetime withdrawal recalled in surveys; the lowest available threshold used; no comparison group to subtract background symptoms; the review is AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_bahji_2020).

inconsistency.note: I2 99.2% overall and 98% within general-population samples, whose estimates run from 7.6% to 34.4%; two analyses of one national survey gave 8.0% and 34.4%. Setting and timeframe explain part of the spread, not all.

The headline 47% is not used as the answer, because it averages cohorts of very different kinds and tracks the average cohort rather than the average participant (card sc_bahji_2020; the review's own fixed-effect total is 0.28); the setting-specific figures are. statement: In randomized trials of people with chronic pain, mostly neuropathic or cancer pain (28 trials, 2,454 participants; 17 at high and 9 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo, in trials with follow-up of at most 15 weeks, are associated with a small reduction in pain. Nabiximols (a THC and CBD spray used in the mouth) was the commonest product (13 of the 28 trials) and nearly all of the pooled trials tested it. In a 2015 meta-analysis of the parallel-group trials (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 37% of people on cannabinoids and 31% on placebo had their pain reduced by at least 30% (254 of 685 against 215 of 685, the crude totals of the 8 trials in the review's forest plot; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), an odds ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 7 of them of nabiximols and 1 of smoked THC, 1,370 people; I2 48%) that does not exclude no difference; the 7 nabiximols trials alone gave 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86), and the one smoked-THC trial, of 50 people, the largest effect (OR 3.43, 1.03 to 11.48). Pain on a 0 to 10 scale was 0.46 points lower with nabiximols (95% CI 0.11 to 0.80 lower; 6 trials, 948 people; I2 59%); the review team rated both outcomes moderate certainty and names no threshold for a clinically important change. More people rated themselves improved overall (OR 2.08, 1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 people; low certainty by the review team), neuropathic-pain scale scores were 3.89 points lower on a 0 to 100 scale (0.47 to 7.32 lower), and the Brief Pain Inventory (-0.17, -0.50 to 0.16) and quality of life (EQ-5D, -0.01, -0.05 to 0.02) did not differ. The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for chronic pain, which its Discussion narrows to neuropathic or cancer pain treated with smoked THC or nabiximols, but the outcomes so rated are either not statistically significant or small. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with long-lasting pain who took a cannabis medicine (in the combined trials, nearly always a THC and CBD mouth spray) scored their pain about half a point lower on a 0 to 10 scale than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo). About 37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%, a difference that could be due to chance. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

comparator: Placebo (one trial against amitriptyline)
outcome: At least 30% pain reduction; pain on 0 to 10 numerical rating scales; Brief Pain Inventory; Neuropathic Pain Scale; patients' global impression of change; quality of life (EQ-5D)
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, parallel-group trials, random effects, cannabinoid against placebo: at least 30% pain reduction 37% vs 31% (254/685 vs 215/685, crude totals in the review's Figure 2; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 1,370 patients; I2 48%; GRADE moderate by the review team); the 7 nabiximols trials alone OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86); smoked-THC trial OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48; 50 patients); in Figure 2, 5 of the 8 trials favour cannabinoids (3 significantly) and 3 favour placebo (none significantly); neuropathic pain OR 1.38 (0.93 to 2.03; 6 trials); nabiximols: 0 to 10 pain scale WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11; 6 trials, 948 patients; I2 59%; moderate); Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16; 3 trials); Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 on 0 to 100 (-7.32 to -0.47; 5 trials); global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 patients; I2 68%; low); EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02; 3 trials).

risk_of_bias.note: Of the 28 pain trials, 17 at high and 9 at unclear risk of bias; across the review, withdrawals were often not handled and only 57% reported adequate blinding of participants, while psychoactive effects (euphoria and dizziness several times more frequent with cannabinoids in the review's adverse-event data) can reveal who had the active drug (card sc_whiting_2015).

inconsistency.note: I2 48% and 59%: moderate heterogeneity. In the responder pool 5 of the 8 trials point towards benefit and 3 towards placebo, none of those 3 significantly (Figure 2), and the review says the continuous results were not consistent across trials; not rated down, because the intervals overlap and the pooled estimates point the same way, but a stricter reading could rate down here.

indirectness.note: Worded for short trials of mostly pharmaceutical products in people with chronic pain; it does not extend to herbal cannabis as most people use it or to long-term use.

imprecision.note: The responder estimate (0.99 to 2.00) includes no difference; the pain-scale difference is precise but small, its whole interval under 1 point on a 10-point scale.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review, which used trial-registry records; many nabiximols trials were registered by the manufacturer, and trial funding is not reported; not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: low. The review team rated these outcomes moderate; the editors also rate down for imprecision, because the outcome that matters most to patients (at least 30% less pain) does not exclude no effect, and the pain-scale reduction, though precise, is small. The largest responder effect comes from the one smoked-THC trial of 50 people; the 7 nabiximols trials alone give OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86). Status replicated: 5 of the 8 responder trials point the same way (3 significantly), with moderate heterogeneity and 3 trials pointing towards placebo without significance (Figure 2, viewed at adjudication); the pain-scale pool has 6 trials whose individual results the article does not show.

statement: In randomized trials of people with multiple sclerosis (11 trials, 2,138 participants; 3 further trials in paraplegia, 142 participants, could not be pooled; of all 14 trials, 7 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo, most often nabiximols (6 of the 14 trials and 4 of the 5 in the Ashworth pool), in trials whose follow-up, where printed, was 3 to 15 weeks, are associated with a small improvement in spasticity as patients rate it, but not detectably as clinicians measure it. In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), patients' own spasticity ratings (numerical rating or visual analogue scales) were 0.76 points lower (95% CI 0.14 to 1.38 lower; 3 trials, 698 people; I2 73%; low certainty by the review team) and more patients rated themselves improved overall (OR 1.44, 1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 people; low), while the Ashworth scale, a clinician's rating of muscle tone, did not clearly change (-0.12, -0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials; I2 0%; moderate; the overall value as corrected by the journal in 2015), nor did the share of people whose rated spasticity fell by at least 30% (OR 1.64, 0.95 to 2.83) or 50% (1.40, 0.81 to 2.41; 2 trials each), activities of daily living (Barthel index: the review prints three separate product estimates and no pooled one, all with intervals that include no difference) or walking speed (-0.86, -3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials). The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for spasticity, but none of the outcomes it rated moderate (Ashworth, Barthel index, walking speed) showed a clear difference. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with MS who took a cannabis medicine, most often a THC and CBD mouth spray, rated their muscle stiffness a little lower (0.76 points on the rating scales used) than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo), and more of them felt better overall. When doctors measured stiffness, there was no clear difference. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

statement: In randomized trials of people receiving chemotherapy (28 trials, 1,772 participants, mostly of nabilone, THC, levonantradol or dronabinol; 23 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo are associated with more people having complete control of nausea and vomiting: in a 2015 meta-analysis of the three placebo-controlled parallel-group trials that could be pooled (dronabinol or nabiximols; Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 47% on cannabinoids against 20% on placebo had a complete response (percentages given only in the abstract, their derivation not described; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 102 patients; I2 0%; low certainty by the review team). Twenty trials compared cannabinoids only with other anti-sickness medicines, most often prochlorperazine (13 of the 20, editors' count from the review's Table 1; 15 trials in all had a prochlorperazine arm). The review says, without pooled figures, that all the trials pointed towards more benefit with cannabinoids than with the other medicines or placebo, though not significantly in all; because these comparisons are not pooled, how cannabinoids compare with those medicines, or with the anti-sickness medicines in use today, is not shown here. A narrative review calls THC an effective treatment for nausea and vomiting with chemotherapy, citing one source, and says, without a cited source, that patients often find marijuana more effective (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In three small trials (102 people having chemotherapy), about 47 in 100 people who took a cannabis medicine (dronabinol or a THC and CBD spray) had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 who took a dummy medicine (placebo). Most of the other trials compared cannabis medicines with other anti-sickness medicines; the review says these leaned towards the cannabis medicines too, but it did not combine them and not every result was clear. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
population: People receiving chemotherapy in randomized trials published up to April 2015
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials (in the pooled placebo comparison, dronabinol or nabiximols; across all trials mostly nabilone, THC, levonantradol and dronabinol); doses are study conditions
comparator: Placebo (pooled); other anti-sickness medicines, mostly prochlorperazine (not pooled)
outcome: Complete response (complete control of nausea and vomiting as each trial defined it)
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (dronabinol or nabiximols) against placebo, parallel-group trials, random effects: complete response 47% vs 20% (given only in the abstract; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 3 trials, 102 patients; I2 0%; GRADE low by the review team). Comparisons with active anti-sickness medicines (20 trials; prochlorperazine in 13 of them, editors' count from Table 1) not pooled in the article; the review says all trials favoured cannabinoids, not significantly in all.

statement: For sleep problems, appetite and weight in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo or other treatments are too few, small or short to show whether they help: in a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), each of these conditions had one to four trials designed for it (four for appetite in HIV, at most two for each of the others) and none for depression, most of them small and many at high risk of bias. Sleep: in 19 placebo-controlled trials for chronic pain or multiple sclerosis, mainly of nabiximols, sleep-quality scores on 0 to 10 scales differed from placebo by -0.58 points in favour of cannabinoids (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials) and sleep-disturbance scores by -0.26, also in their favour (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials), both very low certainty by the review team; of two trials in sleep problems (54 participants), one in sleep apnoea (22 patients; attributed to nabilone in the review, although its reference list points to a dronabinol trial) reported a lower apnoea–hypopnoea index (-19.64, P = .02), and a crossover trial in fibromyalgia found nabilone better than amitriptyline for insomnia (-3.25, -5.26 to -1.24), in the wording the journal corrected in 2016; the review concludes, on low-quality evidence, that cannabinoids may improve sleep. Appetite in HIV: weight gain of 2 kg or more within 6 weeks with dronabinol against placebo, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients), among 4 trials all at high risk of bias. Anxiety: one trial of cannabidiol in 24 people with generalized social anxiety disorder, measured during a simulated public-speaking test with 107 minutes of follow-up (anxiety factor -16.52, P = .01; very low). Depression: in 5 trials for other conditions, 3 found no difference and one found worse depression scores at the highest nabiximols dose (2.50, 0.38 to 4.62) but not at the two lower doses (very low). Psychosis: two trials of cannabidiol (71 participants) found no difference, with intervals too wide to show the absence of an effect (against amisulpride, BPRS -0.10, -9.20 to 8.90; 35 patients). Glaucoma: one crossover trial of 6 people found no difference in eye pressure. Tourette syndrome: two small trials of THC capsules (36 participants) suggested less tic severity on some scales (17 or 18 patients per analysis; low). Epilepsy was not among the review's conditions, and trials of cannabidiol medicines in epilepsy were not among the sources read for this claim; as human evidence a narrative review describes only a small parent survey of cannabidiol-rich cannabis in childhood epilepsy, in which, of 19 families, 2 reported freedom from seizures, 8 a fall in seizures of more than 80% and 6 a fall of 25 to 60%, and it calls safety and efficacy data on cannabis plant products for epilepsy insufficient (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: For sleep problems, appetite in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, there are only a few small, short trials of cannabis medicines each, so it is not known whether they help. Sleep scores in trials for pain or MS were slightly better with the medicine than with a dummy medicine (placebo), but this evidence is very weak. Epilepsy was not part of this review, and trials of a CBD medicine for epilepsy were not read for this answer.

outcome: Sleep quality and disturbance scores, apnoea–hypopnoea index and insomnia; weight gain; anxiety during a public-speaking test; depression scores; psychosis rating scales; eye pressure; tic severity

statement: In randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines for many conditions (62 trials reported adverse events; parallel-group and crossover trials combined), cannabinoids at the highest dose each trial tested, compared with placebo or another medicine, increase short-term side effects (the review's authors word this as an association). Side effects were common in both groups: across the 29 trials with counts for any adverse event in the review's forest plot, 1,438 of 1,779 people on cannabinoids (about 81 in 100) and 1,058 of 1,710 on placebo or another medicine (about 62 in 100) had at least one (crude totals, editors' arithmetic; the review's table gives 3,714 patients for these trials). In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), the odds of any adverse event were 3.03 times higher (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%), of a serious adverse event 1.41 times (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%) and of leaving a trial because of adverse events 2.94 times (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients), with no difference in deaths (1.01, 0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients). Specific effects more frequent with cannabinoids included disorientation (OR 5.41, 2.61 to 11.19), dizziness (5.09, 4.10 to 6.32; 41 studies), euphoria (4.08, 2.18 to 7.64), confusion (4.03, 2.05 to 7.97), drowsiness (3.68, 2.24 to 6.01), dry mouth (3.50, 2.58 to 4.75), somnolence (2.83, 2.05 to 3.91), loss of balance (2.62, 1.12 to 6.13), hallucination (2.19, 1.02 to 4.68; 10 studies), nausea (2.08, 1.63 to 2.65), asthenia (2.03, 1.35 to 3.06), fatigue (2.00, 1.54 to 2.62), vomiting (1.67, 1.13 to 2.47) and diarrhoea (1.65, 1.04 to 2.62); depression, anxiety, paranoia, psychosis and seizures did not differ clearly, with wide intervals (psychosis 1.09, 0.07 to 16.35; 2 studies, 37 patients). Apart from the counts for any adverse event, the review reports odds ratios only, not how many people in 100 had each effect; using the highest dose was the authors' choice of a worst case; and no study of long-term adverse events was found, even among non-randomized studies. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In short trials, side effects were common with both cannabis medicines and the comparison: about 81 in 100 people taking a cannabis medicine and 62 in 100 taking a dummy medicine (placebo) or another medicine had at least one. Cannabis medicines raised the odds of any side effect, and of stopping the trial because of one, about three times, and of a serious one 1.4 times. Disorientation, dizziness, feeling high, confusion, drowsiness and dry mouth were among the most increased; nausea and vomiting were also more common. Deaths did not differ. The review used the highest dose each trial gave, gave counts only for having any side effect, and found no studies of long-term harms.

statement: In healthy volunteers in laboratory studies, evidence is insufficient to say whether CBD taken with or at varying times before THC changes THC's effects, compared with the same amount of THC taken the same way without CBD: results differ between studies and outcomes, and no pattern by amount, route or ratio has been found. A systematic review of such studies (Freeman et al., 2019; searched to February 2019; 16 studies in 23 articles published from 1974 to 2019, 13 crossover and 3 parallel-group, 466 healthy volunteers in all, almost all of whom had used cannabis before, with varied use histories including weekly and daily use; nothing pooled; the editors rate confidence in the review critically low) covers THC swallowed, injected into a vein, smoked, vaporised or sprayed in the mouth, in widely different amounts and ratios. As summarized there, most studies found no significant difference with CBD in THC's blood levels (most of eight studies; one vaporised study of 14 people found a higher peak with CBD), in the rise in heart rate (no difference in nine of ten studies) or in how intoxicated people felt (seven of nine; two small studies, one smoked and one by mouth, found less). Reports of less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects with CBD come mainly from four studies in which THC was swallowed or injected into a vein: groups of 5 given THC by mouth (the most intense grade of effects, such as panic, in 4 of 5 after THC alone against 3 of 15 with CBD added; no statistical test reported in the review), a crossover of 8 people given both by mouth, a pseudo-randomised crossover of 6 people given both into a vein (3 of whom had psychosis-like effects after THC alone), and a parallel trial of 48 people given THC into a vein after CBD or a placebo by mouth, in which the average rise in psychosis-like symptoms did not differ although fewer of those given CBD had a clinically significant rise; the review's discussion nonetheless describes three of these studies as showing significantly fewer people with extreme anxiety or psychosis-like effects. With vaporised THC, a 48-person crossover found no difference in psychosis-like effects, and in the 14-person study anxiety rose 15 minutes after THC with and without CBD and was still raised an hour later only without it. The review reports 14 enrolled in that study, including three who did not complete; outcome-specific analysis sizes are not established here. Separate significant-versus-placebo findings do not by themselves show a difference between the active treatments. Results on memory, attention and movement tasks went in both directions. In a later randomized, double-blind crossover trial in a laboratory, 18 healthy adults who had used cannabis before but not in the previous 30 days (the completers of 22 randomized; Zamarripa et al., 2023) each ate, in random order on days at least a week apart, a placebo brownie, a brownie with a THC-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) and a brownie with a CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD), and swallowed a cocktail of five probe medicines, including the sedative midazolam, 30 minutes later in every session (study conditions only). Compared with the THC-dominant brownie, the CBD-dominant brownie was associated with higher blood levels of THC and of 11-OH-THC, a substance the body makes from THC (peaks 14.8 against 8.2 and 53.9 against 4.5, units not printed in the text: about 1.8 and 12 times higher, editors' arithmetic), and with stronger effects, most of them unwanted. Peak rises from each session's baseline on 0–100 scales, rated by the participants in double-blind sessions, were larger for drug effect (72.8 against 59.2), unpleasant (38.6 against 19.6), feeling sick (26.1 against 11.6), memory trouble (37.8 against 27.4) and difficulty with routine tasks (46.7 against 30.3); scores on an arithmetic task and a divided-attention task were worse (P = .049 and .04), and heart rate rose more (by 25.4 against 10.1 beats a minute). Pleasant and liking ratings did not differ significantly, and anxious (23.9 against 13.3), paranoid (23.4 against 12.0) and sleepy (42.6 against 21.0) ratings, though higher than after placebo, did not differ significantly from the THC-dominant brownie. The placebo brownie with the probe medicines changed no effect measure significantly. Effects were followed for 24 hours: the strongest drug effect came later on average (2.9 against 2.1 hours after the probe medicines; not tested statistically) and total THC exposure (area under the curve) was about 2.5 times higher (editors' arithmetic), but how long the stronger effects lasted is not given in the parts of the paper that could be read. In these conditions the CBD-dominant extract did not soften THC's effects, which the authors present as contrary to common claims that CBD dampens THC's unwanted effects; whether the difference came from CBD, from the extract's other cannabinoids or from changed levels of the probe medicines, which the paper does not report, cannot be told, and the trial tested one amount of CBD, eaten in the same brownie as the THC, in adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days; smoked or vaped cannabis was not tested. This trial's result differs from most earlier studies, and so do its conditions: a large amount of CBD, eaten in a whole-plant extract, with probe medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Lab studies disagree on whether CBD changes how THC feels. In most of 16 older studies, adding CBD made no clear difference to how high people felt, to their heart rate or to THC in their blood. A few small studies, in which THC was swallowed or injected, found less anxiety or fewer paranoid feelings with CBD; studies with vaporised THC found little or no difference. In one later trial, 18 healthy adults who ate THC with a large amount of CBD had more THC in their blood, felt the drug more, felt sicker and had more trouble with memory and simple tasks, but other test medicines, including a sedative, were also given. No pattern by amount or by way of taking it has been found.
population: Healthy volunteers in laboratory studies: 466 in 16 studies from 1974 to 2019 gathered by one systematic review (all but two studies admitted only people with previous cannabis use; frequency varied and included weekly and daily use), and, in one later trial, 18 healthy adults aged 18 to 50 (11 men, 7 women; mean age 30) with past cannabis use but none in the 30 days before the first session (mean 124 days since last use), completers among 22 randomized, at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, United States
exposure: CBD given with or at varying times before the same dose of THC by the same route (swallowed, injected into a vein, smoked, vaporised or sprayed in the mouth, in widely varying amounts and ratios; review studies); in the later trial, a brownie with a CBD-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD; the extract also held about 2% CBC and 1% CBG), followed 30 minutes later by a cocktail of five probe medicines (caffeine, omeprazole, losartan, dextromethorphan, midazolam) (study conditions only)
comparator: The same THC dose by the same route without CBD, or after a placebo pre-treatment, with a placebo condition or a pre-drug baseline (review studies); in the later trial, the same participants after a brownie with a THC-dominant extract carrying the same nominal THC dose (20 mg THC, no detectable CBD) and after a placebo brownie, each with the same probe cocktail
outcome: Blood levels of THC, heart rate, self-rated intoxication, anxiety, psychosis-like symptoms, memory, attention and psychomotor tasks, as each study measured them (review); in the later trial, plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH; peak change from baseline in self-ratings on the Drug Effect Questionnaire (0–100), cognitive task performance and heart rate over 24 hours
magnitude: Freeman et al. (2019), as summarized by the review (no pooled estimates or effect sizes; amounts are study conditions, as printed in its text): pharmacokinetics, mostly no significant change in eight studies; higher peak plasma THC with vaporised THC 13.75 mg plus CBD 13.75 mg than with THC alone (n = 14; area under the curve higher, not significantly); later time to peak THC with an oromucosal spray of THC 10 mg plus CBD 10 mg (n = 24). Pulse: no difference in nine of ten studies (editors' count from the text); differences in both directions in one study with 5 per group. Intoxication: less with CBD in two of nine studies (smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg with CBD 0.150 mg/kg, n = 15; oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with CBD 1 mg/kg, n = 8). Anxiety: grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 after oral THC 30 mg alone against 3 of 15 with oral CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg added (no test reported); a smaller STAI rise after oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with CBD 1 mg/kg (n = 8); vaporised THC 13.75 mg with or without CBD 13.75 mg raised anxiety at 15 minutes, still raised at an hour only without CBD (n = 14). Psychosis-like effects: in 3 of 6 after intravenous THC 1.25 mg, lessened by intravenous CBD 5 mg beforehand (pseudo-randomised crossover); after intravenous THC 1.5 mg, no difference in the mean PANSS rise between oral CBD 600 mg and placebo beforehand, with fewer people showing a rise of at least 3 points in positive symptoms and lower paranoia with CBD (parallel, n = 48); no difference with vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg (crossover, n = 48). These review sample labels are not verified analysis denominators: Arkell enrolled 14 and three did not complete. The reported differences in significance against placebo alone do not establish an active-treatment difference for anxiety. No consistent pattern by route, dose or THC: CBD ratio; the review's own summary of routes and dose ranges disagrees with its Table 1, so no per-route study counts are given here. Zamarripa et al. (2023), CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract, mean (SD): THC peak 14.8 (5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), area under the curve 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9); 11-OH-THC peak 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), area 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4); all P < .001; units not printed in the text (editors' arithmetic: THC peak about 1.8 and area about 2.5 times, 11-OH-THC peak about 12 and area about 10 times higher). Peak change from baseline on 0–100 ratings, CBD-dominant against THC-dominant: drug effect 72.8 against 59.2; unpleasant 38.6 against 19.6; sick 26.1 against 11.6; dry or red eyes 28.8 against 15.9; memory 37.8 against 27.4; routine tasks 46.7 against 30.3 (all Tukey P < .05); anxious 23.9 against 13.3, paranoid 23.4 against 12.0, sleepy 42.6 against 21.0 (not significant). Paced serial addition -22.7 against -6.6 correct (P = .049); divided-attention tracking error 32.7 against 15.9 (higher is worse; P = .04); heart rate +25.4 against +10.1 beats a minute (P = .001). Time of peak drug effect 2.9 against 2.1 hours (not tested). Many printed Cohen's d values for the effects do not match the printed means and SDs (some, such as drug effect, memory and routine tasks against the THC-dominant extract, do), and several printed intervals include zero beside P < .05; the d values are not used.

risk_of_bias.note: The review's 16 studies are seen only through a review the editors rate critically low on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_freeman_2019: English-language, peer-reviewed-only search; risk of bias not weighed in its conclusions); its own ratings (10 low, 6 some concerns) include a pseudo-randomised study rated low, and its text and table disagree in several places. The later trial, RoB 2 some concerns (card sc_zamarripa_2023): only completers analysed after 4 of 22 randomized dropped out and were replaced; 36 outcomes without correction; the abstract, text and table disagree on several results, and many printed effect sizes do not match the printed data.

inconsistency.note: Directions differ: most studies found no difference on most outcomes; four small studies with THC swallowed or injected reported less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects; one vaporised study reported anxiety still raised at one hour only without CBD, without establishing an active-treatment difference from those significance statements, and explicitly worse divided attention with CBD; the later oral trial found higher blood THC and stronger, mostly unwanted effects; the review found no pattern by route, dose or ratio that would explain the differences.

indirectness.note: The review's studies are second-hand (METHODS §6.3); the review concerned acute matched-THC comparisons in screened healthy volunteers with varied cannabis-use histories, including daily use, with laboratory routes, amounts and ratios that rarely match products people use; in the later trial, whole-plant extracts carrying other cannabinoids and a probe cocktail including the sedative midazolam, whose levels are not reported.

imprecision.note: Six of the review's studies had 4 to 8 people per condition and nothing was pooled; the later trial had 18 people, with task differences at P = .049 and .04 and printed intervals that cannot be relied on.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed: the review judged it low because studies reported a mix of significant and non-significant results, which is not a method of detecting it; the later trial was registered (NCT04201197).

grade.reasoning: Randomized within-person and parallel laboratory comparisons start high (METHODS §6.3); the review's studies are seen only second-hand. Down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The rise in blood THC and 11-OH-THC in the later trial, on its own, is large, objective and precise and would rate low (high, minus risk of bias and indirectness). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of CBD on THC's acute effects nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status mixed: 17 studies with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation of the differences. The review (Freeman et al., 2019) is used only for what each study reported, described by route and size, and not for a general claim that CBD protects against THC's anxiety or psychosis-like effects: its discussion calls three studies' results significant where its own summaries give no test for two and no difference in the average for the third. Not yet read: the primary studies, later randomized studies of THC with and without CBD on the reading list (Arkell et al., 2020; Lawn et al., 2023) and a 2026 meta-analysis of blood THC with CBD (Chester et al.).

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis as a teenager lowers IQ later in life, and the question is disputed. In a New Zealand birth cohort (Dunedin; 874 people analysed, born 1972-73; full-scale IQ tested at 7 to 13, when only 7 of 1,037 cohort members had tried cannabis, and again at 38; Meier et al., 2012), IQ rose by 0.05 standard deviations in the 242 people who never used cannabis (99.84 to 100.64) and fell by 0.38 (99.68 to 93.93, about 6 points) in the 38 people (about 4 in 100 of those analysed, editors' arithmetic; 82% men) who met criteria for cannabis dependence at 3 or more of 5 interviews between 18 and 38, with intermediate changes in between (linear trend t = −4.45, adjusted for sex). The trend held when people who had used cannabis in the day or week before testing, or had persistent tobacco, alcohol or hard-drug dependence or schizophrenia, were left out in turn, and after adjustment for education (t = −3.41), but its test statistic about halved (t = −2.20) when use in the past 24 hours, other dependence and schizophrenia were adjusted together, and no adjusted size or interval is reported. The decline was larger when dependence began before 18 (about −0.54 against −0.14 standard deviations at 3 or more interviews; 23 and 14 people; p = .02 by a test the paper does not describe, against p = .44 and .09 at 1 and 2 interviews, with no test of interaction); the 8 points that some reviews quote refer to these 23 people. A simulation by another researcher showed that differences in family socioeconomic status could produce the main pattern with no effect of cannabis, under assumed values (for example a fading schooling boost of about 4 IQ points for lower-status children), with the trend test significant at the 5% level in about half of 500 runs, though how often it produced a trend as strong as Dunedin's (P < 0.0001) is not reported (Rogeberg, 2013); in reply, the original team reported that family socioeconomic status did not significantly predict adolescent-onset dependence (P = 0.56) and was unrelated to IQ change (r = −0.006), and that the trend coefficient barely changed when socioeconomic status or childhood self-control was added, each on its own, or when only the 553 people from middle-class families were analysed (−0.152, then −0.158, −0.151 and −0.155; Moffitt et al., 2013). Two US twin cohorts with lighter, shorter use (ever use by 17 to 20 against never; 789 and 2,277 twins; subtests at 9 to 12 and again at 17 to 20) found that those who used changed by 4.0 and 3.4 points less on Vocabulary than those who never used, and by 2.0 points less on Information (−3.3 to −0.7; given in the larger cohort only), adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, socioeconomic status and cohort, but not on the four other subtests; in the larger cohort lower scores preceded use and the Vocabulary and Information differences shrank to −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6) and −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9) after adjustment for drinking and other drug use (in the other cohort Vocabulary stayed at −3.7); and the twin who used did not differ significantly from the co-twin who did not (identical pairs −5.4, −11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs; −0.7, −3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs), with identical-pair intervals wide enough to include the between-family differences, although in the 99 non-identical pairs of the larger cohort the interval (0.2, −2.8 to 3.3) excluded that cohort's between-family difference of −3.4 (Jackson et al., 2016). In a British twin cohort (1,989 people tested at 5, 12 and 18), the 84 with cannabis dependence at 18 already had lower IQ at 5 and 12 (by 5.23 and 5.61 points, sex-adjusted), their IQ did not fall significantly more between 12 and 18 (−1.73 points, p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 0.9), and in 57 twin pairs in which only one twin was dependent, the twins did not differ at any age (Meier et al., 2018). The three Dunedin papers concern one cohort and count once; the twin cohorts studied mostly light use in late adolescence, while Dunedin studied dependence persisting into midlife. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: This has not been shown either way. In a New Zealand study, people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups between 18 and 38 (about 4 in 100 people in the study) lost about 6 IQ points from their childhood scores, while people who never used gained a little; the loss was larger when dependence began in the teens. Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern; the original team found that family background (parents' jobs) did not change their result. In US and British twin studies of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more IQ than the twin who did not, but these studies could miss a small loss and did not study years of heavy use. Researchers disagree.
population: People followed from childhood in population cohorts: New Zealand (Dunedin, born 1972-73, followed to 38), the United States (two twin cohorts, followed to 17-20) and England and Wales (E-Risk twins, born 1994-95, followed to 18)
exposure: Cannabis use in adolescence and early adulthood as each study defined it: DSM cannabis dependence at up to 5 interviews from 18 to 38, with onset before or after 18 (Dunedin); ever use by 17-20, 30 or more uses, or daily use for 6 months or more (US twins); past-year dependence or frequency at 18 (British twins); amount, potency and route not measured
comparator: Cohort members who never used cannabis (Dunedin; US twins) or were not dependent (British twins); in co-twin analyses, the co-twin who did not use or was not dependent
outcome: Change in IQ from before use (childhood or early adolescence) to 38, 17-20 or 18: full-scale IQ (Dunedin), Wechsler subtests in IQ points (US twins), IQ pro-rated from two subtests (British twins)
magnitude: Dunedin (Meier et al. 2012; IQ change in SD units, IQ points divided by 15, unadjusted group means; trend tests adjusted for sex): never used +0.05 (n = 242); used, never dependent −0.07 (479); dependence at 1 wave −0.11 (80), 2 waves −0.17 (35), 3 or more −0.38 (38; 99.68 to 93.93); trend t = −4.45, P < 0.0001; education-adjusted t = −3.41; multivariable (past-24-hour use, other dependence, schizophrenia) t = −2.20, P = 0.0282; no coefficients or intervals reported. Onset before against after 18 at 3 or more waves about −0.54 (n = 23) against −0.14 (n = 14), p = .02 by an undescribed test (p = .44 and .09 at 1 and 2 waves; bar heights read from a figure). Moffitt et al. 2013 (same cohort): β −0.152 (sex only), −0.158 (plus socioeconomic status), −0.151 (plus childhood self-control), −0.155 (553 from middle-class families); socioeconomic status and adolescent-onset dependence χ2 = 1.15, P = 0.56; socioeconomic status and IQ change r = −0.006. Rogeberg 2013: simulation with no effect of cannabis, trend test significant at 5% in about 50% of 500 runs. Jackson et al. 2016 (ever use against never; IQ points; adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, socioeconomic status and cohort): Vocabulary −4.0 (−6.3 to −1.7; RFAB) and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3; MTFS); Information −2.0 (−3.3 to −0.7; MTFS only); with drinking and other drugs, Vocabulary −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5) and −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6), Information −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9); co-twin Vocabulary, identical pairs −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5; 25 pairs) and −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4; 112 pairs), non-identical −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2; 54) and 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3; 99); 47 pairs discordant for heavy use −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6). Meier et al. 2018 (dependence at 18, 84 against 1,905; sex-adjusted IQ points): age 5 −5.23, age 12 −5.61, age 18 −7.34; change 12 to 18 −1.73 (p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 0.9); 57 discordant pairs, age 18 −1.45 (p = .42; approximately −5.0 to 2.1), change 0.05 (p = .98); frequency, change beta −0.05 (p = .035) in the full sample and −0.02 (p = .46) within pairs.

evidence.locator: Box 1, Does cannabis affect IQ?, paragraphs 1 to 6
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: the review describes three prospective IQ cohorts. Dunedin (1,037 people born 1972–73, assessed at 38): persistent cannabis dependence associated with a decline of up to 6 IQ points from IQ at 7–13 (ref. 54), most evident with onset in adolescence and still apparent in people using less than once a week at 38. A UK birth cohort (2,235 adolescents aged 15–16, born 1991–92): cumulative use not associated with lower IQ once pre-teen IQ and confounders, in particular cigarette and alcohol use, were taken into account, with only 72 reporting more than 50 lifetime uses (ref. 163). A US twin cohort (3,066 people aged 17–20): no IQ difference from IQ at 9–12 within twin pairs discordant for use, with only 47 discordant pairs in which the twin who used had used frequently (ref. 164). The review reads the UK and US studies as suggesting that genetic or environmental factors drive the association, noting their younger participants and fewer exposures, and says all three relied on self-report and did not address potency.
