evidence.extracted: GWPCARE2 (registered NCT02224703): a multicentre, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial at 43 centres, 38 of which enrolled patients (United States 23, Spain 7, Poland 3, the Netherlands 2, Australia 2, Israel 1), recruiting from 13 April 2015 to 10 November 2017: 4-week baseline, 14-week treatment period (2 weeks of dose escalation, 12 of stable dosing), taper of up to 10 days and 4-week safety follow-up. Eligible: age 2 to 18 with a confirmed diagnosis of Dravet syndrome (confirmed, with the seizure types, by the independent Epilepsy Study Consortium), seizures incompletely controlled by current antiepileptic drugs, at least 1 antiepileptic drug, at least 4 convulsive seizures in the 4-week baseline, and epilepsy treatments stable for 4 weeks before screening and throughout; use of recreational or medicinal cannabis in the previous 3 months excluded. Trial conditions: randomized 2:2:1:1 (blocks of 6, stratified by age group 2–5, 6–12 and 13–18 years; computer-generated schedule by an independent statistician, held centrally; allocation by interactive web response system) to plant-derived, highly purified cannabidiol oral solution (Epidiolex in the United States, Epidyolex in the European Union; 100 mg/mL) at 10 or 20 mg/kg/d, or to matching placebo solution (excipients only) at the volume of either dose, in identical 100-mL amber glass bottles, given in 2 equal daily doses for 14 weeks and added to concomitant medicines, whose doses investigators were to keep unchanged except for adverse events; the two placebo groups were pooled for efficacy and safety. Patients, caregivers, investigators, those assessing the data and the sponsor did not know whether a patient received cannabidiol or placebo until trial completion, but were not blinded to the volume each received. After instruction, caregivers recorded the number and type of seizures each day through an interactive voice-response system. Primary outcome: change in convulsive-seizure frequency (tonic–clonic, tonic, clonic or atonic) during the 14-week treatment period compared with baseline, analysed by negative binomial regression on the summed counts and presented as percentage reductions, from baseline in each group and relative to placebo; the primary and three key secondary outcomes (total seizures, at least a 50% reduction in convulsive seizures, caregiver global impression of the overall condition) were tested in a fixed order, each only if the previous one was significant; the other secondary outcomes were exploratory and not adjusted for multiple comparisons; data up to withdrawal were used, without imputation. The sample size, 62 patients per group for 80% power, was calculated for a two-sided Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test.

risk_of_bias.note: Cards sc_devinsky_2017 (updated from its protocol supplement and supplementary appendix) and sc_miller_2020 (updated from its Supplements 1 and 2, first pass) (RoB 2): some concerns in both. Both trials were centrally randomized, with placebo solutions in identical bottles, analysed everyone treated, and had caregivers count the seizures and rate the global impression. Neither reports any test of whether caregivers could tell the arms apart: for the first trial none was planned in the original protocol, the final protocol or the statistical analysis plan (Protocol PDF pp. 156–157, 166, 401–410); in that trial caregivers reported that 9 of 56 children given cannabidiol and 1 of 57 given placebo did not like the medicine at all (Supplementary Appendix p. 6), and somnolence was more frequent (36% against 10%); a post hoc analysis found similar seizure reductions with and without somnolence (38.41% against 38.94%), but with an interval from −28.9 to 22.25 points, within the cannabidiol group only (Supplementary Appendix p. 3). In the second trial families and investigators knew each child's dose level, and somnolence was more frequent with cannabidiol (25% and 23% against 14%), although adverse events overall were about as frequent with placebo (about 9 in 10 in each group). In the first trial the primary end point's window and analysis were changed by protocol amendments in 2014 and 2015 and by the statistical analysis plan, all before unblinding, and the reported primary analysis follows that plan; the planned subgroup analyses (including by clobazam and valproate use), the time to the baseline seizure count and two sensitivity analyses, one of them for data missing from withdrawals, are not reported; and the global impression was tested by a method neither plan names. In the second trial unreported diary days were left out of each child's seizure rate rather than imputed, and how many there were is not reported; filled in, as planned, by the highest of three estimates for each child, they leave the 20 mg/kg/d comparison no longer excluding no difference (ratio to placebo 0.798, 0.616 to 1.033; at 10 mg/kg/d 0.729, 0.563 to 0.943), whereas in the first trial the same kind of imputation kept the result (−22.98, −42.20 to −4.87) (Supplement 2 p. 8; Supplementary Appendix pp. 4–6); the planned imputation under a missing-not-at-random assumption and three planned sensitivity analyses of the caregivers' global impression are described but not shown, and no result of the planned cognitive tests is reported (Supplement 2 pp. 4–5, 12–14; Supplement 1 pp. 127–130, 137–139 of 167). The second trial's primary analysis was changed from the rank-sum test, on which its sample size was based, to negative binomial regression by an amendment of 6 September 2018, after follow-up had ended and before unblinding (Supplement 1 p. 108 of 167); that timing keeps the change from being rated here as selective reporting, and what the analyses each trial replaced show about the robustness of the result is counted under imprecision, not here. The same company designed both trials and ran their analyses, which the status records (replicated by the same team) rather than a further level. These concerns, shared by both trials, could plausibly change the estimates materially.

inconsistency.note: Not rated down: both trials found fewer convulsive seizures with cannabidiol than with placebo, with intervals that exclude no difference in their reported analyses, and every sensitivity analysis in both points the same way; on the one scale the two share, the rank-sum (Hodges–Lehmann) median difference in percentage change at 20 mg/kg/d, the second trial's −19.88 points (−33.92 to −5.29) is close to the first trial's −22.8 (−41.1 to −5.4) (editors' comparison; Supplement 2 p. 8). At least halving was significantly more frequent in the second trial (odds ratios 2.21 and 2.74) but not in the first (2.00, 0.93 to 4.30), with similar point estimates and overlapping intervals. The placebo responses (a median change of −13.3% in the first trial, a model-based reduction of 26.9% in the second) are not on the same scale and are not compared.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for the trials' population (children and young people aged 2 to 18 with Dravet syndrome and convulsive seizures not controlled by their antiepileptic drugs, at specialist centres in the United States, Europe, Australia and Israel), the pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution added to existing antiepileptic drugs, the dose levels tested (20 mg per kg per day in both trials, 10 mg per kg per day in the second only) and 14 weeks; it says nothing about CBD products sold in shops, other doses, adults or other epilepsies.

imprecision.note: Rated down one level (as while only the first trial was on file; not rated down in the previous version, which read the second trial from its article alone). In the reported analyses every interval against placebo for the primary outcome excludes no difference, but the limits nearest to no difference are small (5.4 percentage points in the first trial; relative reductions of 8.4% and 2.9% in the second), so a reduction too small to matter is not excluded, and analyses planned in advance give intervals that include no difference in both trials: in the first, the ANCOVA its protocol named for normally distributed data (−21.99, −45.20 to 1.22) and the last 4 weeks of maintenance (−19.96, −40.74 to 1.25) (Supplementary Appendix pp. 4–6); in the second, at 10 mg/kg/d, the rank-sum test on which its sample size was based and which was its planned primary analysis until amendment 7 (−15.74, −31.27 to 3.68), the rank ANCOVA (−16.9 on the rank scale, −36.3 to 2.4) and the ANCOVA (−15.20, −41.17 to 10.77) (Supplement 2 p. 8; Supplement 1 p. 108 of 167). The 10 mg/kg/d level was tested in one trial only. The trials' primary results are on different scales and are not pooled; at 20 mg/kg/d, the dose given in both, the rank-sum analyses agree (−22.8, −41.1 to −5.4, and −19.88, −33.92 to −5.29; editors' comparison), so the direction of the effect is not in doubt, but its size is. The worst-case imputation result at 20 mg/kg/d concerns missing data and is counted under risk of bias, not here. A reading that judged imprecision only by whether the reported intervals exclude no difference, as the previous version did, would give moderate.

publication_bias.note: Not rated down: both trials were registered (NCT02091375, NCT02224703) and published. Every placebo-controlled trial read comes from the manufacturer's programme and no independent trial is on file; this is recorded in the status (replicated by the same team) and under risk of bias, not as a further level.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one level for risk of bias, shared by both trials: caregiver-counted seizures and caregiver-rated impressions, with no test of blinding in either trial (in the first, none was ever planned, its protocol shows), more side effects with cannabidiol, a taste (palatability) difference in the first trial (9 of 56 against 1 of 57 children did not like the medicine at all) and the dose level known in the second; in the first, the primary end point was amended before unblinding (the reported analysis follows the plan) and planned subgroup and sensitivity analyses were not reported; in the second, unreported diary days were not imputed, and filling them in by the planned worst-case rule leaves the 20 mg/kg/d comparison no longer excluding no difference (ratio to placebo 0.798, 0.616 to 1.033), while its planned missing-not-at-random and caregiver-rating sensitivity analyses are not shown (Supplement 2 pp. 8, 12–14); the manufacturer designed both trials and ran their analyses. Down one level for imprecision, now that the second trial's supplements have been read: the reported intervals exclude no difference, but the limits nearest to it are small, and analyses planned in advance include it in both trials, notably at 10 mg/kg/d the rank-sum test on which the second trial's sample size was based and which was its planned primary analysis until an amendment made after follow-up had ended and before unblinding (−15.74 points, −31.27 to 3.68; Supplement 2 p. 8; Supplement 1 p. 108 of 167). Low (moderate in the previous version, which read the second trial from its article alone; a reading that judged imprecision only by the reported intervals would still give moderate). Rated as worded: this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution, added to existing antiepileptic drugs in Dravet syndrome, reduces caregiver-counted convulsive seizures over 14 weeks compared with placebo. The direction is consistent in both trials and in every sensitivity analysis, and at 20 mg/kg/d, the dose given in both, the rank-sum analyses agree (−22.8 and −19.88 points; editors' comparison), but how large the reduction is, and whether it holds at 10 mg/kg/d, is uncertain. 'Reduces' is kept: the comparisons were randomized and both trials' primary analyses, fixed before unblinding, exclude no difference, so what is uncertain is the size and robustness of the effect rather than its direction (METHODS §6.1). Seizure freedom was rare and is not claimed; 10 mg per kg per day was tested in one trial only, and the two dose levels were not compared statistically, so the claim says nothing about which dose works better or about raising the dose. Nothing is claimed about thinking skills: the second report says cognitive function did not differ, but no cognitive result is shown in the article or its supplements (Supplement 2 pp. 4–5, 13; Supplement 1 pp. 137–139 of 167). Sleepiness-type adverse events were reported more often in children also taking clobazam (Supplement 2 p. 6, with no statistical test), which the report relates to a drug–drug interaction described elsewhere. Status replicated by the same team (METHODS §6.3, §6.4): both trials were sponsored by GW (GW Pharmaceuticals; GW Research Ltd), which designed them and ran the analyses, with the same product, design and caregiver-reported outcome, and overlapping investigators: Ian Miller and Ingrid Scheffer were authors of both reports; Linda Laux and Eric Marsh, authors of the first, were members of the second's study group; Stephen Wright of GW was an author of the first and contributed to the second's design; Daniel Checketts of GW did the second's statistical analysis and is listed in the first's study group. No trial independent of the manufacturer has been read. The authors' statement that cannabidiol lacks the psychoactivity of THC was not tested in either trial and is not used. The trial reports give no result beyond 14 weeks, and the open-label extensions cannot replicate a placebo-controlled result. The trials tell nothing about CBD products sold in shops, whose contents are a separate question; the first trial's protocol describes the product as more than 95% cannabidiol extracted from cannabis plants, typically with less than 0.5% THC, and the first trial's appendix and the second report both caution against extrapolating to other cannabidiol products.

statement: In herbal cannabis and cannabis resin (hashish) analysed in laboratories in 12 studies from seven countries (the USA 5, the Netherlands 2, and the UK, France, Denmark, Italy and New Zealand 1 each), mostly samples seized by police and other law-enforcement agencies, the average concentration of THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, the intoxicating compound) rose between 1970 and 2017, while that of CBD (cannabidiol, which the review's introduction describes as not intoxicating at typical doses) did not detectably change, in a systematic review and meta-analysis that fitted a straight-line yearly trend within each study's own series and pooled these trends across studies (T. P. Freeman et al., 2021; funded by a Society for the Study of Addiction fellowship to the first author; no interests declared, although two of its authors are also authors of two included US studies). Concentrations are percentages of the product's weight, so a rise of 1 percentage point means, for example, THC going from 5% to 6% of the weight; the figures describe the products, not how much THC anyone took in, and the review measured no effect on people. In herbal cannabis (66,747 samples in 7 studies, 1970–2017), THC rose by 0.29 percentage points a year on average (95% CI 0.11 to 0.47), about 2.9 points per decade (1.1 to 4.7; editors' arithmetic); in resin (17,371 samples in 8 studies entered as 10 series, 1975–2017), by 0.57 points a year (0.10 to 1.03), about 5.7 points per decade (1.0 to 10.3; editors' arithmetic). The abstract gives eight studies for herbal cannabis, but the Results name seven and both herbal figures show seven; the paper does not explain the difference (its description of the studies lists a Dutch study as giving data for all herbal cannabis, but that study is not among the seven analysed). The trends varied widely between series (I² 94.2% for herbal cannabis, 79.1% for resin). Herbal THC rose in all four US series (0.17 points a year in 1970–1994, 0.47 in 1995–2007, 0.66 in 1996–2008 and 0.59 in 2008–2017, the last with an interval of 0.02 to 1.16), which carry about 62% of the weight of the pooled estimate (editors' sum of the printed weights), but not in the UK in 1975–1989 (0.04, −0.09 to 0.17) or New Zealand in 1979–1996 (0.01, −0.06 to 0.08); a four-year Italian series was too imprecise to tell (1.66, −0.59 to 3.91). Resin THC rose in the USA in 1993–2007 (1.58, 0.87 to 2.30), France in 1992–2016 (0.62, 0.45 to 0.79) and Denmark in 2000–2017 (1.27, 0.81 to 1.72), but not in the UK in 1975–1989 (−0.03, −0.35 to 0.28) or in imported or Dutch-produced resin bought at random from Dutch retail outlets in 2005–2015 (−0.01, −0.50 to 0.49; −0.69, −2.08 to 0.69); the other resin series were imprecise. Levels also differed between series in the same years: read from the review's figure (approximate), US federal seizures of herbal cannabis averaged about 1.2% THC or less in 1970–1978, while UK samples averaged about 3.4% to 6.3% in 1975–1989, and two US series from the same federal seizure source do not join (about 9.6% in 2007, about 6.0% in 2008); the review prints no levels in its text. CBD showed no detectable change in herbal cannabis (49,434 samples in 5 studies, 1995–2017: −0.01 points a year, −0.02 to 0.01) or resin (11,382 samples in 6 studies, 1992–2017: 0.03, −0.11 to 0.18, an interval that allows anything from a fall of 1.1 to a rise of 1.8 points per decade, editors' arithmetic); the authors describe CBD as very low in herbal cannabis and generally higher in resin, and count the studies with CBD data differently in two places (five in their description of the studies, eight different studies across the two CBD analyses). Ten of the 12 studies used non-random samples, mostly seizures, whose make-up depends on what was seized; only the two Dutch studies bought samples at random from retail outlets, and neither is among the seven in the herbal estimate. The review did not assess the age or storage of samples (the title of one included US study asks whether today's cannabis is more potent simply because it is fresher), searched only peer-reviewed papers, which leaves out monitoring reports published outside journals, fitted only straight-line trends, did not assess publication bias, and did not cover legal markets (too few years of data, although the authors cite early reports, not read here, of substantial rises there), concentrates, edibles or any year after 2017. The authors attribute the rise in herbal cannabis to a growing market share of high-THC sinsemilla relative to traditional herbal cannabis, stated as a finding in the abstract and again in the Discussion's closing paragraph, because separate analyses within sinsemilla (0.26 points a year, −0.09 to 0.61) and within traditional herbal cannabis (0.17, −0.02 to 0.36), 5 studies each, did not show a significant rise; but market share was not measured, both estimates lie close to the overall 0.29 with intervals reaching well above it, and only 3 of the 7 studies in the herbal estimate are among them, so the data do not show this explanation. An earlier meta-analysis of herbal cannabis with data from 1970 to 2009, as this review describes it, found a rise of 0.21 points a year (0.16 to 0.27); it was not read here, and how many series the two share is not stated. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Is cannabis stronger than it used to be? On average yes, up to 2017. A review pooled 12 studies from 7 countries that tested cannabis, mostly cannabis seized by police. THC, the main active part of cannabis, rose by about 0.3 percentage points a year in herbal cannabis (weed), about 3 points every 10 years, and by about 0.6 a year in resin (hash), about 6 points every 10 years; the review did not test whether resin rose more than herbal cannabis. A percentage point is a share of the weight: going from 5% to 6% THC is one point. These numbers describe the cannabis, not how much THC people took in. The rise was not seen everywhere: every US series of weed rose, but weed in the UK (1975 to 1989) and New Zealand (1979 to 1996), and hash bought at random in Dutch shops (2005 to 2015), showed no clear rise. CBD, another substance in cannabis, did not change. Only two Dutch studies picked their samples at random, and the authors' explanation, that stronger kinds of weed took a bigger share of the market, was not measured.
population: Laboratory-tested samples of herbal cannabis (including sinsemilla and traditional herbal cannabis) and cannabis resin (hashish), mostly seized by police and other law-enforcement agencies, in 12 studies from the USA (5), the Netherlands (2), the UK, France, Denmark, Italy and New Zealand (1 each), collected between 1970 and 2017 (66,747 herbal and 17,371 resin samples in the THC analyses); only the two Dutch studies bought samples at random from retail outlets
exposure: Calendar year, within each study's own series, fitted as a straight-line yearly trend
comparator: Earlier years of the same series (each study's first year as the reference); no comparison between countries was modelled
outcome: Mean THC and CBD concentration (percentage of the product's weight) in herbal cannabis, sinsemilla, traditional herbal cannabis and resin, as measured by each study's laboratory
magnitude: T. P. Freeman et al. (2021), random-effects pooled yearly change in percentage points of THC or CBD by weight (95% CI): THC, all herbal cannabis 0.29 (0.11 to 0.47), P < 0.001 as printed (about 0.002 from the printed interval, editors' calculation), 7 studies (8 in the abstract), 66,747 samples, 1970–2017, I² 94.2%, per decade 2.9 (1.1 to 4.7); THC, resin 0.57 (0.10 to 1.03), P = 0.017, 8 studies as 10 series, 17,371 samples, 1975–2017, I² 79.1%, per decade 5.7 (1.0 to 10.3); THC, sinsemilla 0.26 (−0.09 to 0.61), P = 0.141, 5 studies, 15,882 samples, 1986–2017, I² 89.4%; THC, traditional herbal 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.36), P = 0.079, 5 studies, 28,418 samples, 1986–2017, I² 48.1%; CBD, herbal −0.01 (−0.02 to 0.01), P = 0.280, 5 studies, 49,434 samples, 1995–2017, I² 66.0%; CBD, resin 0.03 (−0.11 to 0.18), P = 0.651, 6 studies, 11,382 samples, 1992–2017, I² 82.6%, per decade −1.1 to 1.8 (per-decade figures are editors' arithmetic). evidence.locator: Abstract (Background and aims; Design; Results)
evidence.extracted: Systematic review and meta-analysis registered on PROSPERO (CRD42019130055) of observational studies reporting mean THC and/or CBD concentration in cannabis at three or more annual time points, searched to 27 March 2019. Random-effects meta-regression estimated each study's yearly change for each product, and these were pooled in random-effects models. 12 eligible studies from the USA, UK, Netherlands, France, Denmark, Italy and New Zealand. Herbal cannabis: THC rose by 0.29% each year (95% CI 0.11 to 0.47), P < 0.001, from 66,747 samples in eight studies (so stated in the abstract), 1970–2017. Resin: 0.57% each year (0.10 to 1.03), P = 0.017, 17,371 samples, eight studies, 1975–2017. CBD: no evidence of change in herbal cannabis (−0.01% a year, −0.02 to 0.01, P = 0.280; 49,434 samples, five studies, 1995–2017) or resin (0.03%, −0.11 to 0.18, P = 0.651; 11,382 samples, six studies, 1992–2017). Risk of bias is called low apart from non-random sampling in most studies, with moderate to substantial heterogeneity.

evidence.locator: Methods › Eligibility criteria (p. 2, right column); Information sources and search, and Study selection (p. 3, left column, the latter continuing in the right column); Data collection process (p. 3, right column, continuing on p. 4); Risk of bias and Data analysis (p. 4, left column, the latter continuing in the right column)
evidence.extracted: Included: observational studies giving mean THC and/or CBD concentrations in cannabis at three or more annual time points within the same study (two were planned, raised to three to allow meta-regression within each study); excluded: studies without original data or for which the mean, SD and sample size per year and product could not be obtained, after corresponding authors were asked. Five databases searched from inception to 27 March 2019 by two independent reviewers, limited to peer-reviewed papers, with no language or date limits; some early abstracts published before 1980 could not be obtained in full. Screening and extraction by two reviewers. Because no existing tool suited observational studies of non-human samples, a review-specific risk-of-bias tool with four criteria was applied by one researcher: sampling (random low risk, non-random high risk), at least 19 samples per measurement, consistent sampling location and consistent analytical protocol; the age or storage of samples is not among them. Analysis: within each study, the inverse-variance weighted mean difference of each year from the study's first year was regressed on year as a straight line (random-effects meta-regression), giving a yearly change; the study estimates were pooled in random-effects models with inverse-variance weights, separately for all herbal cannabis, sinsemilla, traditional herbal cannabis and resin; heterogeneity was measured with I².

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_freeman_2021b (AMSTAR 2, first pass): critically low, because the search was limited to peer-reviewed papers without a stated reason, no list of excluded studies is given, the effect of seizure-based sampling is not taken into account in interpretation and publication bias was not assessed. For the samples themselves: 10 of 12 studies used non-random samples, mostly seizures, whose make-up can change with what is targeted; no randomly sampled study is in the herbal estimate; the age and storage of samples and differences between laboratories were not assessed; and two US series from one federal source do not join (about 9.6% in 2007 and 6.0% in 2008, read from Figure 2), so methods alone shift levels. Coverage and measurement could materially change the size of the trend.

inconsistency.note: I² 94.2% (herbal) and 79.1% (resin), with series that differ in direction, not only in size: flat herbal series in the UK (1975–1989) and New Zealand (1979–1996), flat imported resin and an imprecise estimate for randomly sampled Dutch-produced resin (2005–2015; −0.69, −2.08 to 0.69), against rises of 0.17 to 0.66 points a year in the four US herbal series and 0.62 to 1.58 in three resin series. The review offers no explanation beyond splitting by product; with 7 and 8 studies, country and period cannot be separated. The claim reports this variation, but the pooled average depends on which series happen to be included (the US series carry about 62% of the herbal weight).

indirectness.note: Not rated down: worded for what was measured, laboratory concentrations in mostly seized herbal cannabis and resin from seven countries in 1970–2017, and the claim states that legal markets, concentrates, edibles, other countries and years after 2017 are outside it and that the figures describe products, not intake or effects.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: the pooled intervals exclude no change for herbal cannabis (0.11 to 0.47) and resin (0.10 to 1.03) and are narrow for CBD in herbal cannabis (−0.02 to 0.01); the wider interval for CBD in resin (−0.11 to 0.18 a year) and the imprecise single series are reported as such in the claim.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review, and less of a concern for monitoring series than for effect estimates; leaving out agency monitoring reports by searching only peer-reviewed papers is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claim: never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: Descriptive observational evidence (laboratory analyses of product samples, pooled in one systematic review) starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (non-random, mostly seized samples, with no randomly sampled study in the herbal estimate, and the age, storage and laboratory handling of samples unassessed) and one for inconsistency (series that differ in direction, not only in size, without explanation), which is below the floor: very low. 'Describes' because the claim reports a trend in products, not an effect on people; descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect. Rated as worded: average straight-line trends in seized and sampled herbal cannabis and resin from seven countries between 1970 and 2017. The direction of the rise is firmer than its size: every US herbal series rose, as did resin in the USA, France and Denmark, but how much cannabis rose on average depends on which countries and years the included studies happen to cover. The claim does not adopt the authors' explanation that the herbal rise reflects a growing market share of sinsemilla, because market share was not measured and the within-type estimates, from a partly different set of studies, are close to the overall estimate; nor the abstract's description of the samples as international cannabis markets, which the Discussion itself says should not be read as globally representative. Status replicated: rises were found in independent series in several countries (for herbal cannabis, the US federal seizure series and a separate California series; for resin, the USA, France and Denmark), while other series were flat, as the claim reports; three of the four US herbal series share one federal seizure source and count as one. The earlier herbal meta-analysis (data 1970–2009) is reported only as this review describes it and is not counted as independent support; the primary series inside this review must not be cited beside it as independent either. The authors' restatement of the yearly rise in milligrams of THC per gram stays in its evidence anchor and out of the statement and plain text, and no amounts or effects on people are given, so that nothing reads as guidance on strength or amounts. Section 2 (forms and preparations) because the answer concerns what the products contain; the answers on stronger cannabis and psychosis and on stronger cannabis and dependence deal with harms. Stays draft: the study card is first-pass and every anchor awaits a second reader.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis makes people lazy or unmotivated. In the one study read, a single cross-sectional comparison using baseline data from the CannTeen study in Greater London (Skumlien et al., 2023; funded by the UK Medical Research Council, with fellowships and awards to individual authors; one author consults for Cambridge Cognition, one has consulted for Janssen Research and Development and one is employed by a contract research organization), 274 volunteers recruited through school assemblies, posters and flyers and social media were compared: 147 who used cannabis on 1 to 7 days a week over the past 3 months (76 adolescents aged 16 to 17 and 71 adults aged 26 to 29; on average 3.74 and 4.17 days a week; 91% and 84% mostly using strong herbal cannabis, skunk) and 127 controls of the same gender and age groups who had used cannabis fewer than 10 times and not in the past month (63 adolescents and 64 adults). Everyone was tested at least 12 hours after their last cannabis or alcohol use, checked with a saliva drug test, a breath test and their own report (last cannabis use on average 2.41 and 2.56 days before), and people with mental health treatment in the past month, daily psychotropic medication or any other illegal drug used more than twice a month were excluded. In models adjusted for depression, risk-taking, maternal education and alcohol, tobacco and other illegal drug use, the people who used cannabis did not differ detectably from the controls in self-rated apathy, a loss of motivation (Apathy Evaluation Scale; 211 analysed; F(1,201) = 0.05, P = .82, partial eta-squared below .001; Bayes factor 6.48 in favour of no difference), or, in a subsample of 139 (about 35 per group), in how often they accepted offers to press buttons for points later exchanged for chocolates or sweets (137 analysed; Bayes factor 3.78 for no difference), in how much bigger rewards raised their acceptances (112; 3.58), or in how much they liked 30 seconds of a favourite song, a piece of chocolate or candy and a 1-pound coin (135; 5.16); for how much greater effort lowered their acceptances (103; 1.89) and how much they wanted the rewards (135; 2.78), the Bayes factors were below the authors' threshold of 3, so those two results support neither no difference nor a difference. The Bayes factors come from unadjusted two-group comparisons run after the main tests. On self-rated anhedonia, a loss of pleasure (Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale; 268 analysed), the controls scored higher than the people who used cannabis, by 0.55 points before adjustment (F(1,258) = 5.35, P = .02, partial eta-squared .02), a difference the authors call small and possibly not clinically relevant (an earlier study found 14 points between healthy people and people with depression); seven outcomes were tested without correction across them, and P = .02 would not pass a Bonferroni threshold of about .007 (editors' calculation). Adolescents reported more apathy (4.05 points) and anhedonia (3.84 points) than adults whether or not they used cannabis, and no cannabis–control difference was larger in adolescents (interactions P = .54 for apathy and .32 for anhedonia, none significant on the tasks). Days of use a week were not correlated with any of the seven outcomes (r from −.18 to .16). The people who used cannabis also scored higher on risk-taking, smoked tobacco on more days and more often used another illegal drug monthly (59% of adolescents and 25% of adults, against 3% and 2% of controls). What the study could not detect: it measured apathy and anhedonia by questionnaire and motivation by two laboratory tasks with small rewards, not motivation at school or work or as rated by other people; it tested people when not intoxicated and did not single out daily heavy use; its Bayes factors used a default prior that puts half its weight on differences larger than about 0.7 standard deviations, so they weigh against differences of that size rather than small ones; and with no power calculation, about 35 people per group for the tasks and about 105 per group for apathy, differences smaller than about 0.5 and 0.4 standard deviations respectively had less than an 80% chance of being detected (editors' approximation, ignoring the covariates). As a single snapshot, it cannot show what cannabis does to motivation over time, or rule out that people who use cannabis differed before they started: the authors themselves raise the possibilities that people more prone to seek pleasure are more likely to use cannabis and that people who use cannabis may present themselves as more motivated in psychological studies. They also cite, without data shown here, a study in which informants rated people who use cannabis as more apathetic, studies linking adolescent cannabis use to valuing school less and to lower academic motivation, and earlier effort-task studies with mixed results, some finding more effort for rewards in people who use cannabis (none read here). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Does cannabis make people lazy? One study cannot settle this. In London, 147 people aged 16 to 17 or 26 to 29 who used cannabis on 1 to 7 days a week (about 4 on average) were compared with 127 people of the same ages who had used it fewer than 10 times. Tested at least 12 hours after their last use, the people who used cannabis did not rate themselves as less motivated. In tasks done by about half of the volunteers, they were just as willing to press buttons to earn sweets and liked a song, chocolate and a coin as much; two task results were too uncertain to tell either way. They reported very slightly more pleasure in everyday things than the others, a difference the authors say may not matter. Teenagers reported less motivation and less pleasure than adults, whether or not they used cannabis. The study looked at people only once, so it cannot show what cannabis does over time or rule out that people who use it were different to begin with. It did not measure school or work, did not single out heavy daily use, and could have missed small differences.
population: 274 volunteers in Greater London recruited through school assemblies, posters and flyers and social media (baseline of the CannTeen study): 76 adolescents aged 16–17 and 71 adults aged 26–29 who used cannabis on 1 to 7 days a week over the past 3 months (on average 3.74 and 4.17 days; mostly strong herbal cannabis), and 63 adolescent and 64 adult controls of the same gender and age groups with fewer than 10 lifetime cannabis uses and none in the past month; people with past-month mental health treatment, daily psychotropic medication or any other illicit drug used more than twice a month excluded; 268 in at least one analysis
exposure: Regular non-medical cannabis use (1 to 7 days a week over the past 3 months, by timeline follow-back), tested at least 12 hours after last cannabis use (saliva drug test, breath test and self-report); THC content and route not recorded or not analysed
comparator: Controls of the same gender and age groups with fewer than 10 lifetime cannabis uses and none in the past month; within the cannabis groups, days of use a week
outcome: Self-rated apathy (Apathy Evaluation Scale) and anhedonia (Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale); in a subsample, choices to make an effort for sweets (Physical Effort task: total acceptances, reward sensitivity, effort sensitivity) and wanting and liking of a song, chocolate or candy and a 1-pound coin (Real Reward Pleasure task); whether any difference was larger in adolescents than adults
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of cannabis. Skumlien et al. (2023), 2 × 2 analyses of covariance adjusted for depression, risk-taking, maternal education and alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use; cannabis against control: apathy (n = 211) F(1,201) = 0.05, P = .82, partial eta-squared < .001, BF01 6.48; anhedonia (n = 268) F(1,258) = 5.35, P = .02, partial eta-squared .02, controls 0.55 points higher (unadjusted); task outcomes with no significant cannabis-group effect (statistics in supplements, not read) and BF01 for no difference: acceptances (n = 137) 3.78, reward sensitivity (112) 3.58, effort sensitivity (103) 1.89, liking (135) 5.16, wanting (135) 2.78. Adolescents against adults: apathy 4.05 points higher, F(1,201) = 13.89, P < .001, partial eta-squared .065; anhedonia 3.84 higher, F(1,258) = 17.98, P < .001, .065. Interactions: anhedonia F(1,258) = 1.01, P = .32; apathy F(1,201) = 0.39, P = .54; none significant on the tasks. Correlations with days a week of use: anhedonia r = .07 (P = .40), apathy .16 (.10), acceptances −.01 (.93), reward sensitivity .06 (.65), effort sensitivity .03 (.85), wanting −.18 (.15), liking −.18 (.14). No interval for any cannabis–control difference is printed in the main text. Editors' calculations: Bonferroni threshold for seven outcomes .05/7 ≈ .007; smallest standardized difference with 80% power (two-sided alpha .05, no covariates) about 0.39 for apathy (about 105 per group assumed), 0.34 for anhedonia (143 against 125), 0.48 for acceptances and for wanting or liking, 0.53 for reward sensitivity and 0.56 for effort sensitivity (equal groups assumed); a Cauchy prior with scale .707 puts half its weight on standardized differences larger than 0.707.

evidence.locator: Methods › Study Design; Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 11, left column) and 2nd paragraph (p. 11, right column); Procedure (p. 12, left column)
evidence.extracted: Cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from the longitudinal arm of the CannTeen study, with two between-subject factors: age group (adolescents, adults) and cannabis group (cannabis, control). 76 adolescents and 71 adults who used cannabis, and 63 adolescent and 64 adult controls, recruited in the Greater London area through school assemblies, posters and flyers and social media advertisements; adults were 26–29 and adolescents 16–17. All 274 completed the anhedonia questionnaire and 215 the apathy questionnaire; a subsample of 139 (34 adolescents who used cannabis and 35 in each other group) did the two tasks. Cannabis groups: use on 1 to 7 days a week on average over the past 3 months; adults who had used cannabis regularly before 18 were excluded. Controls: had used cannabis or tobacco at least once, fewer than 10 lifetime cannabis uses and none in the month before baseline. Everyone: no daily psychotropic medication, no treatment for a mental health condition, cannabis dependence included, in the past month, and no use of any one illicit drug more than twice a month over the past 3 months. Questionnaires were completed at a baseline behavioural session and the tasks at a baseline imaging session, typically within 2 weeks and always within 2 months, outside the scanner; at the start of every session an instant saliva drug test, a breath test and self-report had to show no alcohol or cannabis for at least 12 hours and no illicit drug for at least 48 hours, or the session was rescheduled.

evidence.locator: Methods › Materials › Questionnaire Measures and Behavioral Tasks (p. 11, right column); Covariates (p. 11, right column, continuing on p. 12, left column)
evidence.extracted: Anhedonia was measured with the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale and apathy with the Apathy Evaluation Scale, both described as reliable and valid in adults and adolescents; higher scores mean more of each. Physical Effort task: offers at three effort and three reward levels to make button presses for points later exchanged for chocolates or sweets, each accepted or rejected; outputs are total acceptances, reward sensitivity (acceptances at the highest minus the lowest reward level) and effort sensitivity (acceptances at the lowest minus the highest effort level). Real Reward Pleasure task: ratings of how much each of three rewards was wanted (30 seconds of a favourite song, a piece of chocolate or candy, a 1-pound coin) and, after receiving each, how pleasurable it was, averaged into wanting and liking scores. Covariates chosen in advance: depression, risk-taking, maternal education and frequency of alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use, all drug use assessed by timeline follow-back.

evidence.locator: Methods › Analyses, 1st paragraph, Missing Data and Statistical Models (left column)
evidence.extracted: Hypotheses and analyses were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (registration not read). Item 4 of the Apathy Evaluation Scale was left out for everyone by experimenter error and imputed; people with reward- or effort-sensitivity scores of 0 or below were left out of those analyses. Each of the seven outcomes was analysed with a 2 × 2 analysis of covariance (cannabis group, age group and their interaction) with the covariates; null results were followed up with post hoc Bayesian independent-samples t tests comparing the cannabis and control groups, and adults and adolescents who used cannabis, with a prior scale of r = .707 and Bayes factors (BF01) of 3 or more read as support for no difference. Correlations of each outcome with days a week of use were also computed. Editors' calculation: a prior with this scale puts half its weight on standardized differences larger than 0.707.

evidence.extracted: Shown for the 268 in at least one analysis: adolescent cannabis group 75, adult cannabis group 68, adolescent controls 62, adult controls 63. Depression (Beck Depression Inventory) 12.77, 7.75, 10.03 and 6.97, higher in adolescents than adults, with no cannabis–control difference marked; risk-taking higher in the cannabis groups; cigarette or roll-up use 2.24, 1.35, 0.52 and 0.45 days a week; monthly use of another illicit drug 44 (59%), 17 (25%), 2 (3.23%) and 1 (2%). evidence.locator: Abstract (Methods, p. 9; Results and Conclusion, p. 10); Significance Statement (p. 10)
evidence.extracted: The abstract gives 274 participants, adults and adolescents who used cannabis on 1 to 7 days a week and gender- and age-matched controls, with anhedonia measured in 274, apathy in 215 and the two tasks in 139 and 137; reports that controls had higher anhedonia (F(1,258) = 5.35, P = .02, partial eta-squared .02) with no other significant cannabis-group effects or interactions; states that the null findings were supported by post hoc Bayesian analyses, although two of the six Bayes factors for no cannabis–control difference (1.89 and 2.78, pp. 12–13) are below the authors' threshold of 3, as are two of the five reported for no adult–adolescent difference (2.60 and 1.09, p. 12), and the Discussion (p. 13) describes the support more cautiously, as broad; and concludes, as a suggestion from the results, that use on 3 to 4 days a week is not associated with apathy, effort-based decision-making for reward, or reward wanting or liking in adults or adolescents; it adds that the cannabis groups had lower anhedonia than controls, at a small effect size. The Significance Statement says the study counters the lazy-stoner stereotype by showing that the groups did not differ on several measures of reward and motivation, and that adolescents were not more sensitive to the 'putatively damaging' effect of cannabis.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 13, left column, continuing in the right column); Discussion › Anhedonia and Apathy, 1st paragraph (p. 13, right column, continuing on p. 15) and 3rd paragraph (p. 15)
evidence.extracted: The people who used cannabis had lower anhedonia than controls by about half a point and adolescents higher anhedonia and apathy than adults by about 4 points on each scale, with no other cannabis-group or interaction effects. The authors offer two explanations for the lower anhedonia, that cannabis may strengthen the reinforcing effects of some rewards or that people more prone to seek pleasure are more likely to use cannabis, and call the difference small (under 1 point, partial eta-squared .02) and possibly not clinically relevant, against a 14-point difference between healthy people and people with depression in an earlier study (not read). They note that more frequent or problematic use might have shown differences, that use averaged 4 days a week, that 56 adolescents (74.7%) and 33 adults (48.5%) met the CUDIT-R cut-off for at least mild cannabis use disorder, that daily use of large quantities differs from non-daily use, that acute effects reported in other studies (not read) might become a lasting state with daily use, and that abstinence was at least 12 hours and typically 2 days.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Anhedonia and Apathy, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors call the relationship between cannabis, anhedonia and apathy likely complex, and say that interpreting earlier results is complicated by the inability to assess causality and by possible confounding or moderating variables: a large longitudinal study (Leventhal et al., 2017; not read) found that anhedonia predicted later cannabis use rather than the reverse; cannabis might affect apathy and anhedonia indirectly through psychosis and depression; self-ratings and observer ratings may differ, since popular beliefs could lead observers to see people who use cannabis as less motivated than they are, and the only study of informant-reported apathy (Meier and White, 2018; not read) found people who use cannabis rated as more apathetic than controls, in contrast with the null self-reported apathy here; and people who use cannabis might sense that others, such as the researcher, see them as demotivated and want to appear more motivated in psychological studies, possibly biasing the present results.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Age-Group Differences, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that long-term frequent use may still have harmful consequences in adolescents: daily use may be linked to more apathy through longer intoxication and could affect educational achievement through time spent using; they cite studies (not read) linking adolescent cannabis use to valuing school less (Pacheco-Colón et al., 2021) and, prospectively, to lower academic motivation (Schaefer et al., 2021), and say adolescent use may be linked to motivational outcomes this study did not assess. They describe the absence of age-by-cannabis interactions in their cross-sectional CannTeen analyses as striking, suggest that the adolescent reward system may not be vulnerable to substantial harm from non-acute use at about 4 days a week, and add that effects on reward processing might be delayed and appear later in life.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph (p. 16, right column, continuing on p. 17, left column); Conclusions (p. 17, left column)
evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: the cross-sectional design, with possible time-lagged effects; pre-existing group differences could have obscured an effect of cannabis, which they consider unlikely given matching and covariates; people using cannabis frequently and matched controls were recruited on purpose, so the sample does not represent the UK or people who use cannabis at large, and it was mostly White, though broadly like the UK census population; associations with quantity of use or cannabinoid content were not assessed, to limit the risk of type 1 errors; younger people, or people using cannabis very frequently, might show impairments not detected here; and whether the two tasks generalize to real-life situations, and their formal reliability and validity, are not established. The Conclusions argue that, with earlier work, the evidence does not support an amotivational syndrome outside intoxication, and call for longitudinal designs, diverse assessments of reward processing, examination of the ecological validity of reward measures, and studies of daily or near-daily use and even younger people.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (left column), 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column) and 4th paragraph (right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors define apathy as a loss of or reduction in motivation and anhedonia as a loss of interest in or pleasure from previously rewarding activities. Their summary of earlier studies (none read here): their own systematic review found only 2 studies comparing behavioural motivation in people who use cannabis and controls, one finding lower motivation in 14 adolescents against 20 controls and one no difference in 40 adults; more recently, adults who used cannabis chose hard trials on an effort task more often than controls in samples of 86 and 60, and frequency of use and use-disorder symptoms went with choosing high-effort trials in 47 young adults. On apathy, their review found some evidence of an association, but results were inconsistent: weak positive correlations with quantity and problematic use but not frequency in 1,168 young adults (largest r = .125 after adjustment), and no relationship in 487 adults or in a longitudinal study of 401 adolescents. The review found stronger evidence of an association between cannabis use and anhedonia in adolescents. In 3,394 adolescents followed over time, with adjustment for mental health and other substance use, anhedonia at 14 predicted later cannabis use but not the reverse.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_skumlien_2023 (ROBINS-E, first pass): high overall, from confounding. A single cross-sectional comparison with no measurement before cannabis use began, so differences that existed beforehand (for example in pleasure-seeking, which the authors raise) cannot be separated from any effect; adjusting for depression and other drug use could remove part of an effect, and other drug use barely overlaps between the groups (59% against 3% of adolescents), so its adjustment leans on the model; volunteers, with exclusions that remove people likely to have more apathy from both groups; self-ratings by people who knew the study's topic (the authors raise self-presentation); and the reward- and effort-sensitivity analyses lost 25 and 34 of the 137 with task data under a rule based on the outcome, with the split by group only in a supplement.

inconsistency.note: Not rated down: one study. The authors' own summary of earlier studies (not read) is mixed, some finding less and some more effort for rewards in people who use cannabis; this is reported in the claim but cannot be rated from the evidence read.

indirectness.note: The question is whether cannabis makes people lazy in daily life; the study measured self-rated apathy and anhedonia and two laboratory tasks with small rewards (sweets, a song, a coin), whose reliability, validity and relevance to real life the authors call unestablished, in people tested when not intoxicated, using on average about 4 days a week, aged 16–17 or 26–29, in London, with people with recent mental health treatment, daily psychotropic medication or frequent other drug use excluded; motivation at school or work and ratings by others were not measured.

imprecision.note: One study with no power calculation; about 35 per group for the tasks; two of six Bayes factors for no difference (1.89 and 2.78) below the authors' threshold; a default prior that weighs against medium-to-large differences only; no intervals for the group differences in the main text; differences smaller than about 0.4 (apathy) to 0.56 (effort sensitivity) standard deviations had less than an 80% chance of detection (editors' approximation).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; pre-registered (registration not read), with all seven outcomes reported, nulls included.

dose_response.note: No gradient: days of use a week were not correlated with any outcome.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence (one cross-sectional comparison) starts low; rated down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. The question asks about a cause, so the relation is insufficient evidence: the study found no detectable difference in self-rated apathy or in effort and liking for small rewards, with Bayes factors favouring no difference in four of six comparisons, but a single snapshot cannot show what cannabis does over time, the measures are far from motivation at school or work, and small differences could have been missed. The study therefore does not show that cannabis makes people lazy, and it does not show that it does not. The abstract's statement that the null findings were supported by post hoc Bayesian analyses is not adopted, because two of the six comparisons of people who use cannabis with controls were inconclusive by the authors' own threshold (and two of five comparisons of adults with adolescents who use cannabis, 2.60 and 1.09, were too), and neither is the Significance Statement's claim to counter the lazy-stoner stereotype, which goes beyond a cross-sectional null. The anhedonia difference (controls slightly higher) is reported but not read as cannabis increasing pleasure: it is small, would not survive a correction for seven outcomes, and the authors offer either an effect of cannabis or self-selection as explanations. Companion analyses of the same participants, which the authors cite, are not independent replications. Status single study. Stays draft: the study card is first-pass and every anchor awaits a second reader.

statement: In 18 adult volunteers in Baltimore, USA (9 women and 9 men, mean age 28), who had used cannabis at some time but not in the previous 6 months by their own account and whose urine was negative before exposure, one hour seated in alternate seats beside six people smoking cannabis cigarettes as they wished, compared with each volunteer's own urine before exposure (there was no unexposed group), was followed by THCCOOH, a breakdown product the body makes from THC, in every volunteer's urine, but only rarely by a positive test at the US federal workplace cut-offs (Cone et al., 2015). Study conditions: a sealed chamber of 3.05 m by 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling; in Session 1, cigarettes of 5.3% THC and no ventilation (10.3 g smoked in the hour by the six people smoking); in Session 2, 11.3% THC and no ventilation (14.4 g); in Session 3, 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour, which the authors liken to home air-conditioning (16.5 g); a different six volunteers in each session, run in that fixed order at weekly or longer intervals; smoke was heavy in Sessions 1 and 2 and visible but greatly reduced in Session 3, and in Session 1 some of the people smoking stopped early after eye irritation, by their own account. Urine was collected from about 1 hour before to 34 hours after (250 specimens, including the 18 taken before exposure, of 252 scheduled) and tested with screening immunoassays at 20 and 50 ng/mL in five laboratories (one assay, CEDIA, also at 75 and 100 ng/mL) and by GC-MS, the confirmation cut-off being the 15 ng/mL of the SAMHSA Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs, whose screening cut-off is 50 ng/mL. THCCOOH became measurable (0.75 ng/mL or more) in all 18 within 0.25 to 3 hours. No specimen screened positive on the CEDIA assay at 100 or 75 ng/mL. At 50 ng/mL, 1 of 250 specimens screened positive, on one of the five laboratories' assays only (the other four reported it negative): one woman's specimen 4 hours after Session 2, which held 46.3 ng/mL by GC-MS, so that under the federal two-step rule (screen at 50, confirm at 15) 1 of the 18 volunteers would have had a positive with that assay and none with the others (editors' count). At the 20 ng/mL screening cut-off, which the authors say some private non-regulated programmes use, positive specimens in Sessions 1, 2 and 3 numbered 12, 22 and 0 on DRI, 6, 8 and 0 on KIMS, 12, 22 and 1 on EMIT II Plus and 6, 12 and 0 on CEDIA; 12 of the 18 volunteers screened positive at least once on at least one assay (5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session), and 3 (with KIMS), 6 (with DRI or CEDIA) or 7 (with EMIT II Plus) of the 18 would have had a screening positive confirmed at 15 ng/mL or more by GC-MS, all of them in the unventilated sessions except one volunteer with EMIT II Plus (editors' counts from Table I). In all, 27 specimens from 7 volunteers reached 15 ng/mL (3, 22 and 2 by session; the paper's 10.8% of 250 counts the 18 specimens taken before exposure, so they are 27 of the 232 taken after it, 11.6%, editors' arithmetic), and peak values per volunteer ranged from 1.3 to 57.5 ng/mL. Screening positives at 20 ng/mL first appeared 1 to 4 hours after exposure and continued for 2 to 22 hours; the latest was in one volunteer's 26-to-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL, positive on one assay); in the last pool, 30 to 34 hours after, no specimen screened positive on the four assays tabulated at 20 ng/mL or reached 15 ng/mL, although THCCOOH was still measurable in 12 of the 18. The authors' summary that positives are likely to be rare, limited to the hours immediately after exposure and confined to circumstances where exposure is obvious fits the 50 ng/mL screen, not a 20 ng/mL screen; 'immediately' understates positives that lasted up to 22 hours and one at 26 to 30 hours; and only obvious exposure was studied. A positive here is a urine result, a breakdown product of THC at or above a set level, not a measure of intoxication; this paper reports no measure of effects (blood, oral fluid, hair and effect measures were reserved for other reports). Differences between sessions cannot be put down to potency or ventilation alone, because the sessions ran in a fixed order with different people and Session 1 burned less cannabis. Funding: SAMHSA, which issues the federal guidelines whose cut-offs were tested; NIDA supplied the cannabis and funded one author; two authors are SAMHSA employees in its Division of Workplace Programs and the first author consults for that division. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one laboratory study in Baltimore, 18 adults who had not used cannabis for at least 6 months each sat for an hour between six people smoking cannabis freely in a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres; a different six sat in each of three sessions, one of them with ventilation like home air conditioning. Afterwards, all 18 had a breakdown product of THC in their urine. At the US government's workplace screening level, only 1 of 250 urine samples screened positive, on just one of five laboratories' tests. At a lower screening level that some private testing programmes use, 12 of the 18 people screened positive at least once, and 3 to 7 of them, depending on the test, would have had the result confirmed by a second laboratory method; all but one of these were in the two sessions without ventilation. A positive urine test is a laboratory result, not a measure of being high, and this paper reports no effects. The smoke was deliberately thick, the room small and sealed, and only 18 people took part, so the study cannot show how often everyday exposure leads to a positive test. The US agency that issues the federal workplace testing guidelines paid for the study, and two of its staff were among the authors.
population: 18 adult volunteers in Baltimore, USA (9 women, 9 men; mean age 28, range 20 to 45), recruited through advertisements, flyers and word of mouth and paid, who had used cannabis at some time but not in the previous 6 months by their own account, with urine negative for cannabis and other drugs at screening and admission and no or minimal tobacco use; six per session, each in one session only
exposure: One hour seated in alternate seats beside six people smoking cannabis cigarettes as they wished, in a sealed chamber of 3.05 m by 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling (study conditions): Session 1, cigarettes of 5.3% THC, no ventilation, 10.3 g smoked in all; Session 2, 11.3% THC, no ventilation, 14.4 g; Session 3, 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour, 16.5 g
comparator: Each volunteer's own urine about 1 hour before exposure (all negative by GC-MS and immunoassay); no unexposed group and no placebo condition; the three sessions differ in potency, ventilation, amount smoked, people and week, in a fixed order
outcome: Urinary THCCOOH by GC-MS (confirmation cut-off 15 ng/mL) and screening immunoassay results at 20, 50, 75 and 100 ng/mL in specimens collected for 34 hours after exposure: specimens and volunteers screening positive at each cut-off, and those whose screening positive would be confirmed at 15 ng/mL
magnitude: Cone et al. (2015), 18 volunteers, 250 specimens (18 before exposure, 232 after): screening positives at 100 and 75 ng/mL (CEDIA only), 0 of 250; at 50 ng/mL, 1 of 250 (printed 0.4%; one of five laboratories' assays), 46.3 ng/mL by GC-MS, so 1 of 18 volunteers positive under the federal 50 and 15 ng/mL cut-offs with that assay (Wilson 95% interval 1.0% to 25.8%, editors' calculation) and 0 of 18 with the other assays; at 20 ng/mL, positive specimens in Sessions 1, 2 and 3: DRI 12, 22, 0; KIMS 6, 8, 0; EMIT II Plus 12, 22, 1; CEDIA 6, 12, 0 (34, 14, 35 and 18 of 250 in all, editors' sums); volunteers with at least one 20 ng/mL screening positive on any of the four assays, 12 of 18 (66.7%; 43.7% to 83.7%; 5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session; editors' count); volunteers with a 20 ng/mL screening positive confirmed at 15 ng/mL or more: KIMS 3, DRI 6, CEDIA 6, EMIT II Plus 7 of 18 (editors' count); specimens at 15 ng/mL or more, 27 (3, 22 and 2 by session) from 7 of 18 volunteers (38.9%; 20.3% to 61.4%), that is 27 of 232 specimens taken after exposure (11.6%; 8.1% to 16.4%) against the printed 10.8% of 250; peak THCCOOH per volunteer by session, mean (range) 11.2 (1.9 to 20.1), 28.3 (5.5 to 57.5) and 7.5 (1.3 to 15.5) ng/mL; THCCOOH measurable (0.75 ng/mL or more) in 18 of 18 within 0.25 to 3 hours and in 12 of 18 in the 30-to-34-hour pool; latest screening positive in one volunteer's 26-to-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL), none in the 30-to-34-hour pools (editors' count). No unexposed group, so no difference from unexposed people can be given.

evidence.locator: Experimental › Participants, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 2) and 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 3); Chamber construction and layout, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Experimental cannabis exposure conditions (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Volunteers were recruited through newspaper advertisements, campus flyers, community bulletin boards and word of mouth, and all were paid. Non-smoking participants were healthy volunteers with lifetime cannabis use but no cannabis or other illicit drug in the previous 6 months by self-report, required to test negative for cannabis and other drugs at screening and at admission, with no or minimal tobacco use: 18 (9 women, 9 men), mean age 28 years (SD 7, range 20 to 45), each in one session only. Eight people who smoke cannabis (self-reported mean 28 days of use in the past month) produced the smoke, six per session (four took part in all three sessions, two in two and two in one). The chamber, of plexiglass, measured 10 by 13 feet (3.05 m by 3.96 m) with a 7-foot (2.13 m) ceiling; its door sealed with magnets and stayed closed except that it was opened briefly for exit and entry when one person in each of Sessions 2 and 3 took a bathroom break of about 5 minutes. Six people smoking and six not smoking sat in alternate seats around a central table; all wore disposable paper clothing and booties. Three 1-hour sessions were held at weekly or greater intervals, with cannabis smoked ad libitum: Session 1 without ventilation, cigarettes of 5.3% THC; Session 2 without ventilation, 11.3% THC; Session 3 with active ventilation comparable to home air-conditioning (11.2 air changes per hour), 11.3% THC.

evidence.extracted: The abstract concludes that extreme exposure can produce positive urine tests at commonly used cut-offs, but that positives are likely to be rare, limited to the hours immediately after exposure, and to occur only where exposure is obvious; THCCOOH generally rose with potency, and ventilation substantially reduced exposure. The Discussion says the conditions were designed as a high-intensity, short-term smoke environment that participants would clearly recognize, with people sitting in close proximity. Limitations stated by the authors: fixed order of conditions, no blinding to ventilation, a single session and few participants per condition, possible social influences among those smoking; exposure varies with potency, amount smoked, duration, room size, ventilation and distance; only an acute 1-hour exposure was studied; vaping may alter exposure; and the results are most representative of short-term extreme exposure and can only partially be extrapolated. The Conclusions say exposure produced positive presumptive tests at 20 ng/mL but only a single positive at 50 ng/mL, and that GC-MS confirmed 15 ng/mL or more in some specimens. Editors' reading: 'rare' fits the 50 ng/mL screen (1 of 250 specimens, 1 of 18 volunteers, on one assay), not 20 ng/mL screening (12 of 18 volunteers at least once; 3 to 7 of 18 confirmed, by assay); 'immediately' understates positives that continued for 2 to 22 hours and one in a 26–30-hour pool; obvious exposure was the only kind studied.

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated down. The claim describes urine results under the study's conditions: objective laboratory measurements, complete (250 of 252 scheduled specimens) and tabulated for every specimen (Table I), with every specimen taken before exposure negative, so the counts at each cut-off can be reproduced, and the editors' recount matches every printed session count. The card's high RoB 2 judgment concerns comparisons between the three sessions (fixed order, a different six people each time, less cannabis smoked in Session 1 after eye irritation, no blinding to ventilation); the claim does not attribute session differences to potency or ventilation. Remaining concerns do not change the counts materially: the only assay positive at 50 ng/mL is not described in the Methods; repeating DRI on the second bottle turned 7 of its 23 true positives at 20 ng/mL into negatives, so results near that cut-off varied between runs; laboratory blinding is not reported; concentrations were not adjusted for urine dilution.

inconsistency.note: One study.

indirectness.note: Rated down one level. The site question asks about other people's smoke in general; the evidence is one deliberately extreme, obvious exposure (one hour, a sealed room of about 12 square metres of floor, six people smoking freely in alternate seats, heavy smoke in two of three sessions), in volunteers who had all used cannabis before, with research cannabis of 5.3% and 11.3% THC, and only urine reported. Everyday, longer, repeated or vaped exposure was not studied, and the authors say the results can only partially be extrapolated. The statement is worded for these conditions.

imprecision.note: Rated down one level: 18 volunteers, 6 per condition, each condition run once. Wilson 95% intervals (editors' calculation): 12 of 18 with a 20 ng/mL screening positive, 43.7% to 83.7%; 7 of 18 with a specimen at 15 ng/mL or more, 20.3% to 61.4%; 1 of 18 positive under the federal two-step rule with one assay, 1.0% to 25.8%.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from one study.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Results were highest in the unventilated 11.3% session, but the sessions also differ in amount smoked, people, week and order, so no gradient can be read.

grade.reasoning: A controlled exposure in volunteers without a placebo or unexposed condition, its three conditions run in a fixed order with different people, does not meet the rule under which within-person laboratory studies start high (placebo-controlled, with randomized or counterbalanced order); what happened to the volunteers' urine is rated as a description of these conditions (METHODS §6.3), starting low. Indirectness −1 (an extreme, obvious exposure in a small sealed room, while the question is about other people's smoke in general) and imprecision −1 (18 volunteers, 6 per condition) bring it to very low, the floor. Not rated down for risk of bias: the urine results are objective, complete and fully tabulated, and the editors' recount from Table I reproduces every printed count; the serious risk of bias of the comparisons between sessions (ROBINS-I; fixed order, different volunteers) is not used, because the claim does not attribute differences to potency or ventilation. Worded as 'describes': the exposure plainly put THCCOOH into urine (every pre-exposure specimen negative, every volunteer measurable within 3 hours), but the claim's point is how many tests would read positive at each cut-off, a count under these conditions. The authors' 'rare' is adopted only for the 50 ng/mL screen, with the counts at 20 ng/mL beside it; 'only where exposure is obvious' is not adopted, because only obvious exposure was studied. The counts of volunteers and of confirmed positives are editors' counts from Table I (minus signs read from the rendered pages and from the PDF's symbol font), to be recomputed by the second reader. Status single study: the authors say earlier passive-exposure studies, mostly with weaker cannabis, also found THC metabolites in non-smokers' urine, but those were not read here. Funding by SAMHSA, which issues the guidelines tested, and the authors' ties to it are given in the statement. Amounts appear only as study conditions, and nothing is phrased as advice about tests.

statement: Of 84 cannabidiol (CBD) extracts sold online in the USA, every unique product with a CBD content on its packaging that internet searches found between 12 September and 15 October 2016 (40 oils, 20 tinctures and 24 vaporization liquids from 31 companies; identical formulations under one brand excluded), the CBD measured by a separate laboratory (Botanacor Services) that received the products under blinded codes (high-performance liquid chromatography in triplicate) was within 10% of the label in 26 (30.95%; 95% CI 22.08% to 41.49%), more than 10% above it in 36 (42.85%; 32.82% to 53.53%; the letter calls these underlabelled) and more than 10% below it in 22 (26.19%; 17.98% to 36.48%; called overlabelled), so 58 of 84 were more than 10% off (69.0%; Wilson 95% interval 58.5% to 77.9%, editors' calculation) (Bonn-Miller et al., 2017, a research letter). Accuracy differed by product type (χ² 16.75, P = .002; printed with 1 degree of freedom where a 3-by-3 table has 4, which give the printed P, editors' calculation): within 10% for 18 of 40 oils, 5 of 20 tinctures and 3 of 24 vaporization liquids, 18 of which held more CBD than labelled. Measured CBD ranged from 0.10 to 655.27 mg/mL (median 9.45) against labels of 1.33 to 800.00 mg/mL (median 15.00). THC, which the letter treats as a cannabinoid not on the labels, was detected in 18 of 84 products (21.43%; 14.01% to 31.35%), at up to 6.43 mg/mL (median 0); cannabidiolic acid in 13 (up to 55.73 mg/mL), cannabigerol in 2, and cannabinol and THC acid in none; the letter does not say whether any of the 18 labels listed THC, or the level at which a cannabinoid counted as detected. What was not measured: no one took any product and no urine or blood was tested, so the letter cannot show whether these products cause intoxication, impairment or a positive drug test; only six cannabinoids were measured, not other contents; one result is given per product, with nothing on batches; and how labels per container or serving, and results by weight, were turned into mg/mL is not described. The authors' statements that the shortfalls could negate any clinical response and that the THC may be enough to cause intoxication or impairment, especially in children, are their inferences, not measurements. No funder is named (the first author is credited with obtaining funding); two authors reported personal fees from organizations the letter lists without describing them (among them Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Tilray, Insys and Aphria), three serve as unpaid board members of the Institute for Research on Cannabinoids, and the letter does not say whether any of these organizations made products in the sample. Products bought only online, in five weeks of 2016, describe that market then, not CBD products in shops or dispensaries, elsewhere or today. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Researchers bought every CBD product with a CBD amount on its label that they found online in the USA in autumn 2016: 84 oils, tinctures and vape liquids from 31 companies. CBD (cannabidiol) is a substance from the cannabis plant. A laboratory that did not know what the labels said measured them. Only 26 (about 3 in 10) held within 10% of the CBD on the label; 36 held more and 22 held less. Vape liquids were most often wrong: 21 of 24 were off by more than 10%. THC was found in 18 products (about 1 in 5). No one took the products and no urine was tested, so the study cannot say whether they cause a high or a positive drug test. The products were bought online in 2016, so products in shops, elsewhere or today may differ. The letter names no funder, and two authors reported fees from organizations it does not describe.

evidence.locator: Introductory paragraph; Methods
evidence.extracted: Aim: to examine the label accuracy of CBD products sold online, including present but unlabelled cannabinoids, buying online to maximize sampling and representativeness of available products. Internet searches (keywords CBD, cannabidiol, oil, tincture, vape) between 12 September and 15 October 2016 identified CBD products for online retail purchase with a CBD content on the packaging; products with the same formulation as another product of the same brand were excluded, and all unique CBD extracts meeting the criteria were bought. Products were stored as their packaging instructed or in a cool, dry place; within 2 weeks of receipt labels were replaced with blinded study identifiers and the products sent to Botanacor Services for analysis of six cannabinoids (cannabidiol, cannabidiolic acid, cannabigerol, cannabinol, THC and THC acid) by high-performance liquid chromatography in triplicate (lower limit of quantification 0.3170% wt/wt or less), after a 10-point method validation; triplicate results were averaged and reported by product weight. A 10% allowable variance, said to be consistent with other herbal products in the US Pharmacopeia and emerging industry standards, defined accurately labelled (90% to 110% of the labelled value), underlabelled (more than 110%) and overlabelled (less than 90%).

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated down (card: editors' checklist for laboratory analyses of products, some concerns overall). Strengths: every unique labelled product found was bought; a separate laboratory, not among the authors' affiliations, analysed blind-coded products in triplicate after a stated method validation; the counts agree with Table 1. Concerns that could move products near the 10% limits but not the overall picture (median deviation 20.42%): the search method and the numbers screened are not reported; how labels per container or serving, and results by weight, were turned into mg/mL is not described; the quantification limit is given only as an upper bound; the chi-squared degrees of freedom are misprinted (statistic and P value are right); no funding statement, beside personal fees that two authors declared from organizations the letter does not describe.

inconsistency.note: One study.

indirectness.note: Rated down one level. One five-week window in 2016, online sales only, no weighting by sales, products without a CBD label excluded and one result per product: this describes what could be bought online in the USA then, not CBD products in shops or dispensaries, elsewhere or today.

imprecision.note: 84 products: 26 within 10% (95% CI 22.08% to 41.49%) and 58 outside it (Wilson 58.5% to 77.9%, editors' calculation); the intervals leave the main finding, that most products were more than 10% off, unchanged. By type the groups are small (20 to 40), and the claim gives them as counts.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from one study.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: A laboratory analysis of products starts low as a description of the products sampled (METHODS §6.3). Indirectness −1 (online only, autumn 2016, unweighted, one result per product) brings it to very low. Not rated down for risk of bias, because blind triplicate analysis by a separate laboratory and complete reporting of the three categories make the counts reliable for these products, with uncertainty only near the 10% limits; nor for imprecision, because the intervals do not change the main finding. Worded as 'describes': it measures product content, not effects in people. The letter's terms run against everyday sense (underlabelled means more CBD than stated), so the claim says which way each product was off. The authors' statements about clinical response and about intoxication or impairment, especially in children, are inferences without measurements (the second rests on one cited report of two children), and their comparison with FDA warning letters cannot be checked from the data shown; none is adopted. The letter does not say whether the 18 products with THC listed it, so unlabelled THC is not asserted. No funder is named; the declared personal fees and board roles are reported as printed, without characterizing the organizations, which the letter does not describe. Status single study.
