statement:
In adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer and 2,985 controls; four of the six studies unpublished) and in Swedish male military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) followed for 40 years, to about age 60 (the pooled analysis as described by the National Academies committee, a narrative review, and not read here, so its figures are second-hand; the cohort from its own paper, read in full), evidence is insufficient to say whether smoking cannabis, compared with not smoking cannabis, changes the incidence of lung cancer.

In the pooled analysis, habitual cannabis smoking (at least 1 joint-year) against non-habitual (under 1 joint-year, including never) gave an odds ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38), and 1.03 (0.51–2.08) among people who did not smoke tobacco; for adenocarcinoma alone the odds ratios were 1.73 (0.75–4.00) for more than 1 joint a day and 1.74 (0.85–3.56) for more than 10 joint-years, not significant. The committee says risk rose with duration and intensity without becoming significant. In the Swedish cohort (the paper itself), 'heavy' use meant reporting, once, at conscription at age 18 to 20, more than 50 uses of cannabis in a lifetime (831 men, 1.7%). These men had a hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for lung cancer against men who reported never using cannabis, adjusted for tobacco smoking (in three bands: none, 1 to 10 and more than 10 cigarettes a day), alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status, each measured only at conscription; unadjusted it was 3.72 (1.96–7.06), and adjusted for tobacco alone 2.24 (1.17–4.29). Ever having used cannabis was not associated with lung cancer once tobacco was counted (1.25, 0.84–1.87, from 1.90 unadjusted), and the lower bands of use showed no rise with more use (fully adjusted, from once to 11 to 50 uses: 1.52, 0.66, 0.68 and 1.68, none significant); the authors report no clear dose–response relationship. Of the men in the heaviest band, 91% also smoked tobacco (62% more than 10 cigarettes a day, against 23% of the men who never used cannabis), and analyses within tobacco groups were unstable or could not be estimated because too few men used cannabis without tobacco: in the paper's Supplemental Table 1, the 678 men who reported using cannabis but no tobacco had one lung cancer between them (in the 216 who had used cannabis once), so no hazard ratio could be estimated for men who had used cannabis more than once without tobacco. Over follow-up from 1970 to 2009 (about 1.9 million person-years), 189 of the 49,321 men had a lung cancer record (about 4 in 1,000; 179 in the analyses); the paper gives no count by cannabis group, so absolute risks by group cannot be given. The committee says studies in an epidemiologic review that are not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk.

The committee graded the evidence 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' between cannabis smoking and the incidence of lung cancer (its wording and its judgment; under it sit the pooled case-control analysis and, in its discussion, the cohort and the review). The editors read 'no statistical association' here as not statistically significant in a pooled estimate whose interval does not exclude an odds ratio of 1.38 (a 38% rise) or, among people who did not smoke tobacco, of 2.08, with a cohort pointing up; it is not a finding that smoking cannabis does not raise the risk, and the chapter's highlights go further than its numbered conclusion. A 2018 commentary sets the committee's wording beside a WHO statement (the WHO report was not read) that a cannabis and tobacco mix may increase cancer risk and that the effect of cannabis alone is unknown.

Not measured and limits, as the committee names them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had few people with heavy long-term smoking (imprecise estimates) and relied on self-report without biological confirmation; in the cohort (confirmed in its paper), cannabis and tobacco use after conscription were not recorded, nor how cannabis was smoked, how much or how strong it was; its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco into their cannabis, which they say would inflate the cannabis-related risk; and the self-reports were not anonymous, which they say may have led to under-reporting, while some men may have over-reported to be exempted from military training. Follow-up ended when the men were 58 to 60 (editors' calculation from birth years 1949 to 1951), younger than the median age of about 70 at a first lung cancer diagnosis that the authors cite; lung cancers came from hospital inpatient records to 2009 and death records to 2006, not from the cancer register; and the 7.6% of men who did not answer the cannabis questions had a lower risk than men who reported never using it (0.41, 0.17–0.99). The committee adds that cancers have a long incubation period that needs long observation, that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, contains carcinogens, that cannabis use has been associated with cigarette smoking (to which 28.6% of US cancer deaths in 2014 have been attributed, in a study it cites), and that replication is needed because exposures are changing and many associations rest on single studies. No source read compares smoking cannabis with other ways of taking it.

Funding as printed: the committee's report was sponsored by US federal agencies and health foundations, with no cannabis or tobacco industry sponsor listed; the cohort paper was funded by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and by the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research, which the paper says had no role in the study, and its authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funding of the pooled analysis is not given in the committee's account and is not known here. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: A 2017 report by a National Academies committee graded the evidence on smoking cannabis and lung cancer as 'moderate evidence of no statistical association'. It mostly rested on a combined analysis of six studies that compared people with lung cancer with people without it, which found no clear difference between people who smoked cannabis habitually and people who did not; the results were also compatible with up to about 38% higher odds of lung cancer. A long study of Swedish men found about twice the rate of lung cancer in men who had said, when called up for military service at 18 to 20, that they had used cannabis more than 50 times, compared with men who said they never had, even after taking into account the tobacco they smoked then. But nearly all of those men also smoked tobacco, men who had used cannabis fewer times showed no clear rise, nobody recorded what anyone smoked later in life, and the study ended when the men were about 60, younger than the age at which lung cancer is usually found. So the evidence cannot show either that smoking cannabis raises the risk of lung cancer or that it does not, and none of these studies can show cause. The committee notes that cannabis use has been associated with cigarette smoking, to which more than a quarter of US cancer deaths in 2014 have been attributed in a study it cites.
population: Adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer, 2,985 controls; four studies unpublished) and men in a Swedish cohort of military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) aged 18 to 20 at the start and followed 40 years, to about age 60 (pooled analysis as described by the National Academies committee; cohort from its own paper)
exposure: Smoking cannabis, self-reported: habitual (at least 1 joint-year) in the pooled analysis; more than 50 lifetime uses reported once, non-anonymously, at conscription at age 18 to 20 in the Swedish cohort (use after conscription, technique, amount, product strength and any tobacco mixed in not recorded)
comparator: Non-habitual cannabis smoking (under 1 joint-year, including never) in the pooled analysis, also within people who did not smoke tobacco; men who reported never using cannabis at conscription in the Swedish cohort (55% of whom smoked tobacco then)
outcome: Incidence of lung cancer (adenocarcinoma analysed separately in the pooled analysis)
magnitude: Pooled analysis of 6 case-control studies (2,159 cases, 2,985 controls; committee's account): habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco OR 1.03 (0.51–2.08); adenocarcinoma only: more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75–4.00), more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85–3.56), not significant. Swedish conscript cohort (the paper; 1970 to 2009, about 1.9 million person-years; 179 lung cancers among 44,257 in the frequency analysis): more than 50 lifetime uses at conscription against never, HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14) fully adjusted (tobacco in three bands, alcohol, respiratory conditions, socioeconomic status, all at conscription); tobacco-adjusted 2.24 (1.17–4.29); crude 3.72 (1.96–7.06). Fully adjusted, lower bands: once 1.52 (0.77–3.01); 2 to 4 times 0.66 (0.27–1.62); 5 to 10 times 0.68 (0.21–2.16); 11 to 50 times 1.68 (0.77–3.66). Ever against never: crude 1.90 (1.30–2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85–1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84–1.87). Tobacco, more than 10 cigarettes a day against none: 5.03 (3.23–7.81). Absolute: 189 lung cancers among 49,321 men by the end of 2009 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000; editors' calculation); no counts by cannabis group. Committee's grade (its wording): moderate evidence of no statistical association.

evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of six case-control studies, four unpublished (2,159 people with lung cancer, 2,985 controls), in the International Lung Cancer Consortium (Zhang et al., 2015): habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking, odds ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco 1.03 (0.51 to 2.08). Habitual means at least 1 joint-year; non-habitual under 1 joint-year, including people who never used cannabis; not smoking tobacco means under 100 cigarettes in a lifetime or the cut-offs of the pooled studies. Adenocarcinoma only: more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75 to 4.00); more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85 to 3.56), described by the pooled analysis's authors as suggestive but not significant. The committee adds that risk rose with duration and intensity, but even people with the heaviest and longest smoking were not at significantly greater risk than people who smoked non-habitually.

evidence.extracted: Method, search: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (PsycINFO for Search 4; the Search 6 listing names only Embase and Medline) covering January 1999 to 2 August 2016; Searches 2 to 6 were combined into a master library of 10,759 unique articles (1,488 first categorised as systematic reviews), first sorted into seven major health endpoint topic areas and later divided into the 11 topic areas of the report's chapters; filtering to the chosen endpoints left 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews. The Search 2 listing limits to English-language human studies from 1999. Method, appraisal: possible systematic reviews were screened with six questions, then assessed on five attributes adapted from other sources (Higgins et al., 2011) and rated good, fair or poor, each independently by at least two members (disagreements settled by deliberation or a third member); only good or fair reviews informed the report. Primary studies were reviewed guided by the Cochrane tool for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies. The report says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review and that literature may have been missed. Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better. The committee says its hierarchy of evidence does not imply how large the observed effect is or how much the health effect matters to individuals or populations, and that its terms reflect the quality, quantity and consistency of the evidence. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several supportive findings from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out with reasonable confidence), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied).

risk_of_bias.note: Pooled analysis: not appraisable here, seen only through the committee's account (a narrative review; METHODS §6.3), with self-reported exposure without biological confirmation and no account of smoking technique or of the cannabis smoked. Swedish cohort, now read in full (card sc_callaghan_2013): ROBINS-E high, for confounding (tobacco measured once, at age 18 to 20, in three bands, with 91% of the heaviest cannabis band also smoking tobacco; the ever-use association disappeared with this adjustment, so residual confounding by tobacco amount and by later smoking is plausible and would run away from the null) and for exposure measurement (one non-anonymous report of lifetime use 40 years before the outcome; no record of use after conscription, of how cannabis was smoked or of tobacco mixed in).

inconsistency.note: The pooled null result (0.96, 0.66–1.38) and the cohort's hazard ratio of 2.12 point different ways, and the committee does not show how the two were weighed; the sources differ in design, exposure definition and timing, which may explain part of it.

indirectness.note: Second-hand reading of the pooled analysis; exposure definitions differ between the two sources (at least 1 joint-year; more than 50 lifetime uses by age 18 to 20); the cohort is of Swedish men followed only to about age 60, with use as it was in 1969–70; the outcome is incidence of lung cancer with self-reported past use.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval (0.66–1.38) and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, 0.51–2.08 include no difference and a rise; the adenocarcinoma intervals (0.75–4.00; 0.85–3.56) are wide; few people with heavy long-term smoking; in the cohort the heaviest band (831 men) gives 1.08–4.14, and too few men used cannabis without tobacco for any estimate in that group.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: four of the six pooled studies are unpublished, which reduces the risk of missing studies, but the pooled analysis was not read.

dose_response.note: Not counted: in the pooled analysis risk rose with duration and intensity, not significantly; in the cohort the bands below more than 50 uses showed no gradient (fully adjusted 1.52, 0.66, 0.68 and 1.68) and the authors report no clear dose–response relationship.

grade.reasoning: Observational (case-control studies and one cohort), so the claim starts low. It rests on the National Academies committee's account of the pooled case-control analysis (a narrative review; the pooled analysis was not read, so its figures are second-hand and its risk of bias cannot be appraised, METHODS §6.3) and on the Swedish cohort's own paper, read in full (ROBINS-E high). Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 pass the floor, so the certainty is very low; any two would give the same. The relation is insufficient evidence (METHODS §6.1): neither an effect nor its absence can be shown with precision, because the pooled interval does not exclude a rise of 38% (and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, an odds ratio of 2.08), while the cohort's raised estimate is confined to its heaviest band, with no gradient below it, no association for ever use once tobacco was counted, tobacco smoked by 91% of that band and no estimate possible for men who did not smoke tobacco. The committee's grade, moderate evidence of no statistical association, is its own judgment and concerns statistical significance; the editors do not adopt it as a finding of no effect (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs precision). Not rated as 'causes': every source is observational and none can show cause. The status is mixed (a pooled null and a cohort that points up in one band, not reconciled by the committee; the cohort paper does not resolve it). With the cohort paper read, the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews; it stays a draft as a section 7 claim held for the senior author.

Not read and without a reference record: Zhang et al. 2015, the pooled analysis (DOI 10.1002/ijc.29036) and Huang et al. 2015, the epidemiologic review (DOI 10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-14-1026). statement: In one laboratory trial of 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (398 days on average), each of whom completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart, cannabis flower inhaled from a desktop vaporizer, compared with the same flower smoked in a small handheld pipe (10 mg or 25 mg of THC loaded, from 13.4% THC flower, taken over 10 minutes; study conditions only), was associated with higher average peak ratings of drug effect on a 0 to 100 scale at the lower amount (69.5 against 45.7; editors' calculation of the difference, 23.8 points, 95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) but with no flagged difference at the higher amount (77.5 against 66.4), and with a larger rise in heart rate at the lower amount (23.3 against 11.3 beats a minute) but not at the higher. Average peak whole-blood THC was also higher after vaporizing (7.5 against 3.8 ng/mL, and 14.4 against 10.2), but the paper reports no test of that difference and the editors' intervals for it include zero. On attention and psychomotor tasks, three contrasts between the methods were flagged, all showing worse performance after vaporizing; at the higher amount both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects, anxiety, memory impairment and throat irritation or coughing over placebo, with no flagged difference between them. Three adverse events were reported, all at the higher amount (vomiting once after each method, hallucinations once after vaporizing), too few to compare. Effects outlasted blood THC, which was back to zero within 4 hours while drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours. Only some contrasts between the methods were flagged, and none was corrected for the 32 outcomes. The authors say that earlier comparisons (not read here) found similar profiles for the two methods, and suggest that those let people adjust their own dose. This trial gave a fixed amount of one flower to people who rarely use cannabis, with one pipe and one vaporizer, in a laboratory, and followed people only through each session. The authors note that the largest amount given was smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (from a survey they cite, not read here). It did not test joints, bongs, portable vaporizers, oil cartridges, concentrates, tobacco mixed in, self-paced or repeated use, or effects on the lungs, and it did not measure how much THC left each device. Funding as printed: a US federal health agency (SAMHSA), which also provided technical assistance on design, analysis, interpretation and manuscript approval; one author reports consulting fees or honoraria from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Insys Therapeutics, Battelle Memorial Institute and Canopy Health Innovations; no industry funding is printed.
plain: In one small laboratory study, 17 healthy adults who rarely use cannabis took the same cannabis flower two ways on different days, smoked in a small pipe and breathed in from a vaporizer, and also had a dummy version of each. At the lower of two amounts, vaporizing gave higher scores for how strong the effect felt, and a bigger rise in heart rate, than smoking; at the higher amount the two ways did not clearly differ. Average blood THC was higher after vaporizing, but the study did not test whether that was more than chance. Both ways made some tasks harder, and three bad reactions were reported (vomiting twice, hallucinations once), too few to compare the two ways. This was one small study in a laboratory with fixed amounts, one pipe and one vaporizer. It did not test joints, vape pens, oil cartridges or concentrates, and says nothing about the lungs or regular use.
population: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days since last use, median 365 days)
exposure: Cannabis flower (13.4% THC) vaporized in a desktop vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, with 10 mg or 25 mg of THC in the material loaded, over 10 minutes (study conditions only)
comparator: The same flower with the same THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe in the same people; each method also had a placebo session (flower under 0.01% THC) as its reference
outcome: Peak ratings of drug effect and other effects, heart rate and blood pressure, whole-blood THC, performance on attention and psychomotor tasks, and adverse events, within 8.5-hour sessions
magnitude: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo 11.2 and 2.1. Vaporized minus smoked, editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg; 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg. Heart rate rise, beats per minute, mean (SD): smoked 11.3 (10.4) and 19.1 (17.1); vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); only the 10 mg difference between methods flagged; editors' unpaired differences 12.0 (4.2 to 19.8) and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5). Peak whole-blood THC, ng/mL, mean (SD): smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4); vaporized 7.5 (5.5) and 14.4 (9.4); no test reported; editors' unpaired differences 3.7 (-0.3 to 7.7) and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9). Differences between methods flagged: 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg; 3 task contrasts (Divided Attention distance at 10 mg; Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg); none corrected across 32 outcomes. Adverse events: 3 reported among 17 people, all in 25 mg sessions. Blood THC back to zero within 4 hours; drug-effect ratings above baseline at 6 hours after both 25 mg conditions.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory trial with counterbalanced method order and randomized dose order starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias -1: RoB 2 'some concerns' in four of six domains (sequence generation not described; method cannot be hidden and the main ratings are self-reported; late registration with 32 uncorrected outcomes). Imprecision -1: 17 people; the lower-amount difference in drug-effect ratings has a wide interval (5.4 to 42.2), the higher-amount difference includes zero, the blood THC difference was not tested, and between-method differences were flagged for only 4 of 20 rating items at the lower amount, 2 at the higher and 3 task contrasts. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for this trial's people and conditions; strict reading: as a claim about vaping against smoking in everyday use it would be indirect and the certainty would be very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias on one trial; the earlier comparisons the authors cite, which they say found similar profiles, were not read and would matter if they had been. Worded as an association rather than 'increases' because only some contrasts were flagged, none was corrected for the number of outcomes, and the trial is small.

statement: In one survey of 2,553 young adults in a Southern California school-based cohort (mean age 19; asked once, between June 2018 and October 2019; 75% took part), people who reported vaping THC or hash oil, or dabs, were more likely to report bronchitic symptoms in the past 12 months (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) than people who reported never doing so, after adjustment for age, sex, race and ethnicity, financial status, body mass index, nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis: adjusted odds ratios 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96) for those whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier, 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56) for 6 months to 30 days earlier, 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47) for 1 or 2 days in the past 30 and 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06) for 3 or more days. Wheeze was raised only in the top band (2.27, 1.17 to 4.37), and shortness of breath was not reliably raised after full adjustment. Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30 was associated with all three symptoms when only age, sex, race, finances and body mass index were adjusted (odds ratios 1.41 to 1.78) and with none after also adjusting for cannabis vaping and smoking (0.85 to 0.96). Overall 17.5% reported bronchitic symptoms (384 of 2,194), 13.0% wheeze and 20.4% shortness of breath; the paper gives no rates by vaping group (editors' rough calculation from its counts: about 12% to 14% of people who never vaped cannabis against about 23% to 31% of those who vaped it on days in the past 30, depending on how people with missing symptom data are counted). The survey was a single snapshot, so which came first is unknown, and symptoms were self-reported with no lung-function test. It did not record the product, device, source or amount vaped, or tobacco mixed into smoked cannabis, and it ran until October 2019, when the national outbreak of vaping-related lung injury (EVALI) was under way, so it cannot show whether the symptoms were linked to the products involved in it. Odds were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier (1.73, against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping in the past 30 days), which argues for caution about reading the link as an effect of recent vaping and points to residual confounding as a possible explanation. A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled; no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this survey is not among its sources) found no study comparing people who vape cannabis with people who do not use it, and none following people who vape over time. Its vaping evidence, second-hand, compares vaping with smoking: in a laboratory crossover (11 adults who smoked cannabis often and 9 occasionally; dried cannabis in a vaporizer), vaporised cannabis raised exhaled carbon monoxide less than smoked cannabis and breathing rate did not change with either; Canadian medical cannabis patients (a survey of 364) rated vaporizing as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and in a one-month study without a control group, 22 people who used cannabis often and had breathing symptoms switched to a vaporizer, and the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness reported fewer symptoms and had a higher FVC, with FEV1 not significantly changed. None of these studied THC oil cartridges or dabs, and the survey's authors say longitudinal research is lacking. Funded by the US National Cancer Institute; no conflicts reported.
plain: In one survey of 2,553 young adults in Southern California, those who said they had vaped cannabis (THC or hash oil, or dabs) were more likely to report long-lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis than those who had never vaped it, even after allowing for nicotine vaping and for smoking cigarettes or cannabis. Wheezing was more common only in people who vaped cannabis on 3 or more days in the last month, and shortness of breath was not clearly more common. Nicotine vaping went with these symptoms until cannabis vaping and smoking were taken into account, and not after that. This was one survey at one point in time, based on what people said, with no breathing test. It did not record what was vaped, how much, or whether tobacco was mixed into joints, and it ran until a national outbreak of vaping-related lung injury in 2019, so it cannot show that vaping caused the symptoms. Even people who had last vaped cannabis more than six months earlier reported more symptoms. A 2024 review of studies by way of use found none that compared people who vape cannabis with people who do not use it, or that followed people who vape over time; small studies that compared vaping with smoking found less carbon monoxide in the breath after vaping and fewer breathing complaints after people switched, but one had no comparison group and none tested oil vapes.
population: 2,553 young adults (mean age 19.3; 58% women; 47% Hispanic) in a Southern California school-based cohort, surveyed once a year after high-school graduation (outcome data for 2,194 to 2,396)
exposure: Self-reported vaping of THC or hash oil in an electronic device, or dabs, by recency and days of use (lifetime but not past 6 months; past 6 months but not past 30 days; 1 or 2 days in the past 30; 3 or more days in the past 30)
comparator: Young adults in the same survey who reported never vaping cannabis (for the nicotine comparison, never vaping nicotine); the full model also adjusts for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis
outcome: Self-reported bronchitic symptoms (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) and wheeze in the previous 12 months, and shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill
magnitude: Bronchitic symptoms, cannabis vaping, full-model adjusted odds ratios against never (95% CI): lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Wheeze: 1.12 (0.61 to 2.03), 1.47 (0.92 to 2.35), 1.84 (0.88 to 3.86), 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37). Shortness of breath: 0.90 (0.57 to 1.40), 1.25 (0.86 to 1.84), 1.55 (0.81 to 2.96), 1.41 (0.80 to 2.48). Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, bronchitic symptoms, wheeze, shortness of breath: sociodemographic model 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full model 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42). Absolute: 17.5% (384 of 2,194) bronchitic symptoms, 13.0% (312 of 2,396) wheeze, 20.4% (488 of 2,389) shortness of breath overall; editors' rough calculation for bronchitic symptoms from Table 2 counts: about 12% to 14% in people who never vaped cannabis, about 27% to 31% (1 or 2 days) and 23% to 27% (3 or more days) in those vaping in the past 30 days, depending on how missing symptom data are counted. Editors' note: odds ratios overstate rate ratios when the outcome is this common. 2024 review by route (second-hand; vaping against smoking, not against no use): less exhaled carbon monoxide after vaporised than smoked cannabis from 0.25 to 6 hours and no route effect on breathing rate (laboratory crossover, 11 and 9 adults); lower perceived respiratory harm (survey of 364 medical cannabis patients); fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90) after a one-month switch in the 12 of 22 who did not develop a respiratory illness, FEV1 not significant (no control group).

Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. The scoping review of Russell 2017 is reported as finding that vaping reduced respiratory symptoms. The text's list of vaping studies also names Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023, which Table 4 gives as edible studies in children. No included study examined THC oil cartridges, followed people who vape for longer than a month, or compared them with people who do not use cannabis; the authors call for research on long-term outcomes of vaping and on vaping-associated lung injury with THC-containing e-liquids. Editors' calculation: two-tailed p values for t(11) = 2.90 and 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 are about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so the printed values match one-tailed tests, and the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups.

evidence.extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled and no appraisal is reported (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high: confounding high (one time point; coarse five-level bands for the other exposures; tobacco in joints and blunts not recorded); self-reported symptoms from people who also reported the exposure; outcome data missing for 14% (bronchitic symptoms), related to vaping and smoking; the stated multiple-testing correction is not shown.

inconsistency.note: One survey.

indirectness.note: Worded for self-reported symptoms in this cohort. Read as a claim about lung disease or lung function, or about other ages and regions, it would be indirect.

imprecision.note: Lower bounds of 1.01 to 1.04 for three of four full-model estimates for bronchitic symptoms; the 1 or 2 day and 3 or more day bands hold 90 and 155 people; most wheeze and breathlessness intervals include 1.

grade.reasoning: Observational and cross-sectional, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1: confounding is high, because one time point and coarse adjustment cannot separate cannabis vaping from other exposures (tobacco in joints and blunts, secondhand smoke, asthma) or from reverse causation, and odds were raised as much in people who last vaped cannabis long before the survey as in people who vaped recently. Imprecision -1: several full-model lower bounds sit at 1.01 to 1.04 and the top bands are small. Not upgraded for a large effect (some odds ratios above 2): the most adjusted model still leaves residual confounding that runs away from the null, there is no clear gradient with recency or frequency, and the lower bounds are close to 1. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for self-reported symptoms in this cohort. Rating: very low. Worded as an association, never as an effect of vaping; no longitudinal study of cannabis vaping was read; the 2024 review by route adds only comparisons of vaping with smoking (a laboratory crossover, a perceived-harm survey and an uncontrolled one-month switch with spirometry), second-hand through a review of critically low confidence, which do not change the rating.

statement: EVALI (e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury) was a surveillance case definition: vaping or dabbing in the previous 90 days, a lung infiltrate on imaging, no other plausible diagnosis, and negative infection testing (confirmed cases) or an infection judged not the sole cause (probable cases). The CDC authors say its high sensitivity likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have had EVALI. By 14 January 2020 the CDC had been told of 2,668 hospitalized patients (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable): median age 24, 66% male; weekly admissions peaked in the week of 15 September 2019 and fell afterwards. Of the 2,022 patients (76%) with information on what they had vaped or dabbed in the previous 3 months, 82% reported a THC-containing product, 57% a nicotine-containing product, 41% both and 14% nicotine only; products were unknown for 24% and were not checked against what was in the devices (in the lung-fluid study, THC or its breakdown products were found in 9 of 11 patients who said they had not used THC products in the 90 days before illness). The CDC authors give three possible reasons for the nicotine-only reports: patients not reporting or not knowing what they vaped, some patients not having EVALI, or accurate reports. Deaths and intensive care are second-hand: CDC figures quoted in the laboratory papers give 52 deaths among about 2,400 reported cases by 12 December 2019 and 47% needing intensive care; the update read gives neither, nor outcomes after discharge. Vitamin E acetate, a form of vitamin E sold online as a diluent or thickener for cannabis oil, was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients in 16 states (94%; editors' exact 95% interval 84% to 99%), including all 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction), and from none of 99 healthy volunteers, none of whom vaped THC (0% to 4%); other additives tested were found in at most one patient. FDA testing, quoted second-hand, found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products. In 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids from cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients, 23 (64%) held vitamin E acetate (16% to 57% by mass) and 13 held none above 1%; 31 of the 36 held at least one pesticide (editors' count), a pattern the authors judge intermittent and not due to a single pesticide. These findings come from different laboratories, patients and sample types and point the same way, but they do not show cause: the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC, so the contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from other features of vaping THC products in 2019; no fluid from people who vaped the same products without injury was tested; none of these studies tested whether inhaling it injures the lung (the authors say laboratory studies are needed); the CDC authors state that "evidence is not sufficient to rule out the contribution of other chemicals of concern" in some cases; and a screen of 38 cartridges listed many other chemicals by library match, without counts per cartridge. The cartridge papers call the products illicit or counterfeit; neither describes how this was established. The sources implicate certain vaping products, mostly THC-containing cartridges, and an additive in them. None tested whether THC or cannabis itself injures the lung, or looked at cannabis smoked or eaten or flower vaporized in dry-herb devices; the one screen with medical-grade cartridges (number not stated) found retinol acetate rather than vitamin E acetate in them, and fewer listed contaminants, though some harmful chemicals were identified. So the sources neither show that other forms of cannabis carry this injury nor show that they are free of it. Funding as printed: CDC authors for the surveillance report; National Cancer Institute, FDA Center for Tobacco Products and Ohio State University for the lung-fluid study; none external for the two cartridge studies; no industry funding is printed.
plain: EVALI was an outbreak of lung injury in people who vaped, mostly in 2019. By January 2020, 2,668 people in hospital had been reported to the US CDC; most were young (median age 24) and two thirds were male. Of those who said what they had vaped, most had used products with THC, and some had used only nicotine products. Vitamin E acetate, an oil sold for thickening cannabis oil, was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients and from none of 99 healthy volunteers, who did not vape THC. It was also found in the liquid of about two thirds of 36 cartridge samples from 10 patients in New York. This does not prove that it caused the injury: these studies did not test that, the volunteers were not people who vaped THC and stayed well, and the CDC says other chemicals are not ruled out. These studies point to certain vaping products (mostly THC cartridges, which the authors call illicit or counterfeit) and an additive in them. They did not test cannabis smoked, eaten or vaporized as plant material. One small screen of medical-grade cartridges did not find the additive in them. So the studies cannot say whether other forms of cannabis carry the same risk.
population: People hospitalized with EVALI in the US (2,668 reported to CDC by 14 January 2020); 51 of them with lung fluid tested in 16 states; 10 New York patients whose cartridges were tested (38 samples)
exposure: Vitamin E acetate found in patients' lung fluid and in vaping cartridge fluid (cartridges that held THC or other cannabinoids)
comparator: Lung fluid from 99 healthy volunteers in an unrelated study, none of whom vaped THC; no comparison cartridges within the cartridge studies
outcome: EVALI (hospitalization with vaping-associated lung injury)
magnitude: Surveillance (CDC, 14 January 2020): 2,668 hospitalized (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable); median age 24 (13 to 85); 66% male; among 2,022 with product information: any THC 82% (1,650), any nicotine 57% (1,162), both 41% (834), THC only 33% (669), nicotine only 14% (274), neither 2% (44); peak 215 admissions in the week of 15 September 2019. Second-hand: 52 deaths among 2,409 reported cases by 12 December 2019 (about 2%, editors' calculation); 47% needed intensive care in an earlier CDC report. Lung fluid (Blount et al.): vitamin E acetate in 48 of 51 patients (94%; editors' exact 95% CI 83.8% to 98.8%) against 0 of 99 healthy volunteers (0% to 3.7%); 25 of 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction; 86.3% to 100%) and 23 of 26 probable cases; THC or metabolites 40 of 47 (85%), including 9 of 11 who reported no THC product use; nicotine or metabolites 30 of 47 (64%); coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39, all other priority substances 0 of 12 to 49. Cartridges (Duffy et al.): vitamin E acetate in 23 of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%; exact 95% CI 46% to 79%, treating fluids as independent) at 16 to 57% by mass, from 10 patients; 13 without it, 12 of which held medium-chain triglyceride oil; 31 of 36 with at least one pesticide (editors' count); update to 12 December 2019 without methods: 101 of 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) from 61 cases; 3 of 6 commercial diluents and thickeners essentially pure vitamin E acetate. Screening (Muthumalage et al.): over 500 chemicals in cartridge liquids; no counts per compound.

risk_of_bias.note: All four study cards are rated high overall: the surveillance report has missing and self-reported product data and a sensitive case definition; the lung-fluid comparison used healthy volunteers from another study, sampled mostly before 2019, none of whom vaped THC; the cartridge studies had no comparison cartridges and gave no per-patient results; the screening paper's identifications are library matches without counts.

inconsistency.note: The studies agree in direction. The share holding vitamin E acetate differs (94% of patients' lung fluid; 64% of 36 cartridge fluids, 69% of 147 in a later update; 49% of case-associated THC product samples in FDA testing as quoted second-hand), which different sample types and sources can explain.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and products sampled.

imprecision.note: 48 of 51 and 0 of 99 are precise as counts.

grade.reasoning: Observational: a surveillance case series, a case-comparator lung-fluid study and laboratory analyses of cartridges, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1 (all four study cards rated high overall); the rating cannot fall below very low. Not upgraded for a large effect: the 94% against 0% contrast has no adjusted model, and the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC and were sampled mostly before 2019, so the contrast probably overstates what separates vitamin E acetate from other features of THC cartridge use in 2019. Not downgraded for inconsistency (the studies agree in direction; the proportions differ for reasons of sample type and source), imprecision (the counts are precise) or indirectness (the claim is worded for the people and products sampled). Strict reading: the presence of vitamin E acetate in nearly all lung fluid tested and in most THC-containing cartridge fluids sampled is consistent across two laboratories, but the rating applies to the association and to the description as worded; that it is the cause or the only cause is a separate claim that none of these studies tests, and is lower still. Status replicated: two independent laboratories (CDC with state laboratories; New York State Department of Health), different patients (New York is not among the 16 states of the lung-fluid study) and different sample types, same direction; a third laboratory (University of Rochester) found it in many but not all cartridge liquids, without counts. The earlier CDC report of 29 patients (whether its patients are among the 51 is not stated) and the New York update of 206 fluids (which presumably includes the 38) are not counted as further replications.

Muthumalage 2020 is a laboratory screening study, not a review as the reading list says. Editors' intervals and deductions need the second reader's recomputation. No awaited PDF is needed for this claim.

statement: At one Colorado university hospital's emergency department, 2012 to 2016, clinicians judged 2,567 visits (visits, not people) to be at least partly due to cannabis; 238 (9.3%) were recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled (135 of these had no route written down and were counted as inhaled). Compared with inhaled visits, edible visits more often involved intoxication (48.3% against 27.8%; difference 20.5 percentage points, 95% CI 13.9 to 27.1), acute psychiatric symptoms (18.0% against 10.9%; 7.1, 2.1 to 12.1) and cardiovascular symptoms (8.0% against 3.1%; 4.9, 1.4 to 8.4), and less often gastrointestinal symptoms (15.1% against 32.3%; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% against 18.0%) or admission to hospital (18.9% against 32.9%); psychiatric symptoms of any kind were similar (26.1% against 24.5%). Severe heart events (heart attack, dangerous heart rhythm) occurred in both groups, with no counts given. Because edibles were under a tenth of the visits, most visits for each of these reasons were inhaled (647 of 762 intoxication visits, 254 of 297 acute psychiatric visits, 73 of 92 cardiovascular visits; editors' arithmetic from the table counts), and the authors write that, given how often inhaled visits occurred and led to admission, education about inhaled cannabis may have the greatest public-health effect. The two groups also differed in who they were (women 51.3% against 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% against 6.6%); a 2016 letter from the same hospital group, cited second-hand in the overview described below and not read, reported that edible-related visits by out-of-state patients rose from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant change for Colorado residents. Against Colorado sales in 2014 to 2016, edibles were 10.7% of this hospital's attributable visits but 0.32% of THC sold by weight, under assumed product contents; the authors call this about 33 times the share expected if the routes were equally likely to lead to a visit, and list its limits (assumed contents, one hospital set against statewide sales, home-grown and illicit supply not counted). A 2016 narrative overview (no stated search or appraisal of studies; its figures are second-hand) quotes another measure, edible units at about 45 percent of Colorado cannabis sales in 2014, without saying how sales were counted, so any such ratio depends on the denominator chosen. No source read here timed effects in patients. The hospital paper and the overview both describe, citing pharmacology work that was not read here, a later and longer effect after eating THC than after inhaling it (the overview: a start within minutes of inhaling against 30 to 90 minutes after eating; the hospital paper: clearance within about 4 hours against about 12). The overview adds that more of the active product 11-OH-THC reaches the blood after eating, which it says may account for stronger, longer-lasting effects; that blood THC after eating is lower than after smoking and tracks intoxication differently from person to person; and that this variation and the delay may lead people to take more than intended before the effect starts, which its abstract says often results in profoundly adverse effects (no count given). The hospital paper cites a consumer survey and an analysis of Twitter posts (neither read) in which people report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping, and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms. The overview relays anecdotal reports from patients, including patients who took cannabis daily, of eating a whole product after feeling no effect from a first serving, and describes one death in Colorado in 2014 (a 19-year-old man; the autopsy named cannabis intoxication a chief contributing factor) after he ate the whole cookie within two hours of a first serving, having not felt intoxicated within an hour (a public-health case report, as cited). The hospital paper cites three deaths linked to edibles from news reports; none of its 2,567 visits ended in death. No source read here counts how often people eat more after a slow start. What these sources cannot show: how many people took each form (shares of visits are not the chance that a form leads to a visit); who took which form (no adjustment); how much was eaten (a dose was charted for 130 of the 2,567 visits, 80 of them edible; the authors could not verify doses, say eaten doses may have been larger than inhaled ones, and were surprised that the charted edible doses were low); what the products contained (not tested in the hospital study; a separate laboratory test of other products found most of them more than 10% away from their labels; see the claim on edible labels); and what happened to people who took cannabis without harm or did not attend hospital (the authors note that most people who take cannabis may have no adverse effect). Route came from chart notes and patients' own accounts, and the authors say counting undocumented routes as inhaled could bias toward more illness in the inhaled group. Inhaled visits were not split by product (flower, vaped oil, concentrates) or checked for tobacco mixed in, and no comparison was made with people who do not use cannabis. The overview states that edible products account for most health-care visits for cannabis intoxication, citing a 2015 viewpoint not read here; the hospital count has edibles at 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%). The overview also infers that eating cannabis does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk, citing no study of people who eat cannabis. A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled or appraised; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this hospital study is not among its sources) also found no study of the lungs of adults who eat cannabis. Its oral-route evidence, second-hand, is a laboratory crossover in which heart rate rose about as much after eating cannabis as after smoking or vaporising it (about 10 to 13 beats a minute above placebo) and breathing rate did not change with route; a survey in which Canadian medical cannabis patients rated eating as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and records of children who ate cannabis products (calls to US poison centres and two hospital chart reviews), in which a fast heart rate was common, some children needed help with breathing, and severe heart and breathing effects were seen at higher doses for their body weight. Its abstract nonetheless says edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects. Follow-up was the visit itself: the hospital data do not follow anyone afterwards, and the overview has no data of its own.   Funding as printed: the hospital paper, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (competitive grant; the paper says the funder had no part in design, analysis, interpretation or dissemination), with the first author's NIH support and membership of the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee; the overview, RTI International internal funds and a US National Institute on Drug Abuse grant, with no conflict statement printed; No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding is printed for the hospital paper or the overview.
plain: At one big Colorado hospital, 2,567 emergency visits over five years were judged to be at least partly due to cannabis. Only 238 of them, about 1 in 11, were linked to eating or drinking cannabis; the rest were linked to smoking or vaping it. Compared with the smoking and vaping visits, the edible visits more often involved being very intoxicated, sudden mental-health symptoms such as acute anxiety or psychosis, or heart symptoms, and less often involved vomiting or being admitted to hospital. But because far more visits involved smoking or vaping, most visits for each of those problems still involved smoking or vaping. Two papers describe a slower start and a longer-lasting effect from eating cannabis than from inhaling it, and some case reports describe people eating more after feeling nothing at first, but no study here timed effects in patients or counted how often people eat more. The hospital study and the overview could not count how many people took each form, how much they took, what was in the product, or who never went to hospital, so they cannot say how likely any form is to lead to a hospital visit, and they did not compare either form with people who do not use cannabis.
population: 2,567 emergency visits (median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% from outside Colorado) to one Colorado university hospital, 2012 to 2016, that clinicians judged at least partly due to cannabis: 238 recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled. Visits, not people (for example, 301 people accounted for 440 of the visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome). Timing and case-report material comes from a 2016 narrative overview citing laboratory studies and case reports (not read).
exposure: Cannabis recorded in the chart as eaten or drunk (edible; 238 visits), from the nursing questionnaire and providers' notes, self-reported and unverified; a dose was charted for 80 of the 238 (study measure only); product contents not tested in the hospital study.
comparator: Visits recorded as inhaled (2,194 documented as smoked or otherwise inhaled, plus 135 with no route written down, counted as inhaled) at the same hospital in the same years. No comparison group of people who took each form and did not attend hospital, and no comparison with people who do not use cannabis; for the sales comparison, flower and edible units sold in Colorado in 2014 to 2016 under assumed THC contents.
outcome: Reasons for the visit coded from the chart (intoxication; acute, acute-on-chronic and chronic psychiatric symptoms; gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; cardiovascular symptoms), admission and length of stay; the later and longer effect after eating as described from cited pharmacology and case reports, not measured in patients.
magnitude: Hospital chart review (Monte 2019), share of each group's visits, edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329), % (difference in percentage points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3 vs 27.8 (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0 vs 10.9 (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0 vs 3.1 (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1 vs 24.5 (1.6; -4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1 vs 32.3 (-17.2; -22.1 to -12.2), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4 vs 18.0 (-9.6; -13.5 to -5.7); admitted 18.9 vs 32.9; women 51.3 vs 33.1; living outside Colorado 40.8 vs 6.6 (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (0 to 121). Severe heart events (myocardial infarction, ventricular dysrhythmia) in both groups, no counts. Edible-attributed visits as a share of all visits for each reason, editors' arithmetic from Table 2 counts: intoxication 115 of 762 (15.1%), acute psychiatric 43 of 297 (14.5%), cardiovascular 19 of 92 (20.7%); edible 238 of 2,567 visits (9.3%). Route recorded in 2,432 of 2,567 visits (94.7%); dose charted in 130 (5.1%), 80 of them edible, 19 of those at 50 mg of THC or more (as charted, unverified; study measure only). Eight symptom groups compared, no correction for multiple comparisons. Colorado sales 2014 to 2016: 219 edible and 1,819 inhaled attributable visits (edible 10.7%); edible 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each); flower-to-edible THC ratio 309 (range 279 to 325); visit share about 33 times the share expected if both routes were equally likely to lead to a visit (authors). Overview (Barrus 2016, narrative, second-hand figures): Colorado 2014 edible units 1.96 million medicinal and 2.85 million retail, said to be about 45 percent of total cannabis sales (measure not stated); timing as cited, inhaled start within minutes and effects tapering within 2 to 3 hours, eaten start 30 to 90 minutes and peak 2 to 4 hours after eating (hospital paper, from the same pharmacology review: clearance about 4 hours after inhaling, about 12 hours after eating); oral bioavailability 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (as cited); 83 percent of tested medicinal edibles more than 10 percent from their labelled THC (second-hand; the paper itself, now read, gives 62 of 75, 82.7%, editors' arithmetic); out-of-state patients' edible-related visits 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits, 2013 to 2014 (second-hand, not read).

Cannabis use is assessed in the nursing assessment questionnaire and the providers' notes; the route was captured from the medical record, and inhalation was presumed when it was not documented. Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image, not read).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Abstract (Limitation)
evidence.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: retrospective design with exposure captured largely through self-report; no comparative community-based exposure cohort; patients presenting to the emergency department differ from the overall population of people who use cannabis, most of whom may have no adverse effects, so a prospective cohort of people who use cannabis and people who do not is needed; doses could not be verified and ingested doses may have been larger than inhaled doses. A dose was documented in 80 edible-attributed visits and in 19 it was 50 mg or higher; the authors were surprised by the low edible doses reported, given the THC content of a typical Colorado joint. Route was presumed inhaled when not documented, which they say could have biased the analyses toward greater toxicity in the inhaled group. The hospital has the second most visits per year in the state and is in an area of high cannabis availability.

risk_of_bias.note: Chart review (Monte 2019): ROBINS-E overall high, with confounding, exposure measurement and selection each high (no adjustment for who took each form; route self-reported and presumed inhaled when not written down; everyone in the data attended an emergency department). Overview (Barrus 2016): a narrative review with no stated search or appraisal and second-hand figures, judged high overall.

inconsistency.note: One data set (route at hospital visits), so consistency cannot be judged. The overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (115 of 762, 15.1%) but rests on a 2015 viewpoint that was not read, so it is shown as a contradicting anchor, not as a second data set.

indirectness.note: Worded for one Colorado hospital, 2012 to 2016, in an area of high cannabis availability. Route is edible against inhaled only (inhaled not split into flower, vaped oil or concentrates). The later and longer effect is cited from pharmacology work that was not read and was not measured in patients; the sales ratio uses assumed product contents.

imprecision.note: 238 edible visits; the intervals for the cardiovascular (1.4 to 8.4 points) and acute psychiatric (2.1 to 12.1) differences are wide for their size; eight symptom groups compared without correction; a dose charted in only 5.1% of visits.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one data set.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The route comparison rests on one chart review at one hospital and a narrative overview with no data of its own. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high for the chart review (no adjustment; route self-reported and presumed inhaled when undocumented; every person in the data attended an emergency department); the overview has no stated search or appraisal and its figures are second-hand. Indirectness -1: one hospital in an area of high availability; edible against inhaled only; timing and the 11-OH-THC explanation come from pharmacology work that was not read and were not measured in patients; the sales ratio rests on assumed contents. Imprecision -1: 238 edible visits, wide intervals for two of the three findings that favour more events with edibles, no correction across eight symptom groups, a dose charted for 5.1% of visits. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one data set per question; the overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (15.1%) but rests on a viewpoint that was not read, so it is shown as a contradicting anchor and flagged. Worded as 'describes' rather than 'increases' or 'is associated with' because the data are shares of visits, not risks, with no count of people taking each form, and the claim combines counts, the authors' interpretation and second-hand pharmacology. The Discussion's causal wording and the 33-fold ratio are the authors' own reading and are reported as such, not adopted.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on one chart review at one hospital (Monte 2019, the only primary study of route read for this claim) and a narrative overview (Barrus 2016: no stated search or appraisal; its timing, label-testing, child-poisoning and out-of-state figures are second-hand). Label accuracy (Vandrey 2015) and children's poison-centre calls (Tweet 2023) are now claims of their own (cl_can_edibles_labels, cl_can_edibles_children), split by the editor on 2026-10-23. The overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (115 of 762, 15.1%); its source, a 2015 viewpoint by the hospital group (Monte, Zane, Heard), was not read, and the conflict is shown as a contradicting anchor, not resolved. The editors' arithmetic (edible shares of visits by reason) needs recomputation by a second reader. Papers cited by the sources (Kim 2016, Hall 2018, Wang 2014, Cao 2016, Grotenhermen 2003) were not read; the hospital group's papers are not independent of each other. Amounts, strengths and timings appear only as study conditions, as measured product content, or as the sources describe them. Funding as printed: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (Monte); RTI International internal funds and a NIDA grant (Barrus). No cannabis-industry funding is printed for Monte or Barrus. The Discussion's causal wording ('lead to') and the 33-fold ratio are the authors' reading; the claim does not adopt them.

statement: A laboratory test of products, read with its July 2015 correction (whose wording is followed where the saved letter differs), measured 75 labelled edible products of 47 brands (baked goods, drinks, candy or chocolate) bought in August to October 2014 at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, in markets the authors call unregulated. Against the THC printed on the package, 13 (17%) were within 10%, 17 (23%) held more than the label said (on average 28% more, at most 55% more) and 45 (60%) held less (on average about half the labelled amount: 47% less in the table's overall row, about 53% less from its city rows, editors' arithmetic; at most 99% less, some with almost none). Products holding more than their label were commonest in Los Angeles (9 of 20) and products holding less in Seattle (18 of 23, where 1 product was within 10%); San Francisco had 8 of 32 within 10% (χ² = 12.94, P = .01). Only 13 products printed a CBD content, and none held it within 10% (4 more, 9 less; editors' arithmetic), although 44 of the 75 contained some CBD. Whole packages were mixed before testing, so the test cannot say how evenly THC was spread between pieces or servings (two samples of the same mixed package differed by more than 10% in 37 products, which were then analysed whole), and it measured no effects in people: the authors' statements that products with less THC may not give the intended medical benefit and that products with more put patients at risk of adverse effects are their inference. The sample was not random and may not generalize, as the authors say, and the cost of the testing was covered by Werc Shop Laboratories, with which four of the six authors are affiliated (see funding). Funding as printed: the label test, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, except the cost of the laboratory testing, which Werc Shop Laboratories covered (four of the six authors are affiliated with Werc Shop Laboratory; the paper says neither funder had any role in the design, conduct, analysis or reporting, while its list of contributions credits two of those four with the concept, design and supervision of the study; one author reported personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings) and travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access; the paper does not say what these organisations do).
plain: A laboratory test of 75 edibles bought in three US cities in 2014 found that only about 1 in 6 held the amount of THC printed on the label: about 1 in 4 held more, and about 3 in 5 held less, some almost none.
population: 75 labelled edible products (products, not people) bought at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, August to October 2014.
exposure: the THC and CBD measured in each whole package by laboratory chromatography.
comparator: the THC or CBD content printed on the package, within 10% counted as accurate.
outcome: measured content within 10% of the label, more than 10% above it, or more than 10% below it.
magnitude: Label test (Vandrey 2015, as corrected in JAMA 2015;314(2):188; products, not people): 75 labelled edibles of 47 brands (22 baked goods, 13 beverages, 40 candy or chocolate; editors' sums), nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in three cities, August to October 2014; measured THC against the label: within 10%, 13 (17%; Wilson 95% CI 10.4 to 27.4, editors' calculation); more than 10% above, 17 (23%; 14.7 to 33.3); more than 10% below, 45 (60%; 48.7 to 70.3); outside 10%, 62 (82.7%; 72.6 to 89.6). Mean deviation (SD): within, -3% (4); above, +28% (13), largest +55%; below, -47% (29) in the overall row, against -52.5% from the city rows (-44%, -55% and -61% for 20, 7 and 18 products; editors' arithmetic), largest -99%. By city, within / above / below: San Francisco 8 / 4 / 20 of 32; Los Angeles 4 / 9 / 7 of 20; Seattle 1 / 4 / 18 of 23 (χ² = 12.94, P = .01; degrees of freedom not printed; 3 of 9 expected counts below 5, editors' calculation). By type, within / above / below: baked goods 2 / 7 / 13; beverages 3 / 2 / 8; candy or chocolate 8 / 8 / 24. CBD detected in 44 (59%); printed on 13, of which 4 above and 9 below the label (none within 10%, editors' arithmetic); median THC:CBD 36:1. Measured THC per package (measured product content): median 54 mg, range under 1 to 1,236 mg; labelled 2 to 1,000 mg. Duplicate samples differed by more than 10% in 37 of 75.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' checklist for a laboratory analysis of products: some concerns overall (non-random sample of products; laboratory method not validated in the letter; two sentences with labels reversed, corrected in July 2015). Not serious enough to downgrade on its own for a measurement of product content.

inconsistency.note: One data set; the 2016 overview's second-hand figure (83% more than 10% from the label) and a newspaper investigation it cites point the same way, but neither is an independent measurement read here.

indirectness.note: 75 products from nine medical dispensaries in three US cities in 2014, in markets the authors call unregulated; it does not describe products sold elsewhere or later, under other rules, or what people actually took.

imprecision.note: 75 products (17% within 10%; 95% CI 10.4 to 27.4, editors' calculation), 20 to 32 per city.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one data set.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). One laboratory test of 75 products: indirectness -1 (three US cities, medical dispensaries, 2014, unregulated markets) and imprecision -1 (75 products, wide interval), so the certainty is very low. Worded as 'describes' because it measures product content, not effects in people; the authors' statements about benefit and risk are their inference.
