statement: In one Colorado field study of 121 adults who already used cannabis at least four times a month (55 using flower, 66 using concentrates; each person chose the form, and a labelled strength was assigned at random within each form), blood THC measured about 13 minutes after they used their own product in their own way at home was higher in the concentrate group than in the flower group (mean 0.32 against 0.14 µg/mL), and so was the active by-product 11-OH-THC, at every time point including before use. Even so, self-rated intoxication (form effect P = .11) and the marijuana effects scale (P = .18) did not differ by form, tension and vigor ratings were lower in the concentrate group, and inhibitory control scores were higher in the flower group at every time, including before use. Delayed verbal recall worsened after use in both groups (form effect P = .65), and eyes-closed balance worsened and was back at its pre-use level by one hour in both (form effect P = .85); the main text reports no effects of labelled strength within a form at its set threshold (P < .01), with the strength tests in a supplement that was not read. The authors offer three untested explanations for similar intoxication despite higher blood THC (greater tolerance in the concentrate group, receptor saturation, individual differences) and read the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within a form as suggesting that people adjust how much they take. The groups were not alike before the session: the concentrate group had used concentrates on 16.5 of the past 30 days against 3.5, had begun regular use at 17.7 years against 20.0 and had about twice the baseline THC metabolite, and it used about half as much product by weight at the session. There was no placebo or no-use session, so changes after use cannot be told apart from repeating the tests; follow-up was one hour; form was not randomised, so earlier differences between the groups may account for some findings; 12 of the 133 people assessed were left out because blood THC after use was very low (9 of 64 on flower, 3 of 69 on concentrates; editors' arithmetic from the group sizes); and people had to have used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction and to use no other drugs or daily tobacco, so the findings do not reach people who use cannabis rarely, are new to it, or do not use it. Tobacco mixed into joints was not recorded and cannabinoids other than THC were not reported. The authors' Conclusions voice concern about long-term effects, which were not measured, and the Abstract and Results print the spread of blood THC as standard errors although the Discussion gives standard deviations. A scoping review done for the State of Colorado searched seven databases to mid-2022 and mapped 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product (225 observational studies, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series; earliest 1971, 60% published 2017 to 2022). Only 54 (12%) examined concentrates and a health outcome directly and 189 (42%) examined THC concentration directly; 63% studied generic cannabis types, and products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, resins) were examined in about 2% to 10% of studies. The median strength studied was 12% THC where given as a percentage (15 mg where given in milligrams), well below the Colorado market strengths the authors cite from other sources for 2020 (flower averaging 19%, concentrates 68%), which they think likely reflects the restriction of research cannabis to a federal supply without concentrates. Only 47% of studies had a control group and 41% reported effect estimates, and most did not capture the elements of use needed to estimate exposure. The review extracted no study results and did not assess bias, so it shows what has been studied and not what was found; its Conclusions say the literature has serious limits in generalisability to the current market and that high-quality evidence bearing on whether to regulate THC concentration is scarce. Searches were English-only, designed to be sensitive rather than specific, and screened with AI assistance, so studies may be missing; the evidence map and the appendix were not read. Of the 452 studies, 25 (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author with a disclosed industry tie, while 24% reported no funding source and 32% no conflict statement. A systematic review of observational studies searched to January 2021 (Petrilli et al., 2022; 20 articles from 16 studies by the editors' count, none rated good quality, no meta-analysis because every study relied on what people said they used and definitions of strength differed) found stronger cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more) associated with psychosis in two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair: against never-use, first-episode psychosis was more likely with skunk-type use in a UK study (adjusted odds ratio 2.91, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) and with types of 10% THC or more across six countries (1.6, 1.2 to 2.2; 4.8 with daily use), but not with hash-type or lower-strength use (0.83; 1.1), and relapse after a first episode was more likely with continued daily use of stronger cannabis (3.28, 1.22 to 9.18, against former use); none of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form. Findings for anxiety and depression varied. The studies of concentrates themselves were all cross-sectional and rated poor: in a 20-country online survey of 181,870 people, those who used butane hash oil more often reported a past diagnosis of anxiety (odds ratio 1.80, 1.60 to 2.01) or depression (1.34, 1.21 to 1.48) than those who used lower-strength herbal cannabis, but not of psychosis (1.11, 0.85 to 1.46); a US sample of 156 found no clear association of concentrate use with psychosis, anxiety or depression symptoms, and another of 191 no difference in anxiety or depression between people who frequently used concentrates and people who frequently used herbal cannabis; in a within-person survey of 574 people, mostly using infrequently, psychosis-like experiences were slightly less frequent with concentrates than with herbal cannabis (Cohen's d 0.12); and among 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin forms went with less residual or late-onset psychosis than dry herbal cannabis (odds ratio 0.21, 0.06 to 0.74). The review's findings on strength and cannabis use disorder are set out in a separate claim. Its authors argue that people taking less of stronger products would weaken rather than inflate these associations, and that people with poorer mental health may choose stronger products. No study read here follows people who use concentrates beyond one hour, compares them with people who do not use cannabis, or reports lung or other long-term physical outcomes for concentrates. Funding as printed: the field study, the US National Institutes of Health and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, with the paper stating that the funders had no role in the study; participants bought their products at one local dispensary that set aside allotments for the study, with no payment declared; the review, the State of Colorado under House Bill 21-1317 (funder not involved), with authors' interests as printed (a paid consultancy for Health Canada on conflict of interest, a paid UpToDate chapter, research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research and a seat on the state health department's marijuana advisory committee); the systematic review, an Economic and Social Research Council doctoral studentship, Cancer Research UK fellowship and project awards and a Wellcome Trust grant (funder without a role), with one author reporting previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and a scientific consulting company doing unrelated work, and its senior author an author of several of the studies it reviews, including the butane hash oil survey. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed for any of the three papers.
plain: In one Colorado study, 121 adults who already used cannabis regularly used their own flower or their own concentrate (a strong extract of cannabis, such as wax or shatter) at home while researchers took blood and ran memory and balance tests. People who used concentrates had more THC in their blood than people who used flower, but they did not rate themselves as more intoxicated, and the memory and balance tests changed in similar ways in both groups. The two groups were not alike to begin with (the concentrate group already used concentrates much more often), nobody had a dummy dose, and people were followed for only an hour, so the study cannot show that concentrates are more or less impairing than flower, or what happens with longer use, and it did not include people who do not use cannabis. A separate review for the state of Colorado found 452 studies that report THC strength, but only 54 looked at concentrates and a health outcome directly; its authors say the strengths studied are well below those now sold, and the review did not check how good the studies were or report what they found. A third paper, a review of studies that asked people which cannabis they used, found that stronger cannabis, such as skunk, was linked to psychosis in studies that compared people with and without psychosis. The studies of concentrates themselves asked people only once, were rated poor, and did not agree: in one large online survey, people who used butane hash oil more often said they had been diagnosed with anxiety or depression than people who used lower-strength herbal cannabis, while two small US studies found no clear link with mental-health symptoms.
population: 121 adults in Colorado (mean age about 28; 42% to 48% women) who used cannabis at least four times a month, had used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction, and used no other non-prescription drugs or daily tobacco (Bidwell 2020); and 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product, 1971 to 2022 (Bero 2023, scoping review); and 16 observational studies in 20 articles of people who use cannabis, people with psychosis and population controls, and people using medical cannabis, in Europe, the Americas and Japan and in online surveys across 20 and 175 countries (Petrilli 2022, systematic review).
exposure: Concentrates (laboratory-tested, labelled 70% or 90% THC, assigned at random within the form; the form itself self-chosen), used in the person's usual way at home (glass rig or tube 92%, hash pen 8%) in one session after 5 days of free use (study conditions only); in the review, studies of concentrates or other high-concentration products and of THC concentration; in the systematic review, self-reported use of concentrates (butane hash oil, concentrates, or liquid or resin forms) or of stronger herbal cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more), as each study defined them.
comparator: Flower (labelled 16% or 24% THC; pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%) in a separate group of regular consumers who chose flower; no placebo or no-use session, and no people who do not use cannabis. In the review, no comparison of outcomes (an inventory of studies). In the systematic review, lower-strength herbal cannabis, hash-type cannabis or never-use, as each study defined them; the concentrate studies compared people who use cannabis in different forms, never with people who do not use cannabis.
outcome: Blood THC and 11-OH-THC, self-rated intoxication and marijuana-effects scale, mood (tension, vigor), delayed verbal recall, inhibitory control and working memory, and balance, before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use. In the review, counts of studies by exposure, outcome, design and reporting. In the systematic review, psychosis (first episode, relapse, symptoms, self-reported diagnosis), psychosis-like experiences, and anxiety and depression (diagnosis or symptoms); its cannabis use disorder findings are in a separate claim.
magnitude: Field study (Bidwell 2020), concentrate group (n = 66) against flower group (n = 55), means before use, about 13 minutes after use (mean 13.3, range 3 to 47) and 1 hour after use. Blood THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.01, 0.32, 0.03; flower 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; form effect F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01. 11-OH-THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.004, 0.011, 0.008; flower 0.001, 0.005, 0.004; form effect P < .001. Self-rated intoxication (scale range inconsistently described in the paper): concentrate 0.14, 2.35, 1.63; flower 0.08, 2.40, 1.93; form effect P = .11. Marijuana effects scale: form effect P = .18. Tension and vigor lower in the concentrate group (P < .01 and P < .001). Delayed verbal recall errors: concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; change after use P < .001; form effect P = .65; form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the set threshold). Eyes-closed sway: concentrate 0.64, 0.69, 0.64; flower 0.63, 0.73, 0.63; quadratic time P < .001; form effect P = .85. Inhibitory control higher in the flower group at every time (P < .001). Thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold of P < .01; no placebo. Baseline, concentrate against flower group: concentrate use on 16.5 vs 3.5 of the past 30 days; regular use begun at 17.7 vs 20.0 years; THC-COOH 0.087 vs 0.044 µg/mL; product used at the session 0.11 g vs 0.22 g (study measure only). Labelled strengths assigned at random within form: flower 16% or 24%, concentrate 70% or 90% THC; groups of 26 to 33 people. 133 assessed (64 flower, 69 concentrate); 12 left out for post-use blood THC below 0.02 µg/mL (9 flower, 3 concentrate). Scoping review (Bero 2023): 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full texts, 452 studies (225 observational, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports, 34 case series); 54 (12%) concentrates and an outcome directly, 189 (42%) THC concentration and an outcome directly, 114 (25%) and 62 (14%) indirectly; control group in 212 (47%); effect estimates in 184 (41%); generic cannabis types in 284 (63%); products typically high in concentration in about 2% to 10%; THC given as a percentage in 172 studies, median 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%), and in milligrams in 113, median 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26); market strengths cited by the authors from other sources for Colorado: flower averaging 14% (2014) to 19% (2020), concentrates 46% to 68%. Funding of the included studies: 25 (6%) cannabis industry, 58 (13%) author with an industry tie, 109 (24%) no funding source reported, 143 (32%) no conflict statement. Outcome domains most studied: mental health 40%, neurologic 30%, pain 29%, cardiometabolic 24%, gastrointestinal 22%, psychosocial 22%, sleep 21%. Systematic review (Petrilli 2022; 16 studies in 20 articles, none rated good): psychosis, adjusted odds ratios against never-use, skunk-type 2.91 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) and hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77) in the UK GAP study; types of 10% THC or more 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2) and under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) in the six-country EU-GEI study, daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6); relapse with continued daily use of stronger cannabis 3.28 (1.22 to 9.18) against former use (58% against 24% relapsed). risk_of_bias.note: Field study (Bidwell 2020): ROBINS-E overall high; confounding and selection each high (self-chosen form, groups differing in concentrate days, years of regular use and baseline THC metabolite; volunteers who had used the strongest product before; 12 people left out by their post-use blood THC), no placebo, thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold, near-threshold results described inconsistently. Scoping review (Bero 2023): AMSTAR 2 critically low (provisional), mainly because it does not assess bias in the studies it maps; it extracts no results. Systematic review (Petrilli 2022): AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional; the list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read); none of its 16 studies was rated good, and its concentrate studies are cross-sectional and rated poor.

inconsistency.note: One field study for the acute comparison; the scoping review reports no results to compare with it. For mental-health outcomes, the concentrate studies in the systematic review disagree with one another (more self-reported anxiety and depression diagnoses with butane hash oil in one survey, no clear association in two small US samples, slightly fewer psychosis-like experiences in a within-person survey, less chronic psychosis in a small clinical sample); they qualify the claim and do not change the rating of its acute finding.

indirectness.note: Regular consumers who had used the strongest assigned product before without a bad reaction, one dispensary in one state, one session of free use, blood measured about 13 minutes and 1 hour after use; impairment inferred from change in the same people without a placebo; the review's counts concern studies, not health effects.

imprecision.note: 121 people, 26 to 33 in each strength group; the reported null form effects (intoxication, recall, balance) come from a study not designed to show equivalence and give no confidence intervals; results at P = .02 and P = .05 are unresolved.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one field study.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The field study randomised labelled strength within each form but not the form, so the concentrate-against-flower comparison that this claim reports is observational. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high (self-chosen form with baseline differences in concentrate use, years of regular use and THC metabolite; selected volunteers; no placebo or no-use session; exclusion of 12 people by an outcome; thirteen outcomes at a fixed threshold). The scoping review adds counts of what has been studied and no results, and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (provisional: the appendix was not read) chiefly because it does not appraise the studies it maps. Indirectness -1: regular consumers, one dispensary, one session, blood at about 13 minutes and 1 hour, impairment inferred without a placebo. Imprecision -1: 121 people, 26 to 33 per strength group, no confidence intervals, null form effects from a study not built to show equivalence, results at P = .02 and P = .05 unresolved. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one field study. Worded as 'is associated with' because each person chose the form and the groups differed at baseline; the statement of what the scoping review found is a statement about the literature, not about health effects. The systematic review added in version 0.3.0 (Petrilli 2022; AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional) qualifies the claim without changing its rating: the psychosis associations it reports for stronger cannabis come from case-control and cohort studies that did not look at concentrates as a separate form, and its studies of concentrates and mental health are cross-sectional, rated poor and inconsistent with one another.

statement: In people who use cannabis, using cannabis of higher strength, as each study defined it (stronger herbal types such as skunk or sinsemilla, types of 10% THC or more, hash in one survey, liquid or resin forms in one clinical sample, or concentrates), compared with lower-strength cannabis, is associated with more signs of cannabis use disorder in four of the six studies found by a systematic review searched to January 2021 (Petrilli et al., 2022), all of them cross-sectional, one rated fair and five poor. In a UK annual drug survey of 2,514 people, each extra day a month of using skunk went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.25 points higher (scale 0 to 15, 3 or more taken to indicate dependence; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.36), with no association for grass or resin (adjusted for age and gender); in a survey of 55,240 people from 175 countries, the groups using sinsemilla or hashish alongside herbal cannabis scored 0.16 and 0.26 points higher than the group using herbal cannabis only (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added); in a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24, people who used stronger cannabis were more likely to report recent cannabis problems on a screening test (adjusted odds ratio 4.08, 95% CI 1.41 to 11.81, adjusted for frequency of use, age at first use, sex and childhood socio-economic position); and among 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, people who used liquid or resin forms more often had a dependence syndrome than people who used dry herbal cannabis (odds ratio 6.85, 95% CI 1.87 to 25.15 in the table, 1.19 to 25.15 in the text; no adjustment listed). The two studies that compared concentrates with herbal cannabis found no clear difference: in 156 US adults, neither concentrate nor stronger herbal use was associated with use-disorder symptoms (the interval printed for concentrates does not contain its own estimate), and in 191 US adults, people who frequently used concentrates did not report significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3, with few symptoms overall). Every study relied on what people said they used; none measured THC in their cannabis or how much they took in, only one adjusted for the amount used, and no study followed people over time or compared them with people who do not use cannabis. The review's Discussion says higher-strength use was "consistently associated with an increased risk of CUD", which is stronger than these results. Its senior author is an author of three of the four studies that found an association (the two surveys and the UK sample, which another review author led); the Japanese study and the two studies that found no clear difference are by other groups. A later narrative review (Inman & Cservenka, online 2024; 27 articles found through PubMed and citation searches, not appraised) says that studies have consistently linked concentrate use with a higher cannabis use disorder risk than other forms, citing mainly the survey of 191 people as showing more symptoms, together with US college and web surveys that compare people by how often they use concentrates; it does not cite the systematic review. It finds little information on cannabis use disorder with edibles and argues only by analogy with slower-acting forms of other drugs, and concludes that how often people use cannabis remains the most reliable predictor across all forms and that a causal role of strength is not established. As a base rate, a meta-analysis of 21 general-population studies from high-income countries (Leung et al., 2020; studies published 2009 to 2020, over half from the US, mostly DSM-IV) puts the share of people who had used cannabis who met criteria for cannabis use disorder at 22 in 100 (95% CI 18 to 26) and for dependence at 13 in 100 (10 to 15), pooling lifetime, past-year and past-month measures, with single studies ranging from 4.5 in 100 (US adults aged 50 or more) to 41 in 100 (21-year-olds in one Australian cohort); dependence was 33 in 100 (22 to 44) in two cohorts of young people who used weekly or daily, against 18 in 100 (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use. That review found no population study that estimated the risk by the strength of the cannabis used, and it did not appraise the studies it pooled. Funding as printed: the systematic review, an Economic and Social Research Council doctoral studentship, Cancer Research UK fellowship and project awards and a Wellcome Trust grant (funder without a role), with one author reporting previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and a consulting company doing unrelated work; the narrative review, no funding and no conflicts; the meta-analysis, University of Queensland and NHMRC fellowships and Australian Government Drug and Alcohol Program funding of the authors' centre, with no conflicts. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Some studies asked people which kind of cannabis they mostly used and checked for signs of cannabis use disorder, when cannabis use gets hard to control and causes problems. In four of six such studies, people who used cannabis with more THC, such as skunk, had more signs of the disorder; the two studies that compared concentrates (strong extracts such as wax or shatter) with plant cannabis found no clear difference. All six asked people only once, relied on what they said they used and did not measure THC, so they cannot show that stronger cannabis causes the disorder. A later review says concentrates are linked to more problems, but it leans mostly on one of those two studies; it says little is known yet about edibles, and that how often people use cannabis is the most reliable sign of risk. For comparison, large surveys in richer countries found that about 22 in 100 people who had used cannabis had a cannabis use disorder, and about 13 in 100 were dependent; none of those surveys looked at how strong the cannabis was.
population: People who use cannabis: respondents to drug surveys (a UK annual survey, n = 2,514; a survey across 175 countries, n = 55,240), a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24, US convenience samples of 156 and 191 adults, and 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (Petrilli 2022, six cross-sectional studies); US surveys of college students, high-school students, adults and web samples (Inman 2026, narrative review); and, for the base rate, people who had ever, recently or regularly used cannabis in 21 general-population studies from the US, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, the Netherlands, Ireland and France (Leung 2020).
exposure: Self-reported use of higher-strength cannabis as each study defined it: skunk, sinsemilla or other stronger herbal types; types typically of 10% THC or more; hash classed with stronger types in one survey; liquid or resin forms in one clinical sample; concentrates (including butane hash oil) in the two US samples and the narrative review, which also compares flower and edibles as forms. Strength bands are study definitions only. For the base rate, any cannabis use (ever, past year or month, or weekly or daily).
comparator: Lower-strength cannabis as each study defined it (grass, resin or herbal types; types typically under 10% THC; dry herbal cannabis); in the two concentrate studies, people who use herbal cannabis (frequently, in one). No study compared with people who do not use cannabis. For the base rate, none (a share of people who had used cannabis).
outcome: Signs of cannabis use disorder: Severity of Dependence Scale scores (0 to 15; 3 or more taken to indicate dependence), recent problems on the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test, a MINI cannabis screening test, a self-report symptom questionnaire, or ICD-10 dependence syndrome by clinical interview; for the base rate, DSM-III-R, DSM-IV (abuse or dependence) or DSM-5 cannabis use disorder from structured interviews.
magnitude: Systematic review (Petrilli 2022), six cross-sectional studies, higher against lower strength: Severity of Dependence Scale b 0.254 (95% CI 0.161 to 0.357) per extra day a month of skunk use, grass 0.020 (-0.029 to 0.070), resin 0.025 (-0.019 to 0.067) (UK survey, 2,514; poor); b 0.155 (0.100 to 0.209) for sinsemilla with herbal and 0.262 (0.188 to 0.337) for hashish with herbal against herbal only (175-country survey, 55,240; poor); recent problems, adjusted odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81) (UK sample, 1,087; fair); dependence syndrome, odds ratio 6.85 (1.87 to 25.15 in Table 2; 1.19 to 25.15 in the text) for liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis (71 Japanese patients; poor); no association in 156 US adults (stronger herbal r 0.09, -0.12 to 0.30; concentrates -0.05, interval printed as -0.35 to -0.26; poor); no significant difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use in 191 US adults (mean symptoms 2.1 against 1.3; poor). Narrative review (Inman 2026): no effect sizes. Base rate (Leung 2020; 21 studies, 153 data points, high-income countries): cannabis use disorder 22 in 100 (18 to 26), abuse 13 in 100 (8 to 18), dependence 13 in 100 (10 to 15) among people who had used cannabis; use disorder by design and recall period, 17 in 100 (12 to 23) to 28 in 100 (10 to 48); dependence with weekly or daily use 33 in 100 (22 to 44) in two cohorts of young people and 18 in 100 (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies; single studies from 4.5 in 100 (use disorder, US adults aged 50 or more) to 41.1 in 100 (lifetime use disorder, Australian 21-year-olds). No estimate by strength or form exists in these sources.

risk_of_bias.note: Petrilli 2022 (AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional) rates five of the six cannabis use disorder studies poor and one fair: self-reported product type as the exposure, cross-sectional designs, self-selected online or convenience samples and a clinical sample, confounder adjustment ranging from none to frequency and amount, and no measure of THC intake. Inman 2026 is a narrative review rated high risk on the editors' checklist. Leung 2020 (AMSTAR 2 critically low, provisional) did not appraise the surveys it pooled.

inconsistency.note: Four studies find more signs of the disorder with higher strength and two find no clear difference; the two null studies are the only direct comparisons of concentrates with herbal cannabis, and the two reviews describe one of them differently (no significant difference against more symptoms). The direction is otherwise consistent.

indirectness.note: Strength is inferred from self-reported product type, not measured THC or THC intake; four of the six outcomes are screening or severity scales rather than diagnoses; the samples are online, convenience or clinical; and the base rate comes from general-population surveys in high-income countries that did not measure strength or form.

imprecision.note: The two large surveys give narrow intervals; the smaller studies' wide intervals (1.41 to 11.81; 1.87 to 25.15) are reported. Not downgraded further: the certainty is already at its floor.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: no meta-analysis of strength and cannabis use disorder, and the systematic review did not examine it.

dose_response.note: The per-day gradient in one survey concerns how often stronger cannabis is used, not strength itself, and comes from a poor-quality cross-sectional study.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias -1: cross-sectional studies with self-reported exposure, five of six rated poor, adjustment ranging from none to frequency and amount, and a narrative review and a pooled prevalence without appraisal. Inconsistency -1: two of six studies, the only direct comparisons of concentrates with herbal cannabis, find no clear difference, and the two reviews disagree on one of them. Indirectness -1: product type as a proxy for THC, screening scales for four of six outcomes, selected samples, and a base rate not split by strength. These downgrades pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for imprecision or publication bias, and no upgrade (the one gradient mixes strength with frequency of use). Overlapping evidence: three of the four studies that found an association share an author with the review and two of them are described as annual drug surveys, so they are not fully independent replications. Worded 'is associated with' because no study can show direction. The base rate (Leung 2020) is given as a description of the populations sampled; as a description it rests on unappraised surveys pooled across recall periods and DSM versions and would itself be rated low at best.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice; strengths and THC bands appear only as study definitions. Split from cl_can_concentrates as the batch 10 brief allows: dependence by strength and form is a different outcome and body of evidence from that claim's acute comparison of concentrates with flower. Rests on one systematic review without meta-analysis (Petrilli 2022: AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional, appendix not read), one narrative review (Inman 2026: editors' checklist high) and one meta-analysis of prevalence used as the base rate (Leung 2020: AMSTAR 2 critically low, provisional; read from the journal pre-proof, supplements S1 to S6 not read). The two reviews describe Bidwell et al. 2018 (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004) differently; reading it would settle that. Three of the four studies that found an association share an author with Petrilli 2022: a reason to read closely, not to discount. The Leung anchors could later move to a section 8 base-rate claim on cannabis use disorder (editor's choice).

statement: In dried cannabis flower that licensed growers sent for state compliance testing to six commercial laboratories in six US states (Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington; December 2013 to January 2021; 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results), the Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category that one consumer cannabis website's strain database links to each strain name, matched by name to the growers' own sample names (so the category is the website's, not necessarily what each package said; 73.4% of samples could be given one), was barely related to the samples' terpene profiles, the mix of the compounds the authors describe as responsible for cannabis's smell (Smith et al., 2022). THC and CBD content were not compared between the categories, and no effects on people were measured. In the 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results, a score of how much more samples resemble others with the same label than samples with the nearest other label (the silhouette score, from −1 to 1) averaged −0.03 for the categories, with most samples below zero, against 0.27 when samples were grouped by their most abundant terpene and 0.38 for three groups found by a clustering method in the same terpene data, which the authors expected to separate better; the category analysis also counted 12,322 samples (29.9%) that had no category as a group of their own. Strain names carried more information: for 26 of the 41 names attached to at least five growers with at least five samples each, products sold under the same name by different growers were more alike in terpene profile than names shuffled at random, 13 did not differ from chance and 2 (LSD and Durban Poison) were less alike than chance (editors' count of the significance marks in the paper's figure); even randomly paired products were fairly similar, at about 0.69 on a 0-to-1 similarity scale (read from the figure). Among 12,063 THC-dominant products with a category, Sativa products made up 30.9% of the terpinolene-rich group against 15.0% overall, yet that group was still mostly Hybrid (55.8%), and the test the paper reports for this appears to have been computed on percentages rather than counts (editors' calculation). The six laboratories' methods were not standardized, which the authors say prevents them from separating laboratory from regional differences, and the corresponding author is employed by the website that supplied the categories and strain names. In a small Dutch study, two cultivars that a seed company's website describes as Sativa-dominant (Amnesia) and Indica-dominant (White Widow), bought at ten coffee shops in four cities on two visits about two months apart (35 samples), differed in terpenes and minor cannabinoids but had similar THC (about 17% and 16% of the weight); many compounds varied by more than 25% between purchases of the same name, 3 samples had the chemistry of the other cultivar and were left out as presumed mix-ups, and of three pharmacy varieties one, bred from a variety with a large share of Sativa genes, resembled the Indica-dominant cultivar (Hazekamp & Fischedick, 2012; no statistical tests of these differences; the first author worked for the grower of the pharmacy varieties). Neither study measured how the products felt, so neither can say whether the labels predict effects. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do indica and sativa labels tell you what's in your weed? Mostly not. In lab tests of 41,201 THC-rich flower samples from six US states, samples that a strain website calls indica, hybrid or sativa were mixed together in their terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell: on average, a sample was about as close to another label's samples as to its own. Strain names did somewhat better: for 26 of 41 names sold by at least five growers, products from different growers were more alike than chance, but for 13 they were not, and 2 names were less alike than chance. Sativa labels were twice as common among terpinolene-rich products, though even there most were labelled hybrid. The study compared only these smell compounds, not THC or CBD, used the website's labels rather than the packages, and measured no effects on people. A small Dutch study found that two coffee-shop strains, one described as sativa-type and one as indica-type, differed in terpenes but had similar THC, and varied a lot from purchase to purchase.
population: Dried female cannabis flower submitted by licensed growers (3,319 producers) for state compliance testing at six commercial laboratories in Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington, December 2013 to January 2021: 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results, 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results in the label analysis, and 13,401 THC-dominant products (one producer's samples under one name, averaged), 12,063 of them with a category; 41 strain names in the name analysis. Also 35 samples of two cultivars bought at ten Dutch coffee shops in four cities (purchase dates not given; paper received November 2011) and three Dutch pharmacy varieties
exposure: The Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category and the popular strain name that a consumer cannabis website's strain database attaches to each name, matched to growers' sample names by string matching and an expert dictionary of name variants (not read from packages); in the Dutch study, the name under which a sample was bought and each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background as given by a seed company's website
comparator: Samples with other categories or names; groupings built from the same terpene data (each sample's most abundant terpene; three clusters found by k-means); names shuffled at random across growers (200 repetitions); in the Dutch study, the other cultivar and three pharmacy varieties grown under controlled conditions
outcome: How closely samples sharing a label resembled each other in terpene profile (silhouette score; cosine similarity between growers' products against shuffled names; share of a name's products in its most common terpene cluster; category shares by cluster); in the Dutch study, separation of the two cultivars in a principal component analysis of 28 compounds, THC content and variation between purchases. No effects on people were measured

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated down separately: the category result rests on 41,201 samples and is visible in the raw scatter (Fig 6A). Unstandardized methods across six laboratories and repeat submissions by the same producer add noise and dependence, and the cluster χ² and some effect sizes are unreliable (card sc_smith_2022, JBI moderate), but these weaken the secondary associations, which the statement words with their limits. The Dutch study is at high risk of bias (small unsystematic sample, post hoc exclusions, no tests, a conflict of interest; card sc_hazekamp_2012) and only qualifies the claim.

inconsistency.note: The Dutch study points the same way on variation within names, and on THC not telling its two cultivars apart; with two cultivars it cannot test the categories in general.

indirectness.note: Rated down one level: the categories tested are those a consumer website's database attaches to strain names, matched by name, not the labels printed on packages or given at sale; only terpenes were compared, not THC or CBD; the products are compliance-tested flower from six US states in 2013–2021; and nothing about effects was measured, although effects are what people usually mean by the labels.

imprecision.note: A very large sample for the category result; no intervals are printed, but the score sits near zero by a wide margin. The name results rest on 41 names and are given as counts.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one analysis of laboratory records; the cleaned data and code are stated to be public.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claim: never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: Descriptive analysis of product records (cross-sectional): starts low; indirectness −1 (website categories matched by name, terpenes only, US compliance-tested flower in 2013–2021, no effects), which gives very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. 'Describes' because the claim reports how labels and chemistry line up in products, not an effect on people. The central finding, that the categories barely separate terpene profiles, is firmer than the secondary ones: the strain-name counts are the editors' count of figure marks (the paper gives one summary test, and the recount agrees with the first reader's), and the Sativa-terpinolene association rests on a test that appears to use percentages. The claim does not adopt the authors' conclusions about effects and marketing, which go beyond the chemistry measured, nor the Dutch study's estimate that 20% of coffee-shop visits gave an unreliable product, which counts presumed mix-ups the authors concede may be genuine. Status single study: the Dutch study tested two cultivars and qualifies the claim; the earlier label studies the US paper describes were not read.
